Pre-requisite: Knowledge of vector algebra, functions, limits, differentiation and integration of
functions.
Course Objective:
This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus. This
course will help the students achieve sound understanding of the concepts of calculus, develop
problem solving skills and apply the concepts and techniques of calculus to solve problems within
Engineering domain. This course will equip the students with intermediate to advanced level
concepts and aligned tools to help them tackle advanced mathematics and related applications.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the fundamental concepts of differential calculus for functions of one variable,
including limits, derivatives, Mean Value Theorems, Taylor and Maclaurin series, and
LHospital’s rule. (K2)
2. Solve problems involving functions of several variables using partial differentiation, Taylor
series expansion, and techniques for finding maxima and minima, including Lagrange’s
method of undetermined multipliers. (K3)
3. Use Beta and Gamma functions to solve problems in single-variable calculus. (K2)
4. Compute and interpret double and triple integrals, including change of variables and
coordinate transformations, and apply them to determine areas and volumes. (K3)
5. Examine vector functions using gradient, divergence, curl, and scalar potential and apply
fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to
evaluate integrals. (K3)
6. Integrate concepts from differential, integral, and vector calculus to formulate and solve real-
world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences. (K3)
Detailed Syllabus

1.   Differential Calculus of functions of one variable

Course Objectives:
The knowledge of Physics relevant to engineering is critical for converting ideas into technology.
An understanding of Physics also helps engineers understand the working and the limitations of
existing devices and techniques, eventually leading to innovations and improvements. This
course aims to help students understand the basic concepts of physics thoroughly and lay the
foundations for the various engineering courses.

principles of semiconductor devices. (K2)

diffraction grating applications. (K3)

real-world communication and engineering problems. (K3)

recognize their applications in basic engineering problems related to electromagnetism.
(K2)
5. Explore the properties and applications of modern engineering materials like
nanomaterials, superconductors, and dielectrics. (K3)
6. Gauge theoretical principles through laboratory experimentation, enhancing problem-

Pre-requisite: Fundamental knowledge of physics, chemistry, and mathematics.
Course Objective:
To introduce students to modern biology with an emphasis on the evolution of biology as a multi-
disciplinary field, to make them aware of the application of engineering principles in biology. This
will encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems with engineering
tools. They will also be exposed to the application of engineering principles in biology and
engineering robust solutions inspired by biological examples.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Identify the principles of biomimicry and explain their applications in engineering and
sustainable design, demonstrating an understanding of biologically inspired solutions. (K1)
2. Classify the fundamental building blocks of life (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic
acids) and describe their structural and functional roles in cellular processes and metabolism.
(K2)
3. Explain the molecular basis of genetic information transfer, including DNA replication,
transcription, and translation, and interpret Mendel's laws and their significance in genetics. (K2)
4. Describe the mechanisms of enzyme action, enzyme-substrate interactions, and enzyme
inhibition, and discuss their industrial and biological applications. (K2)
5. Explain the principles of metabolism and energy transactions, and categorize microorganisms
based on their characteristics, growth kinetics, and applications in biotechnology and drug
discovery. (K1)

processes, and ecosystems. Sustainable engineering.

Unity in diversity of life, Molecules of life. Structure and functions of   04

Course Objective:
The course would enable students to get a brief introduction of the Indian Constitution and its
principles. The students would have knowledge of concept of ‘State’ and interdependencies of
its institutions vis a vis their relation with fundamental rights.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Recall the historical evolution of India’s democratic values, emphasizing the foundational
principles of justice, equality, and liberty as enshrined in the Preamble of the Constitution.
(K1)
2. Understand the fundamental rights enshrined in the Constitution, their permissible
restrictions, and how these rights are balanced with duties, to grasp their application
within societal and professional frameworks. (K2)

maintaining the basic structure of the Constitution in real-world professional contexts. (K3)

Course Objective
The main objective of this course is to equip the students with the ability to solve, assemble and
test simple AC and DC electrical circuits. Further, the course also enables the student to obtain
a basic understanding of the working principle and applications of electronics
devices.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain the fundamental concepts of DC circuits, including Kirchhoff’s laws and network
theorems, (Understand- Level 2)
2. Interpret the principles of AC circuit analysis, including resonance and three-phase systems,
(Understand- Level 2)
3. Illustrate the working principles of transformers and different types of electrical machines,
(Understand- Level 2)
4. Explain the basic operation of analog electronic components, including rectifiers, transistors
and operational amplifiers. (Understand- Level 2)
5. Make use of logic gates and Boolean expressions for digital circuits.

phase quantities.
3   Transformers and Electrical Machines   6

induction motors.

technology. An understanding of Physics also helps engineers understand the working and
the limitations of existing devices and techniques, which eventually leads to new
innovations and improvements. This course aims to make students understand the basic
concepts of Physics thoroughly with a view to lay foundations for the various engineering
courses.

with a scientific outlook,
2. Identify and apply different processes of physics that have wide applications in
industrial and technological sectors,

Pre-requisite: -
Course Objective
The course aims to introduce digital fabrication tools and methods. It familiarizes the students with
various principles of 3D printing along with solid modeling, part slicing and fabrication using
Fused deposition modelling (FDM) process.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe FDM Technology
2. Prepare given model for 3D printing
3. Create products of complex geometries using 3D printer
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Digital Manufacturing and Technical Design   02
Overview of 3D printing laboratory equipment, pre-fabricating requirements
– printer bed size, hardware and materials required.
2   3D Printing Process Steps   06
3D printing concepts for converting CAD model into real parts, process steps
involved in 3DP, creation of solid model, conversion to STL file, slicing the file
or select a STL model from online resources, machine set up, build.
3   3D Printing with Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM)   10
Operating principle and workflow of a Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) 3D
Printing machine, effect of layer thickness, infill density, part orientation and
overhang angles on FDM printed parts, study of lithophane.
4   Project Involving Ideation, Design and 3D Printing   12
Briefing of idea, designing of product, solid model creation, final fabrication
using 3D printer.
Total   30
Text Books
1.   Noorani, Rafiq, 3D Printing: Technology, Applications, and Selection, 1st edition, CRC Press, 2017.
2. Filemon Schöffer, Ben Redwood, Brian Garret, The 3D Printing Handbook: Technologies, design
and applications, 3D Hubs, 2017
Reference Books
1. Chua, C. L., Lim, K., Rapid Prototyping: Principles and Applications, 3rd Edition, World Scientific
Publishing Co. Pte. Ltd., 2010
A.Y. 2024-25
SVKM’s Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
Laboratory Work
6 to 8 laboratory exercises (and a mini project) based on the syllabus.
List of Experiments
1) To design an object using an open source software (Tinkercad).
2) To understand the working of slicing software (Repetier Host)
3) To examine the effect of layer thickness, infill density and orientation on build time and
material consumption.
4) To generate code for designed object using Repetier host software for 3D printing.
5) To study the components of a Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) 3D Printing machine.
6) To prepare FDM machine for printing the given object.
7) To print object using FDM machine.
8) To carry out post processing on the printed object.
9) To evaluate the effect of overhang angles on build quality of polylactic acid (PLA) and
Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) parts made using FDM.
10) To build parts of same geometry in PLA and ABS and compare the bending strength.
11) To create an object using lithophane technique.
12) Mini project.

Course Objective
The main objective of this course is to equip the students with the ability to solve, assemble
and test simple AC and DC electrical circuits. Further, the course also enables the student
to obtain a basic understanding of the working principle and applications of electronics
devices.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Interpret DC circuits, theorems and time domain analysis of first order RL circuit
2. Analyse series and parallel AC circuits and summarize star/delta configurations
3. Comprehend the principles of transformer and electrical machines
4. Review the construction, working principle and applications of electronics devices
and logic circuits
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1 DC Circuits
Electrical circuit elements (R, L and C), voltage and current sources,
Kirchhoff’s current law, Kirchhoff’s voltage laws, Analysis of simple
circuits with dc excitation, Superposition Theorem, Thevenin’s   6
Theorems, Norton’s Theorems. Time-domain analysis of first-order RL
circuits.
2 AC Circuits
Generation of alternating emf, instantaneous, rms, peak, average values
and related other terms, vector representation of AC quantities, Steady   8
state analysis of R, L, C series and parallel circuits, resonance. Generation
of three-phase emf, star connection, delta connection, relationship
between line and phase quantities.
3   Transformers and Electrical Machines
Construction and working of single-phase transformer Ideal and practical
transformer, equivalent circuit, Losses in transformers,
4   Generation of rotating magnetic fields, Construction and working of a   6
three-phase induction motor, Single-phase induction motor, construction
and working, DC motor construction, working and types.
5   Analog Electronics (no mathematical treatment and design)
Half and full wave rectifiers, special purpose diodes -zener regulator, BJT
and its applications, amplifier, oscillator, overview of opto-electronics
devices, opto-couplers, concepts of transducer, Operational amplifier   5
(IC-741), Inverting and Non-Inverting, Comparator, Timer (IC-555) and
multivibrators.
6   Digital Electronics
Logic gates, concept of universal logic; implementation of Boolean
5
expressions using logic gates, application of digital circuits: e.g., adder,
subtractor, multiplexer, de-multiplexer, Analog to Digital Converter,
Digital to Analog Converter.
Total   30

1. D. C. Kulshreshtha, Basic Electrical Engineering, 1st Edition, McGraw Hill
Education, 2017.
2. E. Hughes, Electrical and Electronics Technology, 10th Edition, Pearson Education,
2013.
3. Boylstad R.L., Nashelsky L., Electronic Devices and Circuit Theory, 12th Edition,
Pearson, 2012
4. M. Morris Mano, Digital Logic and Computer Design, 10th Edition, PHI, 2008.
Reference Books
1. V. D. Toro, Electrical Engineering Fundamentals, 2nd Edition, Pearson Education India,
PHI, 2015.
2. B. L. Theraja, Fundamentals of Electrical Engineering and Electronics, 24th Edition, S.
Chand & Co, 2012
3. Jacob Millman & Halkias, Electronic Devices & Circuits, 2nd Edition, Tata McGraw
Hill, 2013.

8 to 10 practical exercises (and a practicum) based on the syllabus.

Course Objective
The course would enable students to get a brief introduction of the Indian Constitution and its principles. The
students would have knowledge of concept of ‘State’ and interdependencies of its institutions vis a vis their
relation with fundamental rights.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to
1. understand the historic evolution of the Indian Constitution, its drafting, nature and to understand the
principles mentioned in its Preamble,
2. inculcate fundamental rights in its true sense and also the permissible restrictions upon it so as to enjoy
these rights within permissible limits while simultaneously performing their duties and to apply these
principles into their professional lives,
3. ingrain the structure of our polity and role of Judiciary in maintaining the basic structure of the
Constitution,
4. attain knowledge of the Emergency provisions, when and how it is imposed, to know the additional
powers the bestowed upon the Government at times of Emergency and to understand the Amendment
procedure.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Nature, Characteristics and Sources of Indian Constitution   2
2.   6
Fundamental rights and Fundamental duties – Concept of State, Right to
Equality under Articles 14 and 15, Right to certain freedoms under Article 19, Right
to Life and liberty under Article 21, Right to religion under Article 25 and 26, Right
to remedy under Article 32 and Fundamental duties

Judges, Independence of Judiciary, Jurisdictions of Supreme Court and High Courts
4.   4
Emergency Provisions – Concept of National Emergency under Article 352, Financial
Emergency under Article 360 and President rule under Article 356 of the Constitution
Total   15

Course Objective
This course examines the basic nature of reasoning and the fallacies which prevent good reasoning and decision
making. Both the theory and practice of critical thinking are covered. Emphasis will be on understanding the
logical structure of an argument and on recognizing the influence of bias and emotional persuasion on decision
making.
Course Outcomes

Course Objective

The principal objective of this course is to provide a basic understanding of biological mechanisms of living
organisms from the perspective of engineers. To encourage engineering students to think about solving
biological problems with engineering tools. To make them aware of the application of engineering principles
in biology and engineering robust solutions inspired by biological examples.

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the manifestations are diverse
2. identify and classify microorganisms while understanding molecular basis of DNA as a genetic
material for information transfer
3. classify enzymes and distinguish between different mechanisms of enzyme action

Detailed Syllabus

Unit Description Duration

1 Introduction 03

Convey that Biology is as important a scientific discipline as Mathematics, Physics
and Chemistry Bring out the fundamental differences between science and
engineering by drawing a comparison between eye and camera, Bird flying and
aircraft. Mention the most exciting aspect of biology as an independent scientific
discipline. Why we need to study biology? Discuss how biological observations of
18th Century that lead to major discoveries. Examples from -Brownian motion and
the origin of thermodynamics by referring to the original observation of Robert
Brown and Julius Mayor. These examples will highlight the fundamental
importance of observations in any scientific inquiry.

ecological be highlighted. Hierarchy of life | forms at

phenomenological level. A common thread weaves _ this hierarchy
Classification.Discuss classification based on (a) Cellularity-Unicellular or
multicellular (b) ultrastructure- prokaryotes or eucaryotes. (c) energy and Carbon
utilization -Autotrophs, heterotrophs, lithotropes (d) Ammonia excretion -
aminotelic, uricoteliec, ureotelic (e) Habitata- acquatic or terrestrial (e) Molecular
taxonomy- three major kingdoms of life. A given organism can come under
different category based on classification. Model organisms for the study of biology
come from different groups. E. coli, S.cerevisiae, D. Melanogaster, C. elegance, A.

Thaliana, M. musculus
06

3 Genetics

Convey that "Genetics is to biology what Newton's laws are to Physical Sciences"
Mendel's laws, Concept of segregation and independent assortment. Concept of
allele. Gene mapping, Gene interaction, Epistasis. Meiosis and Mitosis be taught as
a part of genetics. Emphasis to be give not to the mechanics of cell division nor the
phases but how genetic material passes from parent to offspring. Concepts of
recessiveness and dominance. Concept of mapping of phenotype to genes. Discuss
about the single gene disorders in humans. Discuss the concept of complementation
using human genetics.

06

4 Biomolecules
Convey that all forms of life has the same building blocks and yet the manifestations
are as diverse as one can imagine Molecules of life. In this context discuss
monomeric units and polymeric structures. Discuss about sugars, starch and 05
cellulose. Amino acids and proteins. Nucleotides and DNA/RNA. Two carbon

05

6 Information Transfer
The molecular basis of coding and decoding genetic information is universal
Molecular basis of information transfer. DNA as a genetic material. Hierarchy of
DNA structure- from single stranded to double helix to nucleosomes. Concept of 06

complementation and recombination.

7 Macromolecular analysis
How to analyses biological processes at the reductionistic level Proteins- structure
and function. Hierarch in protein structure. Primary secondary, tertiary and
quaternary structure. Proteins as enzymes, transporters, receptors and structural
elements.

05

8 Metabolism

The fundamental principles of energy transactions are the same in physical and
biological world. Thermodynamics as applied to biological systems. Exothermic
and endothermic versus endergonic and exergonic reactions. Concept of Keq and
its relation to standard free energy. Spontaneity. ATP as an energy currency. This
should include the breakdown of glucose to CO2 + H2O (Glycolysis and Krebs
cycle) and synthesis of glucose from CO2 and H2O (Photosynthesis). Energy

05

Concept of single celled organisms. Concept of species and strains. Identification
and classification of microorganisms. Microscopy. Ecological aspects of single

Pre-requisite: -
Course Objectives
This course is aimed at providing basic understanding of the fundamentals of Engineering
Graphics; mainly visualization, graphics theory, standards & conventions of drawing, the tools of
drawing and the use of drawings in engineering applications. The course has been structured to
include sufficient simulations which would aid the student in visualization of three-dimensional
objects and developing the drawing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Interpret and communicate drawings effectively using different types of curves, lines, planes
2. Analyze the concepts of projections and section of right regular solids with their
development
3. Apply the techniques, skills, and modern tools to create projections of machine components
with the help of software
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Engineering Drawing   04
Principles of engineering graphics and their significance, usage of drawing
instruments, lettering, numbering;
Conic sections (ellipse, parabola, hyperbola - general method only)
including the rectangular hyperbola; cycloid, epi-cycloid, hypo-cycloid and
involutes.
2.   Projections of Lines and Planes   05
Introduction to projections of points, conventions; points locating in all
quadrants.
Projections of Lines
Introduction, lines inclined to one plane and parallel to other plane, lines
inclined to both planes.
Projections of Planes
Introduction, types of planes, plane surface inclined to both reference planes,
projection of auxiliary planes
3.   Projections of Regular Solids   05
Introduction to projection of regular solids, types of solids; Projections of
regular solids (prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones) covering those inclined
to both the reference planes
4.   Section and Development of Regular Solids   04
Introduction to section and development of regular solids;
Section of regular prisms, pyramids, cylinders, cones;
Development of surfaces of right regular solids namely prisms, pyramids,
cylinders and cones.
5.   Orthographic Projections   04
Principles of orthographic projections, conventions used in quadrant
formation, conversion of isometric models to orthographic views and
viceversa, orthographic views of geometrical solids and objects from
industry.
6.   Sectional Orthographic Projections   04
Principles of sectional orthographic projection, need of sectional views,
types of sections, hatching of sectioned part and principles, sectional
orthographic views of geometrical solids and objects from industry.
7.   Isometric Projections   04
Principles of isometric projection-isometric scale, isometric views,
conventions; isometric views of lines, planes, simple and compound solids;
conversion of orthographic views to isometric models to and vice-versa;
isometrics projections of given views.
Total   30
Text Books
1. N. D. Bhatt, V. M. Panchal and P. R. Ingle, Engineering Drawing, 53rd Edition, Charotar
Publishing House, 2014.
Reference Books
1. M. B. Shah and B. C. Rana, Engineering Drawing, 2nd Edition, Pearson Education, 2014.
2. K. Venugopal and V. Prabhu Raja, Engineering Drawing + AutoCAD, 6th edition, New Age
International (P) Ltd. Publishers, 2011.
Laboratory Work
8 to 10 experiments based on the syllabus.

electromagnetism. The course also intends to focus on understanding the concept and working of the
transformer, measuring devices, and sensors. The course concludes with a case study discussion of IoT
applications.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1.   Explain DC network theorems and apply them to solve DC circuits
2.   Understand AC fundamentals and use them to solve AC circuits
3.   Understand the operating principle of the transformer
4.   Describe various measuring devices and sensors
5.   Understand the application of computer science and electrical engineering principles in real-time
application

1   Introduction to DC Circuit Fundamentals:
Definitions: Electrical Potential and Potential Difference, Current, Work, Power
and Energy, Active and Passive Elements and Circuits, Linear and Non-linear

Method for DC Network Analysis   07

Concept of Leading and Lagging AC Quantities

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of vector algebra, functions, limits, differentiation and integration of
functions.
Course Objective:
This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus. This
course will help the students achieve sound understanding of the concepts of calculus, develop
problem solving skills and apply the concepts and techniques of calculus to solve problems within
Engineering domain. This course will equip the students with intermediate to advanced level
concepts and aligned tools to help them tackle advanced mathematics and related applications.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Demonstrate the fundamental concepts of differential calculus for functions of one variable.
2. Solve problems involving functions of several variables using partial differentiation, Taylor
series expansion, and techniques for finding maxima and minima, including Lagrange’s method
of undetermined multipliers.
3. Use Beta and Gamma functions to solve problems in single-variable calculus.
4. Compute and interpret double and triple integrals, including change of variables and coordinate
transformations, and apply them to determine areas and volumes.
5. Examine vector functions using gradient, divergence, curl, and scalar potential and apply
fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to evaluate
integrals.
6. Integrate concepts from differential, integral, and vector calculus to formulate and solve real-
world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences.

Course Objective
This course aims to equip students with practical skills in electronics prototyping and provides hands-on
experience with essential tools, measuring instruments, PCB design, and fabrication techniques.
Additionally, students will gain knowledge in PC hardware assembly, Arduino-based circuit
programming, and aerial robotics, including drone assembly and flight basics.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Understand and demonstrate the use of essential hand tools, measuring instruments, and
prototyping equipment for circuit design and testing, (Understand - Level 2)
2. Design and fabricate single-sided PCBs by selecting appropriate circuit components, routing
layouts using open-source software, and assembling electronic circuits, (Create- Level 6)
3. Analyze and troubleshoot common electrical and electronic components used in industrial
applications, including wiring systems and protection devices, (Apply- Level 3)
4. Assemble, configure, and troubleshoot PC hardware by understanding the functionality of
components such as CPU, RAM, motherboard, power supply, storage devices, and input/output
peripherals, (Understand - Level 2)
5. Develop and implement Arduino-based projects by coding and interfacing various sensors for
real-world applications, (Create- Level 6)
6. Assemble and configure aerial robotic systems (drones/UAVs) by understanding flight
principles, selecting appropriate components, and performing test flights in a controlled
environment. (Understand - Level 2)

Course Objective
The objective of this course is to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of operating
system principles, including process management, CPU scheduling, synchronization, deadlock
handling, memory management, and I/O systems. The course aims to develop students’ ability to
analyze core operating system mechanisms and to relate theoretical concepts to real-world operating
systems such as UNIX, mobile platforms, and modern heterogeneous computing environments.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain the fundamental concepts of operating systems, including OS evolution, system calls, and
resource management.
2. Analyze process management and CPU scheduling techniques, including process states, context
switching, threads, and scheduling algorithms such as FCFS, SJF, Priority, and Round Robin.
3. Apply process synchronization and concurrency control mechanisms using critical sections,
semaphores, monitors, and message passing to solve classical IPC problems.
4. Evaluate deadlock handling strategies and memory management techniques, including deadlock
prevention, avoidance (Banker’s algorithm), paging, segmentation, virtual memory, and page
replacement algorithms.
5. Compare I/O management, disk scheduling, and file management strategies, and relate operating
system concepts to real-world case studies such as UNIX, mobile operating systems, and
heterogeneous architectures.

Prerequisite: Linear Algebra, Calculus, Probability
Course Objective
This course introduces students to the basic ideas of information, uncertainty, and entropy that are
essential for understanding data and decision-making in Artificial Intelligence. Students learn how
information measures like mutual information and KL divergence are used in learning, prediction, and
evaluation. The course emphasizes simple statistical reasoning to understand how information flows
through learning systems and how uncertainty limits performance. By the end, students will appreciate
why information theory forms a fundamental mathematical basis for modern AI methods.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to
1. Explain the basic concepts of information, uncertainty, and entropy.
2. Apply mutual information and KL divergence to compare probability distributions in learning
problems.
3. Analyze information flow in simple learning systems using Markov assumptions and the Data
Processing Inequality.
4. Describe how information flow and error bounds influence performance in basic classification
tasks.
Detailed Syllabus

definition and properties, Joint entropy, conditional entropy, chain rules, Mutual

of Gaussian variables (with ML interpretation)

inequality, Connection of KL divergence to: Variational inference (e.g., VAEs),
2.   05

functions, Information per coin toss, multiple hypothesis testing, Lower bounds
related to inference (Stein’s lemma – conceptual)

Pre-requisite: Linear Algebra and Ordinary Differential Equations
Course Objective
The principal objective of the course is to develop students' logical reasoning and problem-solving
skills by introducing fundamental concepts of discrete mathematics essential for computer science
and engineering applications. It provides a strong foundation in set theory, logic, combinatorics,
graph theory, and abstract algebra, enabling students to analyze and construct mathematical
arguments. Through the study of proof techniques, recurrence relations, and discrete structures,
students will gain the ability to model computational problems and prove the correctness of
algorithms. The course also highlights the practical applications of discrete mathematics in real-
world contexts, such as data structures, cryptography, network security, and algorithm design,
equipping students for advanced studies and careers in computing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Apply fundamental concepts of set theory, relations, and functions to solve mathematical
and computational problems.
2. Construct valid mathematical arguments using propositional and predicate logic, proof
techniques, and induction methods.
3. Analyze combinatorial structures and recurrence relations to model and solve discrete
problems in engineering applications.
4. Implement graph and tree algorithms to solve optimization and network-related problems.
5. Demonstrate an understanding of abstract algebraic structures and their applications in
coding theory.

Course Objective
This course provides the fundamental knowledge of computer networks through understanding each
layer of computer network architecture, and transmission systems to network applications. It also
focuses on congestion control techniques, protocols, and application layer functions.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Identify fundamental concepts of computer networks, network topologies, and OSI & TCP/IP
models. (L3- Applying)
2. Explain error detection and correction techniques along with multiple access protocols used in
the data link layer. (L2- Understanding)
3. Classify IPv4 & IPv6 addressing, subnetting, and routing algorithms for efficient network
design. (L4- Analyzing)
4. Compare transport layer protocols such as TCP and UDP, including congestion control
mechanisms. (L4- Analyzing)
5. Demonstrate the functionalities of application layer protocols such as HTTP, DNS, FTP, and
SMTP for network communication. (L2-Understanding)

problem-solving through structured project work. Students will engage in stakeholder analysis,

sustainability. Emphasizing collaboration and ethical responsibility, the course prepares students for
industry and community-driven challenges by enhancing their project management, communication,
and critical thinking abilities.

Course Objective

This course provides an introduction to time series analysis. It will educate students on how to choose an
appropriate forecasting method in a particular environment and then apply it using necessary computations.
It aims to equip students with various forecasting techniques and knowledge on modern statistical methods
for analyzing time series data. It will also provide directions to Improve forecasting using better statistical
models based on statistical analysis

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain the fundamental components of time series data, such as trend, seasonality, and
autocorrelation, and visualize them using various plotting techniques.
2. Apply time series regression models, exponential smoothing, ARMA, ARIMA, and SARIMA models
to forecast univariate and seasonal data.
3. Analyze stationary and non-stationary time series processes using ACF, PACF, unit root tests, and
diagnostics to identify appropriate forecasting models.
4. Evaluate forecasting performance of hierarchical and grouped time series models using
reconciliation methods and compare with alternative approaches.
5. Design advanced forecasting solutions using complex seasonality, the Prophet model, VARs,
bootstrapping, and bagging on real-world datasets using statistical software.

feasibility study, analysis, design, development and validation so as to enhance the technical skill sets in

harness workflow automation, create apps, grasp the distinctions between attended and unattended

process analysis and selection

Course Objective
This course provides an introduction to time series analysis. It will educate students on how to choose an
appropriate forecasting method in a particular environment and then apply it using necessary computations.
It aims to equip students with various forecasting techniques and knowledge on modern statistical methods
for analyzing time series data. It will also provide directions to Improve forecasting using better statistical
models based on statistical analysis
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –

autocorrelation, and visualize them using various plotting techniques.

harness workflow automation, create apps, grasp the distinctions between attended and unattended
bots, and comprehend the symbiotic relationship between RPA and Artificial Intelligence (AI).

Course Objective
The course would enable students to get a brief introduction of the Indian Constitution and its principles.
The students would have knowledge of concept of ‘State’ and interdependencies of its institutions vis a
vis their relation with fundamental rights.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the historic evolution of the Indian Constitution, its drafting, nature and to
understand the principles mentioned in its Preamble
2. Inculcate fundamental rights in its true sense and also the permissible restrictions upon it so as to
enjoy these rights within permissible limits while simultaneously performing their duties and to
apply these principles into their professional lives
3. Ingrain the structure of our polity and role of Judiciary in maintaining the basic structure of the
Constitution
4. Attain knowledge of the Emergency provisions, when and how it is imposed, to know the
additional powers the bestowed upon the Government at times of Emergency and to understand
the Amendment procedure

and 26, Right to remedy under Article 32 and Fundamental duties

the Constitution

Course Objective

The principal objective of this course is to provide a basic understanding of biological mechanisms of living
organisms from the perspective of engineers. To encourage engineering students to think about solving
biological problems with engineering tools. To make them aware of the application of engineering principles
in biology and engineering robust solutions inspired by biological examples.

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. convey that all forms of life have the same building blocks and yet the manifestations are diverse
2. identify and classify microorganisms while understanding molecular basis of DNA as a genetic
material for information transfer
3. classify enzymes and distinguish between different mechanisms of enzyme action

Detailed Syllabus
Unit Description Duration
1 Introduction

Convey that Biology is as important a scientific discipline as Mathematics, Physics
and Chemistry Bring out the fundamental differences between science and
engineering by drawing a comparison between eye and camera, Bird flying and
aircraft. Mention the most exciting aspect of biology as an independent scientific
discipline. Why we need to study biology? Discuss how biological observations of
18th Century that lead to major discoveries. Examples from -Brownian motion and
the origin of thermodynamics by referring to the original observation of Robert
Brown and Julius Mayor. These examples will highlight the fundamental
importance of observations in any scientific inquiry.

a part of genetics. Emphasis to be give not to the mechanics of cell division nor the

using human genetics.

monomeric units and polymeric structures. Discuss about sugars, starch and 05
cellulose. Amino acids and proteins. Nucleotides and DNA/RNA. Two carbon

The aim of the course is that the student should understand working principle, characteristics and simple
applications of basic electronic devices. The course also helps students to understand the application of

assembling and testing simple circuits
Course Outcomes

1. Examine the working of P – N junction diode and its applications
2. Differentiate various configurations and biasing circuits of Bi-polar Junction Transistor
3. Recognize various types of Field Effect Transistors and its configurations
4. Describe various basic digital electronic circuits

Course Objective
The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) by
covering its foundational concepts and advanced applications. Students will gain insight into the
historical development and evolution of RPA, along with a deep appreciation for the benefits and
challenges of its implementation. By delving into RPA tools and their features, students will learn to
harness workflow automation, create apps, grasp the distinctions between attended and unattended
bots, and comprehend the symbiotic relationship between RPA and Artificial Intelligence (AI).
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Demonstrate understanding of fundamental RPA concepts, historical evolution, benefits and
process analysis and selection
2. Analyze RPA tools, design bot workflows, and apply decision-making strategies, constructing
optimized automation processes
3. Create user-centric app interfaces, develop integrated app functionalities aligned with RPA
workflows, and deploy applications within operational frameworks

implementations, and making informed decisions regarding automation practices.

This course provides knowledge of evolutionary computation techniques such as mechanisms of
natural evolution--including genetic recombination, mutation, and natural selection--to automatically
produce solutions to a wide range of problems. The students will explore several evolutionary
computation techniques and apply them to practical problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain the concepts Evolutionary computations and algorithms.
2. Use the concepts of variation and selection techniques for particular classes of problems.
3. Implement various evolutionary algorithms including ant colony optimization and swarm
optimization algorithms.
4. Apply the principles of evolutionary and genetic programming for real life problems.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of vector algebra, functions, limits, differentiation and integration of
functions.
Course Objective:
This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus. This
course will help the students achieve sound understanding of the concepts of calculus, develop
problem solving skills and apply the concepts and techniques of calculus to solve problems within
Engineering domain. This course will equip the students with intermediate to advanced level
concepts and aligned tools to help them tackle advanced mathematics and related applications.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Demonstrate the fundamental concepts of differential calculus for functions of one variable.
2. Solve problems involving functions of several variables using partial differentiation, Taylor
series expansion, and techniques for finding maxima and minima, including Lagrange’s method
of undetermined multipliers.
3. Use Beta and Gamma functions to solve problems in single-variable calculus.
4. Compute and interpret double and triple integrals, including change of variables and coordinate
transformations, and apply them to determine areas and volumes.
5. Examine vector functions using gradient, divergence, curl, and scalar potential and apply
fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to evaluate
integrals.
6. Integrate concepts from differential, integral, and vector calculus to formulate and solve real-
world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences.

1.   Differential Calculus of functions of one variable

Pre-requisite: Fundamental knowledge of physics, chemistry, and mathematics.
Course Objective:
To introduce students to modern biology with an emphasis on the evolution of biology as a multi-
disciplinary field, to make them aware of the application of engineering principles in biology. This
will encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems with engineering
tools. They will also be exposed to the application of engineering principles in biology and
engineering robust solutions inspired by biological examples.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Identify the principles of biomimicry and explain their applications in engineering and
sustainable design, demonstrating an understanding of biologically inspired solutions. (K1)
2. Classify the fundamental building blocks of life (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic
acids) and describe their structural and functional roles in cellular processes and metabolism.

3. Explain the molecular basis of genetic information transfer, including DNA replication,
transcription, and translation, and interpret Mendel's laws and their significance in genetics. (K2)
4. Describe the mechanisms of enzyme action, enzyme-substrate interactions, and enzyme
inhibition, and discuss their industrial and biological applications. (K2)
5. Explain the principles of metabolism and energy transactions, and categorize microorganisms
based on their characteristics, growth kinetics, and applications in biotechnology and drug
discovery. (K1)

processes, and ecosystems. Sustainable engineering.

Course Objective

functions of management. This course also aims to understand issues dealing with small-scale economic
phenomena and concepts such as prices and output of firms, industries and resource owners along with
examining market impact of technological change with regards to understand broader aspects of the
economy and its environment.

based on classical and modern theories. (K2, K3)

Pre-requisite: Fundamental knowledge of physics, chemistry, and mathematics.
Course Objective:
To introduce students to modern biology with an emphasis on the evolution of biology as a multi-
disciplinary field, to make them aware of the application of engineering principles in biology. This
will encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems with engineering
tools. They will also be exposed to the application of engineering principles in biology and
engineering robust solutions inspired by biological examples.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Identify the principles of biomimicry and explain their applications in engineering and
sustainable design, demonstrating an understanding of biologically inspired solutions. (K1)
2. Classify the fundamental building blocks of life (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic
acids) and describe their structural and functional roles in cellular processes and metabolism.
(K2)
3. Explain the molecular basis of genetic information transfer, including DNA replication,
transcription, and translation, and interpret Mendel's laws and their significance in genetics. (K2)
4. Describe the mechanisms of enzyme action, enzyme-substrate interactions, and enzyme
inhibition, and discuss their industrial and biological applications. (K2)
5. Explain the principles of metabolism and energy transactions, and categorize microorganisms
based on their characteristics, growth kinetics, and applications in biotechnology and drug
discovery. (K1)

Pre-requisite: Physics, Chemistry, Mathematics
Course Objective
The aim of this course is to foster a holistic understanding of the composition and working of the
Earth and be able to differentiate between minerals, rock types and landscape types with reference to
their genesis. Also, the course focuses on the application of plate tectonic theory to differentiate
structural features in rocks, decipher seismicity probabilities and predict geological hazards,
fundamentals of Geo-Economics and use geological principles in Civil Engineering.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Differentiate between Earth materials, Earth processes and landscapes
2. Explain structural geology and tectonics
3. Discuss natural disasters based on geological parameters
4. Test and interpret Earth Materials
5. Test and interpret Geological Maps
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Geology   01
Theories of the formation of the Earth; Compositional layering and the internal
structure of the Earth, Rock Cycle; Carbon Cycle; work of Geological Survey of
India
2   Mineralogy and Physical Geology   08
Introduction to minerals, Bowen’s Reaction Series, physical properties;
common rock forming mineral classes; introduction to crystallography, mineral
Provinces, fundamentals of economic geology, India’s mineral deposits,
weathering and Erosion, Types, factors and products of erosion and deposition;
work of running water, sea, wind, glacier, groundwater, aquifer types, recharge
3   Igneous Petrology   05
Depth-wise classification of igneous rocks, Volcanic eruption types and ejected
materials, Concept of hot springs and geysers, Magma types, Basis of expressing
Igneous texture, Types of igneous textures, Igneous intrusive and extrusive
structures, common igneous rocks like Basalt, Granite, Mantle generated rocks
Sedimentary Petrology
Modes of formation of sedimentary rocks, Mineralogical composition of
sedimentary rocks, Basis of expressing sedimentary textures, Types of
sedimentary textures, Sedimentary structures, Classification of sedimentary
rocks, Sedimentary Facies and Provenance, Common sedimentary rocks like
Sandstone, Limestone, Breccia, Fossiliferous rocks

schists, gneisses, marble.
4   Structural Geology   06
Folds, Faults, Joints, Unconformities: Types, classification
Geological maps: fundamentals, symbols and basic interpretation
Introduction to cartography; Introduction to ArcGIS, QGIS

Evolution of the theory of plate tectonics

Pre-requisite: NIL
Course Objective
The course provide basic orientation towards microeconomic principles and help them understand the
functions of management. This course also aims to understand issues dealing with small-scale economic
phenomena and concepts such as prices and output of firms, industries and resource owners along with
examining market impact of technological change with regards to understand broader aspects of the
economy and its environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand Fundamental Economic Concepts - Explain the basic concepts of economics,
including scarcity of resources, economic systems, and demand-supply analysis. (K1, K2)
2. Demonstrate Consumer and Producer Behavior - Apply utility analysis and production
theories to understand consumer decision-making and cost structures in different market
conditions (K2, K3)
3. Illustrate Market Structures and Pricing Mechanisms - Differentiate between market
structures such as monopoly, oligopoly, perfect and imperfect competition, and explain
price and output determination. (K2, K3)
4. Apply Management Principles in Decision-Making - Demonstrate an understanding of
management functions such as planning, organizing, decision-making, and leadership
based on classical and modern theories. (K2, K3)
5. Understand the Role of Business Functions in Organizational Success - Examine the
significance of key business functions such as finance, marketing, human resources, and
operations, and their interdependence in achieving organizational objectives. (K1, K2)

Pre-requisite: Strength of Materials; Engineering Mechanics
Course Objective
This course explains the concept of influence lines and plastic analysis. It also aims to acquire
knowledge of analysis for determinate and indeterminate structures and deflections of structures.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Apply knowledge of general theorems related to elastic structures
2. Examine the deflections of statically determinate structures
3. Construct influence lines diagrams for determinate beams
4. Analyze indeterminate structures by flexibility and stiffness method
5. Analyze column for various end conditions
6. Analyze beams using plastic theory
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
General theorems
Types of structures occurring in practice and their classification. Stable and
unstable structure, static and kinematic determinacy and indeterminacy of
structure. Symmetric   structure, symmetrical and   anti-symmetrical   loads,
1   distinction between linear and non-linear behaviour of material and geometric   06
non- linearity.
Theorems relating to elastic structures, principle of virtual work. Strain energy
in elastic structures, stresses due to axial load & impact load. Complementary
energy, Castigliano’s theorem, Betti’s and Maxwell’s reciprocal theorems,
principle of superposition.
Deflection of statically determinate structures
2   Deflection of determinate pin jointed and rigid jointed frames by principle of   08
virtual work (unit load method) and Castigliano’s theorem. Deflection due to
temperature change.
Rolling loads and Influence lines for statically determinate structures
Influence lines for cantilevers, simply supported, overhanging beams, criteria for   04
3   maximum shear force and bending moment at a section, absolute maximum shear
force and bending moment under moving loads (udl and series of point loads) for
simply supported beams.
Analysis of indeterminate structures by flexibility method
Flexibility coefficients and their use in formulation of compatibility equations.   08
4
Theorem of three moments, application of above methods to propped cantilevers,
fixed beams, continuous beams including effect of settlement of supports.

5   equilibrium equations, direct stiffness method, slope deflection method, Moment
distribution method. Application of the above methods to indeterminate beams
and simple rigid jointed non-sway frames excluding the effect of settlement of
supports.
Plastic Analysis
Introduction, Definitions of plastic hinge and plastic moment capacity,
6   Assumptions, Shape Factor for general sections. Collapse load and basic theorems   05
for finding collapse loads. Methods of plastic analysis – static method and
kinematic method, application of above method for beams.
Columns and struts
7   Euler’s theory for long columns, columns with different end conditions, effective   04
length and slenderness ratio of columns, Rankine’s theory for column.

adaptation and mitigation.

Pre-requisite: Fundamental knowledge of physics, chemistry, and mathematics.
Course Objective:
To introduce students to modem biology with an emphasis on evolution of biology as a multi-
disciplinary field, to make them aware of application of engineering principles in biology. This will
encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems with engineering tools. They
will also be exposed to the application of engineering principles in biology and engineering robust
solutions, inspired by biological
examples.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Identify key principles of biomimicry and develop engineering solutions for different fields
2. Classify microorganisms and their molecular properties and analyze the role of DNA as
genetic material in transferring information among living organisms
3. Describe the fundamental building blocks of life, including carbohydrates, amino acids,
proteins, and lipids, and illustrate their functions in cellular processes and metabolism
Detailed Syllabus

1.   Introduction to Biomimicry
Applications of biology in engineering, Biology as an independent scientific
discipline, Importance of studying biology, Exploring biological discoveries of
the 19th century: Brownian motion and beyond. Applications of biology:   09
Biotechnology, Bioremediation, Bioinformatics, etc., Biologically inspired
engineering. Biomimicry in engineering using designs, processes, and
ecosystems. Sustainable engineering. Case study: The Kingfisher's beak inspired
high-speed Bullet trains.
2.   The fundamental building blocks of life
Unity in diversity of life, Molecules of life. Structure and functions of
carbohydrates, amino acids, proteins, and lipids. Hierarchy in protein structure.   06
Primary secondary, tertiary, and quaternary structure. Proteins as enzymes,
transporters, receptors, and structural elements. Nucleotides and DNA/RNA.
3.   Genetics and Information Transfer
Genetics as the foundation of biology, Mendel's laws, Segregation and

DNA.

Catalysis as a crucial element for life, Enzymology, Enzyme-catalyzed
06
reactions, Enzyme-substrate complex, Mechanism of action, Enzyme

Metabolism: catabolism and anabolism, Principles of energy transactions, ATP as
06
energy currency, ATP cycle, Cellular respiration, Anaerobic respiration, Aerobic
respiration, Metabolic regulation, Bioenergetics.

Introduction to biological classification: criteria of organization and hierarchy of
life. Ecological aspects of single-celled organisms, Identification, and
classification of microorganisms, Microbial growth kinetics, Microbial

Pre-requisite: Physics, Chemistry, Mathematics
Course Objective
The aim of this course is to foster a holistic understanding of the composition and working of the Earth
and be able to differentiate between minerals, rock types and landscape types with reference to their
genesis. Also, the course focuses on the application of plate tectonic theory to differentiate structural
features in rocks, decipher seismicity probabilities and predict geological hazards, fundamentals of
Geo-Economics and use geological principles in Civil Engineering.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. differentiate between Earth materials, Earth processes and landscapes
2. explain structural geology and tectonics
3. discuss natural disasters based on geological parameters
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Geology   01
Theories of the formation of the Earth; Compositional layering and the internal
structure of the Earth, Rock Cycle; Carbon Cycle; work of Geological Survey of
India
2   Mineralogy and Physical Geology   08
Introduction to minerals, Bowen’s Reaction Series, physical properties; common
rock forming mineral classes; introduction to crystallography, mineral
Provinces, fundamentals of economic geology, India’s mineral deposits,
weathering and Erosion, Types, factors and products of erosion and deposition;
work of running water, sea, wind, glacier, groundwater, aquifer types, recharge
3   Igneous Petrology   05
Depth-wise classification of igneous rocks, Volcanic eruption types and ejected
materials, Concept of hot springs and geysers, Magma types, Basis of expressing
Igneous texture, Types of igneous textures, Igneous intrusive and extrusive
structures, common igneous rocks like Basalt, Granite, Mantle generated rocks
Sedimentary Petrology
Modes of formation of sedimentary rocks, Mineralogical composition of
sedimentary rocks, Basis of expressing sedimentary textures, Types of
sedimentary textures, Sedimentary structures, Classification of sedimentary
rocks, Sedimentary Facies and Provenance, Common sedimentary rocks like
Sandstone, Limestone, Breccia, Fossiliferous rocks
AY 2024 - 25
SVKM’s Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
Metamorphic Petrology
Agents of metamorphism, Types of metamorphism, Metamorphic grades and
facies, Metamorphic textures, structures, common metamorphic rocks like schists,
gneisses, marble.
4   Structural Geology   06
Folds, Faults, Joints, Unconformities: Types, classification
Geological maps: fundamentals, symbols and basic interpretation
Introduction to cartography; Introduction to ArcGIS, QGIS
5   Plate tectonic theory   03
Evolution of the theory of plate tectonics
Types of plate movements
Plate Tectonic Theory Case Studies: Himalayas, Andes, New Zealand, Atlantic
Ocean
6   Historical Geology   02
Stratigraphy: Theories, Deccan Basalt, Cuddapah, Vidhyan, Himalayas, Theories
of mass extinction and Ice Ages
7   Geological Hazards and Exploration   05
Types, Causes, mitigation, Case Studies for landslides, Earthquakes, Tsunami,
Floods: Direct and Indirect methods of Geophysical exploration, Site selection,
geological considerations and hazards; Case Studies of dams, reservoirs and
tunnels

Course Objective
This course aims to instill in students a sound knowledge of probability theory and statistical
techniques. It equips the students with intermediate to advanced level concepts and tools in
probability and statistics that help them tackle relevant problems within engineering domain.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Solve problems involving random variables, probability distributions and testing of
hypothesis, correlation and regression
2. Identify suitable probability distribution and testing techniques to solve related problems
3. Apply knowledge of random variables, probability distributions, measures of central
tendency, correlation and regression to solve real life problems
4. Analyse data samples using statistical methods
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Basic Probability
03
Probability spaces, conditional probability, independence; Bayes theorem.
2 Random variables and Probability Distributions
Discrete random variables, probability mass function, cumulative distribution
function, Independent random variables, Continuous random variables,   06
distribution functions and densities, expectation, variance, raw and central
moments of random variables, Binomial distribution, Poisson approximation to
the binomial distribution, Normal distribution.
3   Bivariate Distributions   02
Definition of Bivariate Distribution and their properties, Conditional densities.
4   Basic Statistics
Measures of Central tendency; Moments, Moment generating function,
skewness, kurtosis.   02
Mean and variance of Binomial distribution & Poisson distribution, Moments,
skewness & kurtosis for Normal distribution.

5   Testing of hypothesis
Point estimation, Interval estimate and Confidence interval, Criteria for good
estimates, Null and Alternate hypothesis, Test Statistic, Type I and Type II
errors, One-tailed and two-tailed test, Critical region, Large sample statistical   12
test for mean, Large sample statistical test for proportion, t-test for small
samples, Test for variance- F test, Chi-square test for Goodness of fit and
independence of attributes, Analysis of variance.
6   Linear Statistical Models
Scatter diagram, Linear regression and correlation, Least squares method, Rank   05
correlation, Multiple regression.

gaps.

fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and
verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a
report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and
synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her work carried out before examiners.

also aims to impart knowledge of the effect of compaction, consolidation and shear characteristics of
soil.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Determine index properties of soils and interpret their engineering behavior
2. Classify soils and evaluate their suitability for geotechnical applications
3. Analyze the soil – water characteristics and its effect on soil behavior
4. Compare compaction and consolidation of soils and examine shear strength characteristics

3. Evaluate deformations in various structures

techniques. It equips the students with intermediate to advanced level concepts and tools in
probability and statistics that help them tackle relevant problems within engineering domain.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Solve problems involving random variables, probability distributions and testing of
hypothesis, correlation and regression
2. Identify suitable probability distribution and testing techniques to solve related problems
3. Apply knowledge of random variables, probability distributions, measures of central
tendency, correlation and regression to solve real life problems
4. Analyse data samples using statistical methods

2 Random variables and Probability Distributions   06
Discrete random variables, probability mass function, cumulative distribution
function, Independent random variables, Continuous random variables,
distribution functions and densities, expectation, variance, raw and central
moments of random variables, Binomial distribution, Poisson approximation
to the binomial distribution, Normal distribution.

skewness, kurtosis.

skewness & kurtosis for Normal distribution.

Objectives:
This course intends to build a deep understanding of the Smart City concept and the technology
that underpins it. The course is designed to help the students develop innovative concepts and
prototypes for a sustainable smart city
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Decode the Smart City concept & different models of Smart cities in the world
2. Application of technological innovations for smart city enablement
3. Identify and measure requirements of a smart city.
4. Project work: Generate innovative solutions for smart city as projects outcome
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1. “Smart City” – Various perspectives and definitions, Characteristics of a   3
smart city: What makes a city Smart? What are the different models of Smart
city development – existing city into Smart city, New green field project,
enhancing a “town” into a Smart City.
2. Components of a smart city: Pillars of a smart city – Institutional, Physical,   3
Social, Economic, Infrastructure, Factors that make smart cities possible, Use
of technology and automation.
3.   Identification of smart cities: Framework and KPI for smart city   3
development – 1: Conditions precedent for smart city development,
Benchmarks for smart cities, Government policies, Mapping of smart cities
through Transport, Infrastructure, Water Management, energy, health,
hygiene & sanitation, education, governance, social & cultural fabric and
disaster management. Measurement of key parameters (KPI) for smart cities

analytic/optimization and visualization technologies
6. Understanding Financial sustainability of Smart cities, the PPP model   3
for smart city development
7. Case Studies of Existing best practices in cities in India   3
8. Case Studies of Existing Smart cities of the world   3
Like Singapore, London – UK, Barcelona etc.
9.   Project work begins : Students get divided into teams, each team will study   3
one of the ten aspects of Smart city- Transport, Infrastructure, Water
Management , energy, health, hygiene & sanitation, education, governance,
social & cultural fabric and disaster management: Project work begins -
Briefing to students on the sub-themes and allotted projects related to any one
area for an in- depth study by each team. The stage gates and timelines for the
project defined along with the evaluation criteria at each deliverable.
10. Sector analysis - Project wise: Presentation of secondary research on the   3
specific area picked up by the student teams
11. Primary Research work - Project wise: Expert interviews, focus group   3
discussions, ethnographic study to understand the needs and aspirations of
people from the future cities.
12. Ideation for Innovative concept proposals for resolving issues in Smart   3
cities: Observation on post-it notes, Clustering, Analysis and ideation for new
concept ideas
13. Initial Concept development for solutions: Students develop concepts   3
around proposed solutions for various pain points identified in their
respective domain areas
14. Feasibility Analysis of the Concepts developed: Concepts developed initially   3

Objectives:
1. Interpret multidisciplinary scientific bases of climatic change: basic mechanisms that govern the
climate system and its responses to drivers of change
2. Analyse paleo-climatic change and assess recent historical variability to project future climate
projections
3. Investigate the impact of climate change on communities of human population and global
economy
4. Gain insight into legal and Financial aspects of Climate change
5. Investigate fundamentals of the fields of Geo-engineering
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Explain how the climate system works and understand the physical basis of climate change
2. Investigate climate projections from the past and predict possible future climate change on Earth
3. Analyse how human activities are influencing Climate Change and Global Warming
4. Evaluate global climate change policy and its implementation, options for mitigation and
adaptation
5. Evaluate aspects of Climate change finance
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Climate Change Science:   08
 Human contribution to climate change; units of temperature, energy and
light;
 Overview of important greenhouse gases and their main sources, Earth
Energy Budget and Energy balance model, Radiative transfer, Naked planet
climate model, Nuclear winter
 Anthropogenic Drivers of Climate Change: Main observed changes in the
climate since the industrial revolution.
 Future trends and Impacts of Climate Change: Projected future trends and
impacts of climate change on surface temperature, precipitation, ocean pH
2   Paleo-Climate:   03
   Principles of Paleo-climate studies: Polar Regions and Sea level rise, Ice Ages
   Paleoclimate and Proxy Measurements
 Tree Rings, Borehole temperatures and Interglacial cycles
3   Climate and Changing Weather:   06
 Concepts of Heat transport, Coriolis Acceleration, Geostrophic motion, Ice
albedo, water vapour feedback, aerosols
 Global Wind Systems: Trade Winds and the Hadley Cell, the Highs and
Lows of the Westerlies, the Vital Importance of Monsoon Rains
 Cloud Formation and Climate: Hurricanes and Global Warming

 Global ice sheet degradation: rates, reasons
4   Climate Change Legalities:   06
 The Climate Change Policy Framework: Overview of how the international
legal and policy framework to address climate change developed over time
and key issues under negotiation.
 Key provisions of the UNFCCC, its organizational structure, and different
Party groups under the Convention.
 Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement, COP Simulation
 Towards a Post-2020 Regime
 India’s role in climate change mitigation

4, To impart knowledge about the effect of compaction and consolidation

5. To gain the knowledge of shear characteristics of soil

Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:

1. Identify and determine index properties of soils and interpret their engineering behaviour

2. Classify soils and evaluate their suitability for geotechnical applications

3. Analyse the soil — water characteristics and its effect on soil behaviour

4, Distinguish between compaction and consolidation of soils and examine shear strength

characteristics
Detailed Syllabus:
Unit | Description Duration
1. Introduction: 01

Definitions: soils, soil mechanics, soil engineering, rock mechanics, scope
of soil engineering, comparison between soil & rock, Formation of Soil:
Residual Soils and their zones, Transported soil and its Types

2. | Basic Definitions & Relationship: 06
Soil as three phase system in terms of weight, volume, void ratio, porosity,
Definitions: moisture content, densities, unit weights, degree of saturation,
void ratio, porosity, specific gravity, mass specific gravity etc. Relationship
between volume- weight, void ratio-moisture content, unit weight-percent air
voids, saturation-moisture content, moisture content-specific gravity etc.,
Determination of various parameters such as moisture content by Oven Dry
Method, Specific gravity by Pycnometer method, Unit weight by core cutter
method

3. | Plasticity Characteristics of Soil: 03
Introduction to definitions of: plasticity of soil, consistency limits- liquid limit,
plastic limit, shrinkage limit, plasticity, liquidity and consistency indices,
flow & toughness indices, Use of consistency limits.

4. | Classification of Soils: 03
Introduction of soil classification:, Textural Classification, Unified Soil
Classification, Indian standard soil classification system, Sieve analysis,
particle size distribution- its use and interpretation.

5. | Permeability of Soils: 03
Introduction to hydraulic head, Darcy’s law, Discharge velocity and seepage
velocity and relation between them, factors affecting permeability of soil,

water table, Fluctuation of effective stress, effective stress in soils saturated
by capillary action, seepage pressure, critical hydraulic gradient, quick sand
condition.

7. | Compaction of Soils: 02
Introduction, theory of compaction, laboratory determination of optimum
moisture content and maximum dry density. Standard and Modified
Compaction Tests, Factors affecting compaction, Compaction in the field,

primary & secondary consolidation , Terzaghi’s spring analogy for

consolidation.

9, | Shear Strength: 04
Principal planes and principal stresses, Mohr-Coulomb theory, types of
shear tests, direct shear test, merits & demerits of direct shear test , tri-axial
compression tests, drainage conditions of UU, CU and CD tests, unconfined
compression test, vane shear test.

Introduction, methods of investigation, methods of boring, soil samplers
and sampling, number and disposition of borings, borehole logs,

Torsion of circular shafts - solid and hollow, stresses and strains in shaft when

Application to members subjected to eccentric loads and chimneys, core of

General equations for transformation of stress, principles planes and principal
stresses, maximum shear stress, Mohr’s circle.

Uniform linear acceleration, liquid container subjected to constant
horizontal and vertical acceleration, constant rotation with vertical axis,

Loss of head through pipes, Darcy Weisbach equation, Minor losses,

structures

e Analyse the indeterminate structures using advanced methods of analysis
e Plot the influence lines diagram for indeterminate beams
e Analyse the portal frames using approximate methods

Detailed Syllabus:
Unit | Description Duration
1. Introduction to Stiffness Method in Matrix Form: 13

Basic concepts of stiffness coefficients, member stiffness matrix
for member of plane truss, member of rigid jointed plane frame,
member of plane grid and member of space frame.

Properties of stiffness matrix, co-ordinate transformation matrix,
stiffness matrix in local and global co-ordinate axes system,
assemblage of structural stiffness matrix and application of
boundary conditions.

Joint loads, Equivalent joint loads, method of solution for
displacements and computation of internal forces in members.
Application of stiffness method to beams, pin jointed trusses,
rigid jointed plane frames and simple plane grid structures.

2, Conventional Form of Stiffness Method, Modified Moment 07
Distribution Method:
Symmetric structure, Symmetric and anti-symmetric loads,
Modification of stiffness and carryover factors for symmetric and
anti-symmetric loads both for sway and non-sway cases for
frames with different support conditions.
Application to frames involving side sways.

Flexibility Method in Matrix Form: 06

Review of concepts of flexibility coefficients, Selection of primary
structure, concept of structure flexibility matrix, compatibility
equations, solution for redundant forces, computational of
internal forces, and joint displacements. Application to pin
jointed trusses and rigid jointed plane frames for different
loading including the effect of settlement of support,

temperature changes and elastic supports.

Conventional Form of Flexibility Method: 08

Elastic Center Method and its application to rectangular box,
rigid jointed portal frames and fixed arches.

Column Anology Method and its application to analysis of non
prismatic beams, simple rectangular frames, determination of
stiffness coefficients and carry over factors for non prismatic

beam members.

Influence Line Diagrams for Indeterminate Structures: 06

Muller Breslau’s Principle for drawing influence line diagrams
for statically indeterminate structures. Influence Lines Diagrams
for propped cantilevers, fixed beams and continuous beams.

Approximate Methods for Analysis of Building Frames: 05
Approximate methods for gravity loads: Substitute frame and
equivalent frames. Approximate methods for lateral loads: Portal

and cantilever method.

Total 45

Program: _B. Tech. (Civil Engineering) Semester: VIII
Course: Elective - III (Structural Dynamics ) Code : BTCI08004
Teaching Scheme Evaluation Scheme (Marks & Weightage)
Theory Internal Continuous
Lecture | Practical | Tutorial | Credit (3 Hrs, Assessment (ICA) as per
60 Marks) | Institute Norms (50 Marks)
3 0 2 4 100 % 40%
Objectives:
e To impart knowledge of the structural dynamics in civil engineering
structures

e To study the behaviour of single degree of freedom system
© To know the behaviour of structures idealized as multiple degree of freedom

system
e To understand the behaviour of system with distributed masses

Outcomes:
After successful completion of this course, students should be able to

e Determine the dynamic properties of vibratory structures.
e Describe the response of a structures subjected to dynamic loads and base

excitation
Detailed Syllabus:
Unit | Description Duration
1, Introduction: 02

Introduction to structural dynamics, definition of basic problem
in dynamics, static v/s dynamic loads, different types of
dynamic loads.

2. Single degree of Freedom (SDOF) systems: 18
Undamped vibration of SDOF system, natural frequency and
period of vibration, damping in structures, viscous damping and
coulomb damping, effect of damping on frequency of vibration
and amplitude of vibration, logarithmic decrement. Forced
vibration, response to harmonic forces, periodic loading,
dynamic load factors, response of structure subjected to general
dynamic load, Duhamel's integral, numerical evaluation of
dynamics response of SDOF systems subjected to different types
of dynamic loads. Introduction to frequency domain analysis,

NMIMS
Mumbai

-BTECH /CIVIL/2015-16/SEM-VIII/ Page 6
response of structure in frequency domain subjected to general
periodic and non-periodic / impulsive forces of short duration,
use of complex frequency response function. Use of Fourier
Series for periodic forces, introduction to vibration isolation.
Distributed mass system idealized as SDOF system, use of
Rayleigh's method, response of SDOF system subjected to
ground motion.

3: Generiilized Single-Degree of Freedom System: Generalized 06
properties, assemblages of rigid bodies, systems with distributed
mass and elasticity, expressions for generalized system
properties.

4, Lumped mass multi degree of freedom (MDOF) system: Coupled 13
and uncoupled systems, direct determination of frequencies of
vibration and mode shapes, orthogonality principle, vibration of
MDOF systems with initial conditions, approximate methods of
determination of natural frequencies of vibration and mode
shapes-vector iteration methods, energy methods and use of
Lagrange's method in writing equations of motions. Decoupling
of equations of motion, modal equation of motion, concept of
modal mass and modal stiffness, forced vibration of MDOF
system, modal analysis, application to multi storey rigid frames
subjected to lateral dynamic loads.

5. Structure with distributed mass system: Use of partial 06
differential equation, free vibration analysis of single span beams
with various boundary conditions, determination of frequencies
of vibration and mode shapes, forced vibration of single span
beams subjected to the action of specified dynamic loads.

Total 45
Text Books:
1, Anil K. Chopra (2007), “Dynamics of Structures 3 Edition”, Prentice Hall
India

Reference Books:
_ 1. Craig R.R. (2006), “Fundamentals of Structural Dynamics 2nd Edition”, John

Wiley & Sons
2. Cloguh & Penzein (2010), “Dynamics of Structures”, Computers and Structures
3. John M. Biggs (2011), “Structural Dynamics”, Tata McGraw Hill

1. Minimum seven assignments covering the prescribed syllabus

measures, seismic design considerations, allowable ductility
demand, ductility capacity, reinforcement detailing for members

and joints as per IS 13920

Unit Description Duration

Course :   Engineering Mathematics - III   Code : BTAB03001
Teaching Scheme   Evaluation Scheme
