Pre-requisite
1. Theory of semiconductor materials, their atomic structures and properties.
2. DC circuit analysis, AC fundamentals.
Course Objectives
The aim of the course is that the student should understand working principle,
characteristics and simple applications of basic electronic devices. The course also
helps students to understand the application of these devices in advanced circuits such
as amplifiers. It also intends to impart hands on experience in assembling and testing
simple circuits.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to
1. describe the fundamentals of semiconductors,
2. understand characteristics and working of diodes, BJTs and FETs and solve
simple circuits,
3. describe operational amplifier and illustrate its applications,
4. describe digital electronics fundamentals.
Detailed Syllabus:

Energy band theory, Fermi levels; Conductors, Semiconductors &
Insulators: electrical properties, band diagrams. Semiconductors:
intrinsic &   extrinsic, energy band   diagram, P&N-type   04
semiconductors, drift & diffusion carriers.

4.   Field Effect Transistors: Concept of Field Effect Transistors

Course Objective

Macroeconomics.
Course Outcomes

1. describe how microeconomic models can be used to consider fundamental
economic choices of households and firms,

whole,

Course Objectives
The students will study basic components of the environment and various types of
pollution affecting the environment. They will also study how to differentiate various
types of waste and ways to manage these wastes. In addition, the students will learn
the impact studies associated with the environment and social issues, and methods to
manage them. They will also be acquainted with various legal aspects associated with
the environment and study the roles of various stakeholders associated with the
environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to
1. discuss various types of environmental Pollution, natural resources and its
misuse,
2. demonstrate a plan for water management, promotion of recycle and reuse,
generation of less waste, avoiding electricity waste,
3. demonstrate a slogan, poster and plan activities for environmental protection
and social issues.

Prerequisite: Programming, Computer Organization and Architecture
Course Objective
This course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of operating system principles, including
process management, memory management, file systems, synchronization, system security, and storage
management. Students will develop the analytical skills necessary to design, evaluate, and optimize
operating system components for efficient and secure operation.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the students will be able to –
1.Explain the fundamental concepts of operating systems. (K2)
2.Analyze the various process management techniques and concurrency mechanisms. (K4)
3.Explain synchronization, deadlock handling, and resource allocation methods for efficient process
execution. (K2)
4.Apply knowledge of memory management techniques and page replacement algorithms to
optimize system performance. (K3)
5.Implement I/O management strategies and disk scheduling algorithms for system   performance
improvement. (K3)
6.Utilize case studies to understand the architecture, file system and security mechanisms of
operating system. (K2)
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Operating system:   03
OS objectives and functions, evolution of operating system, Basic concepts:
Processes, Files, System Calls, Basic architectural concepts of an OS, Concept of
Virtual Machine, Resource Manager view,
Process view and hierarchical view of an OS, Real-Time Operating Systems   02
(RTOS) and lightweight OS
2   Process and Process Scheduling:   04
Definition, Process Relationship, Different states of a Process, Process State
transitions, Process Control Block (PCB), Context switching
Process Scheduling: objectives, Types of Schedulers, Scheduling criteria, Pre-
emptive and non-pre-emptive Scheduling algorithms - FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Priority,
and Round Robin. Multilevel scheduling
Thread: Definition, Various states, Benefits of threads, Types of threads   02

Peterson’s Solution, The Producer / Consumer Problem, Event Counters,
Monitors, Message Passing, examples on live locks.
Classical IPC Problems: Reader’s & Writer Problem, Barber’s shop problem   02
4   Deadlock:   02
Definition, Necessary and sufficient conditions for Deadlock, Deadlock
Prevention
Deadlock Avoidance: Banker’s algorithm, Deadlock detection and Recovery,   04
Dinning Philosopher Problem
5   Memory Management:   04
Basic concepts
Memory allocation: Contiguous Memory allocation – Fixed and variable
partition– Internal and External fragmentation and Compaction.
Basics of Virtual Memory – Hardware and control structures – Locality of
reference, Page allocation, Partitioning, Paging, Page fault, Working Set,
Segmentation, Demand paging, Thrashing.
Page Replacement algorithms: Optimal, First in First Out (FIFO), Belady's   02
anomaly, Least Recently used (LRU), Not Recently Used ( NRU).

Pre-requisite: Linear Algebra and Ordinary Differential Equations
Course Objective
The principal objective of the course is to develop students' logical reasoning and problem-solving
skills by introducing fundamental concepts of discrete mathematics essential for computer science
and engineering applications. It provides a strong foundation in set theory, logic, combinatorics,
graph theory, and abstract algebra, enabling students to analyze and construct mathematical
arguments. Through the study of proof techniques, recurrence relations, and discrete structures,
students will gain the ability to model computational problems and prove the correctness of
algorithms. The course also highlights the practical applications of discrete mathematics in real-
world contexts, such as data structures, cryptography, network security, and algorithm design,
equipping students for advanced studies and careers in computing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Apply fundamental concepts of set theory, relations, and functions to solve mathematical
and computational problems.
2. Construct valid mathematical arguments using propositional and predicate logic, proof
techniques, and induction methods.
3. Analyze combinatorial structures and recurrence relations to model and solve discrete
problems in engineering applications.
4. Implement graph and tree algorithms to solve optimization and network-related problems.
5. Demonstrate an understanding of abstract algebraic structures and their applications in
coding theory.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year
students’ learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate
with the required practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think
critically, solve challenging problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral
communication skills, teamwork and planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary
areas which will help broaden their scope and learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the
research gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design
and fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop
algorithms and verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be
required to submit a report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation,
analysis functional simulation and synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her
work carried out before examiners.

4. Analyze the different protocols of the layered architecture of computer networks

Course Objective
This course provides the fundamental knowledge of computer networks through
understanding each layer of computer network architecture, and transmission systems to
network applications. It also focuses on congestion control techniques, protocols, and
application layer functions.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain the concepts of computer networks, topologies and data communication.
2. Analyze the various error detection and correction and medium access techniques.
3. Apply network layer addressing and routing techniques to different network
topologies.
4. Analyze the different protocols of the layered architecture of computer networks.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of vector algebra, functions, limits, differentiation and integration of
functions.
Course Objective:
This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus. This
course will help the students achieve sound understanding of the concepts of calculus, develop
problem solving skills and apply the concepts and techniques of calculus to solve problems within
Engineering domain. This course will equip the students with intermediate to advanced level
concepts and aligned tools to help them tackle advanced mathematics and related applications.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the fundamental concepts of differential calculus for functions of one variable,
including limits, derivatives, Mean Value Theorems, Taylor and Maclaurin series, and
LHospital’s rule. (K2)
2. Solve problems involving functions of several variables using partial differentiation, Taylor
series expansion, and techniques for finding maxima and minima, including Lagrange’s
method of undetermined multipliers. (K3)
3. Use Beta and Gamma functions to solve problems in single-variable calculus. (K2)
4. Compute and interpret double and triple integrals, including change of variables and
coordinate transformations, and apply them to determine areas and volumes. (K3)
5. Examine vector functions using gradient, divergence, curl, and scalar potential and apply
fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to
evaluate integrals. (K3)
6. Integrate concepts from differential, integral, and vector calculus to formulate and solve real-
world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences. (K3)

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of 12th grade level Physics
Course Objectives:
The knowledge of Physics relevant to engineering is critical for converting ideas into technology.
An understanding of Physics also helps engineers understand the working and the limitations of
existing devices and techniques, eventually leading to innovations and improvements. This
course aims to help students understand the basic concepts of physics thoroughly and lay the
foundations for the various engineering courses.

principles of semiconductor devices. (K2)

grating applications. (K3)

real-world communication and engineering problems. (K3)

recognize their applications in basic engineering problems related to electromagnetism. (K2)
5. Explore the properties and applications of modern engineering materials like nanomaterials,
superconductors, and dielectrics. (K3)
6. Gauge theoretical principles through laboratory experimentation, enhancing problem-
solving abilities and technical proficiency in modern physics applications. (K3)

Course Objective
This course aims to equip students with practical skills in electronics prototyping and provides hands-on
experience with essential tools, measuring instruments, PCB design, and fabrication techniques.
Additionally, students will gain knowledge in PC hardware assembly, Arduino-based circuit
programming, and aerial robotics, including drone assembly and flight basics.

prototyping equipment for circuit design and testing, (Understand - Level 2)

real-world applications, (Create- Level 6)

principles, selecting appropriate components, and performing test flights in a controlled
environment. (Understand - Level 2)

Pre-requisite: Linear Algebra and Ordinary Differential Equations
Course Objective
The principal objective of the course is to develop students' logical reasoning and problem-solving
skills by introducing fundamental concepts of discrete mathematics essential for computer science
and engineering applications. It provides a strong foundation in set theory, logic, combinatorics,
graph theory, and abstract algebra, enabling students to analyze and construct mathematical
arguments. Through the study of proof techniques, recurrence relations, and discrete structures,
students will gain the ability to model computational problems and prove the correctness of
algorithms. The course also highlights the practical applications of discrete mathematics in real-
world contexts, such as data structures, cryptography, network security, and algorithm design,
equipping students for advanced studies and careers in computing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Apply fundamental concepts of set theory, relations, and functions to solve mathematical
and computational problems.
2. Construct valid mathematical arguments using propositional and predicate logic, proof
techniques, and induction methods.
3. Analyze combinatorial structures and recurrence relations to model and solve discrete
problems in engineering applications.
4. Implement graph and tree algorithms to solve optimization and network-related problems.
5. Demonstrate an understanding of abstract algebraic structures and their applications in
coding theory.

Course Objective
This course aims to provide fundamental knowledge of computer networks by exploring network
architectures, classifications, and key models such as OSI and TCP/IP. It covers network layer
functionalities such as data transmission, error detection, flow control, addressing, routing and transport
layer functionalities. Additionally, the course introduces emerging network technologies and network
security fundamentals.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the students will be able to -
1.Explain the fundamental concepts of Computer Networks. (K2)
2.Analyze and Implement Data Link Layer Protocols to ensure reliable transmission. (K4)
3.Apply and evaluate network layer functions and routing algorithms (K3)
4.Describe and differentiate various Transport and Application Layer Mechanisms (K2)
5.Explain the concepts of future Networking Technologies (K2)

Course Objective
This theory course introduces the internal structure, functioning, and organization of computer
systems. It covers data representation, instruction execution, CPU architecture, memory hierarchy, and
I/O organization. The course forms the foundation for advanced topics such as operating systems,
embedded systems, and computer architecture design.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Identify the major functional units of a computer system and their roles.
2. Explain number systems, data representation formats, and basic arithmetic operations
used in computer hardware.
3. Illustrate instruction formats, addressing modes, and the complete instruction execution
cycle.
4. Analyze the impact of memory hierarchy, cache mapping techniques, and virtual
memory performance.
5. Differentiate between various I/O mechanisms such as programmed I/O, interrupt-
driven I/O, and DMA.
6. Evaluate processor performance considering pipelining, hazards, and RISC vs. CISC
design principles.

Security posture of an organization is affected by end user’s action. Human users are considered
as the weakest link in the cybersecurity. Students should also understand legal aspects of
cybersecurity as it guides the developments of security programs and solutions. This course
provides an understanding of the human and legal aspect of cybersecurity. Students will be
exposed to various national and international laws relevant to cybersecurity from a layman’s
perspective.

After successful completion of the course, student would be able to -

2. Explain ITA 2000 and ITAA 2008

Course Objective
Image and video evidence is a growing concern during an investigation as more and more of our
lives are captured in some form. From cell phones to CCTV security cameras in public places to
cell phone cameras, our everyday activities are constantly being recorded. This evidence, when
properly collected and analysed, can be crucial in solving crimes. This course will introduce
students to the concepts of video and image forensics. The course will cover how to properly
identify, collect, and handle digital video and image evidence in a way that maintains evidence
integrity and is consistent with best practices in the field.

After successful completion of the course, student would be able to -

designers. This course looks at application of theories from other domains like economics and
behavioural science to the cybersecurity context.

Pre-requisite: Fundamentals of C Language
Course Objective
This course teaches the fundamentals of secure programming in C. Students will learn how a C
program runs “under-the-hood” by analysing at the machine-level representation. The coding
standards and design principles of secure programming are explored so that security can be built-
in the design time to avoid security vulnerabilities.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain the fundamentals of secure programming
2. Analyse C programs for security vulnerabilities
3. Implement security attacks
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   04
Philosophy of Secure Programming, Security Policies and Procedures,
Motivation behind Software Security, Examples of Vulnerabilities, A Tour of
Computer Systems, Secure Programming Design Principles.
2.   Representing Information   04
Bits and Bytes, Hexadecimal Notation, Addressing and Byte Ordering, Integer
Security, Integer Arithmetic, Integer Overflow and Security Vulnerabilities.
3.   Machine-Level Representation of C Programs and Optimizing Program   08
Performance
Conditional Statements, Switch-Case Statements, Loops, Procedures, Array
Allocation and Access, Eliminating Loop Inefficiencies, reducing Procedure
Calls, Eliminating Unneeded Memory References, Loop Unrolling, Enhancing
Parallelism, Memory Performance, Stack-based Buffer Overflow.
4.   Data Pointer and Function Pointer Vulnerabilities   04
Smashing the stack by exploiting pointers, Dynamic Memory Allocation and
security.
5.   Linking   03
Load-time exploitation, Basics of static and dynamic linking.
6.   Format String Vulnerabilities   03
Stack layout of variadic functions, Exploit the formatted output string and
buffer overflow vulnerabilities.

Pre-requisite: Basic knowledge of technology
Course Objective
We live in a technology enabled world where data is collected and process as we interact with any
technology product or service. This data is used by the companies to predict our tastes, our habits,
or future possible health problems. This use of data has created a big privacy threat. Various
governments have developed stringent privacy laws like GDPR to protect the privacy of their
citizens. Effective information privacy is very difficult. Globally organizations are approaching
privacy problem based on two concepts: Privacy by design and privacy engineering. In this course
students will be exposed to both the concepts.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Identify data privacy threats and suggest their countermeasures
2. Implement various privacy models
3. Design privacy program for an organization
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   06
Data privacy need and concepts, privacy by design principles, information
privacy requirements and guidelines, information privacy threats and
vulnerabilities, privacy risk assessment, privacy and security control
selection, privacy integration, testing and evaluation, trade-offs between
privacy and security, usable privacy.
2.   Data Privacy Attacks and Models   07
The evolving threat environment, privacy threat taxonomy, NIST threat
model, privacy attacks (Linkage Attack, re-identification Attack, Statistical
Attack), De-identification of direct identifiers,
Basic Privacy Models K- Anonymity, L-Diversity, t-closeness, Differential
Privacy, Generalisation, Suppression, Perturbation, Randomization.
3.   Online Privacy   07
The online eco-system for personal data, online privacy threats, online
privacy requirements, privacy notices and tracking, Privacy Preserving Data
Sharing and Publications, Privacy Preserving Access Control Models.
4.   Information Privacy Management   05
Information privacy governance, privacy roles, privacy program plan, key
areas of privacy management, privacy policy, NIST privacy framework,

The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), US Privacy laws
(COPPA, HIPPA and others), The China Personal Information Protection
Law, Draft Indian Personal Data Protection Bill, 2019.
Total   30

Abstract properties of pairings. Pairing-friendly elliptic curves. Generating

Baby step-giant step. Pollard rho. Menezes-Okamoto-Vanstone and Frey-

Pre-requisite: Digital Forensics Fundamentals
Course Objective
Image and video evidence is a growing concern during an investigation as more and more of our
lives are captured in some form. From cell phones to CCTV security cameras in public places to
cell phone cameras, our everyday activities are constantly being recorded. This evidence, when
properly collected and analysed, can be crucial in solving crimes. This course will introduce
students to the concepts of video and image forensics. The course will cover how to properly
identify, collect, and handle digital video and image evidence in a way that maintains evidence
integrity and is consistent with best practices in the field.
Course Outcomes
After successful completion of the course, student would be able to -
1. Forensically extract image and video evidence from given media
2. Perform image and video authentication and detect tampering
3. Create and detect deepfake

analysis of digital images and video, protocols and guidelines related to
collection, recovery, enhancement, analysis, and interpretation of image and
video evidence.

issues related to video recordings (Data losses and impairments, visual
distortions and artefacts, video quality evaluation metrics) Various categories

camera, mode of capture, and environmental conditions at the time of
recording, video analytics algorithms.

image and video manipulation and their detection techniques (i.e., various

Pre-requisite: Basic knowledge of technology
Course Objective
We live in a technology enabled world where data is collected and process as we interact with any
technology product or service. This data is used by the companies to predict our tastes, our habits,
or future possible health problems. This use of data has created a big privacy threat. Various
governments have developed stringent privacy laws like GDPR to protect the privacy of their
citizens. Effective information privacy is very difficult. Globally organizations are approaching
privacy problem based on two concepts: Privacy by design and privacy engineering. In this course
students will be exposed to both the concepts.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Identify data privacy threats and suggest their countermeasures
2. Implement various privacy models
3. Design privacy program for an organization
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   06
Data privacy need and concepts, privacy by design principles, information
privacy requirements and guidelines, information privacy threats and
vulnerabilities, privacy risk assessment, privacy and security control
selection, privacy integration, testing and evaluation, trade-offs between
privacy and security, usable privacy.
2.   Data Privacy Attacks and Models   07
The evolving threat environment, privacy threat taxonomy, NIST threat
model, privacy attacks (Linkage Attack, re-identification Attack, Statistical
Attack), De-identification of direct identifiers,
Basic Privacy Models K- Anonymity, L-Diversity, t-closeness, Differential
Privacy, Generalisation, Suppression, Perturbation, Randomization.
3.   Online Privacy   07
The online eco-system for personal data, online privacy threats, online
privacy requirements, privacy notices and tracking, Privacy Preserving Data
Sharing and Publications, Privacy Preserving Access Control Models.
4.   Information Privacy Management   05
Information privacy governance, privacy roles, privacy program plan, key
areas of privacy management, privacy policy, NIST privacy framework,
OASIS privacy management model, privacy awareness training and
education.
5.   Legal and Regulatory Requirements   05

Pre-requisite: Digital Forensics Fundamentals
Course Objective
Image and video evidence is a growing concern during an investigation as more and more of our
lives are captured in some form. From cell phones to CCTV security cameras in public places to
cell phone cameras, our everyday activities are constantly being recorded. This evidence, when
properly collected and analysed, can be crucial in solving crimes. This course will introduce
students to the concepts of video and image forensics. The course will cover how to properly
identify, collect, and handle digital video and image evidence in a way that maintains evidence
integrity and is consistent with best practices in the field.
Course Outcomes
After successful completion of the course, student would be able to -
1. Forensically extract image and video evidence from given media
2. Perform image and video authentication and detect tampering
3. Create and detect deepfake
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   4
Image and Video as legal evidence and related issues, principles of forensic
analysis of digital images and video, protocols and guidelines related to
collection, recovery, enhancement, analysis, and interpretation of image and
video evidence.
2.   Fundamentals of image and video processing and analytics   8
Basic concepts, image and video formats and standards, Overview of technical
issues related to video recordings (Data losses and impairments, visual
distortions and artefacts, video quality evaluation metrics) Various categories
of digital videos, based on the kind of recording device, placement of the
camera, mode of capture, and environmental conditions at the time of
recording, video analytics algorithms.
3.   Image and Video Authentication and Tamper Detection   12
Image and Video Source and Content Authentication, basic Tamper Detection
and their limitations (Hash value analysis, Hex editor analysis, Metadata
analysis, and Error Level Analysis (ELA)), Study of various methods of digital
image and video manipulation and their detection techniques (i.e., various
kinds of forgeries such as copy paste aka splicing, object removal forgeries,
upscale-crop, and resampling, frame-based tampering, Re-compression and
transcoding detection, etc.)
4.   Deepfake Detection   6
Introduction to deepfake technology, deepfake creation process and detection
methods.
Total   30

Pre-requisite: Fundamental Knowledge of Cybersecurity
Course Objective
Technical challenges of the cybersecurity are better understood as compared to human challenges.
Cybersecurity is fundamentally a problem of human interaction with technology. This course
provides an overview of human interactions with cybersecurity technology, from users to system
designers. This course looks at application of theories from other domains like economics and
behavioural science to the cybersecurity context.
Course Outcomes
After successful completion of the course, student would be able to -
1. Apply various theories from other domains to cybersecurity decision making
2. Apply game theory to cybersecurity context
3. Design cybersecurity awareness campaign using marketing and behavioural theories
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Economics   6
Classical and Behavioural economics, asymmetric information, auction theory,
the economics of security and dependability, application of Kahneman-Tversky
approach to cybersecurity, Heuristics and biases in cybersecurity decision
making.
2. Game Theory and Cybersecurity   8
Introduction, payoff, matrix games, mixed strategy, Saddle point, dominated
strategies, applications of game theory to cybersecurity.
3.   Personality Theory and Cybersecurity   5
Personality traits and cybersecurity, Profiling in the cybersecurity context,
profiling matrices, ABCD Analysis
4.   Marketing and Communications for Cybersecurity Awareness Campaign   6
The communication conundrum,   similarity between marketing and
cybersecurity awareness campaigns, tracking   results and measuring
effectiveness.
5.   Behaviour Management for Security Awareness Leaders   5
System 1 and System 2 thinking, working with human nature, Fogg Behaviour
Model, Nudge and frames, designing and debugging behaviour, tracking
results and measuring effectiveness.

Pre-requisite: Nil

Course Objective
In this course students will get acquainted with the various systems of forces. It is designed for the
students to understand the concept of static equilibrium and apply the equations of motion to rigid

bodies.

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Determine the resultant of various systems of forces
2. Analyse the system of forces in equilibrium
3. Evaluate the displacement, velocity and acceleration of a moving bodies
4. Determine the forces developed on rigid bodies subjected to displacements and rotations

Detailed Syllabus
Unit | Description Duration
1. | System of Forces 05

Rectangular components of forces in space, moment, couple, Varignon’s theorem,
resolution of forces, resultant of force system (coplanar, non-coplanar), concept
of virtual work, principle of virtual work.

2. | Application of System of Forces and Equilibrium 08
Conditions of equilibrium, types of support, loads and beams, free body
diagrams, support reactions.

Friction

Laws of friction, angle of friction, angle of repose, cone of friction, equilibrium of
bodies on rough horizontal and inclined plane, application to inclined planes,
wedges, ladder & screw jack.

Analysis of Pin Jointed Plane Trusses

Perfect truss, analysis using method of joints and method of sections.

3. | Centroid and Moment of Inertia 03
Centroid, moment of inertia, polar moment of inertia, and product of inertia,
parallel and perpendicular axis theorem.

4. | Kinematics of Particle 07
Velocity and acceleration in terms of rectangular coordinate system, rectilinear
motion, curvilinear motion, projectile motion, tangential and normal component
of acceleration, acceleration - time, velocity- time graphs and their uses, relative
velocity

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering

Kinematics of Rigid Bodies

Translation, pure rotation and plane motion of rigid bodies, instantaneous centre
of rotation for the velocity for bodies in plane motion, link mechanisms (up to
two links).

5. | Kinetics of Particles 07
Newton’s laws of motion, D’Alembert’s principle, equation of dynamic
equilibrium, linear motion, curvilinear motion.

Kinetics of Rigid Bodies
D’Alembert’s principle for bodies under translational motion, rotational motion
about a fixed axis and plane motion.

Pre-requisite: Theory of semiconductor materials, their atomic structures and properties DC circuit

Course Objective
The aim of the course is that the student should understand working principle, characteristics and simple
applications of basic electronic devices. The course also helps students to understand the application of
these devices in advanced circuits such as amplifiers. It also intends to impart hands on experience in
assembling and testing simple circuits
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Examine the working of P – N junction diode and its applications
2. Differentiate various configurations and biasing circuits of Bi-polar Junction Transistor
3. Recognize various types of Field Effect Transistors and its configurations
4. Describe various basic digital electronic circuits
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Diodes and Diode Circuits
Formation of P-N junction, energy band diagram, built-in-potential,
forward and reverse biased P-N junction, formation of depletion zone, V-I   08
characteristics, Zener breakdown, Avalanche breakdown and its reverse
characteristics; Junction capacitance and Varactor diode. Simple diode
circuits, load line, linear piecewise model; Rectifier circuits: half wave, full
wave, PIV, DC voltage and current, ripple factor, efficiency, idea of
regulation.
2   Bipolar Junction Transistors
Formation of PNP / NPN junctions, energy band diagram; transistor
mechanism and principle of transistors, CE, CB, CC configuration,   08
transistor characteristics: cut-off active and saturation mode, transistor
action, injection efficiency, base transport factor and current amplification
factors for CB and CE modes. Biasing and Bias stability: calculation of
stability factor.
3   Field Effect Transistors
Concept of Field Effect Transistors (channel width modulation), Gate   08
isolation types, JFET Structure and characteristics, MOSFET Structure and
characteristics, depletion and enhancement   type; CS, CG, CD
configurations; CMOS: Basic Principles
4   Digital Electronics Fundamentals
Difference between analog and digital signals, Logic ICs, half and full   06
adder/subtractor, multiplexers, demultiplexers, flip-flops, shift registers,
counters

Pre-requisite: Probability theory, descriptive statistics, random variables, differentiation and
integration of functions.
Course Objective
This course will help students to develop sound knowledge and skills in theoretical, computational
and application-oriented statistics. The course will equip the students with intermediate to advanced
level concepts in statistics using probability theory and basic concepts in statistics that will help them
to tackle relevant problems within engineering domain.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to-
1. Explain the concepts of sampling techniques, estimation, sufficient statistic parametric and non-
parametric inference
2. Solve problems involving correlation, linear and multiple regression estimation techniques and
time series
3. Apply knowledge of time series, parametric and non-parametric inference to analyze statistical
data
4. Use various concepts in R programming to analyze statistical data samples
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Sampling Techniques
Random sampling, Sampling from finite and infinite populations, Estimates and
standard error (sampling with replacement and sampling without replacement),   03
Sampling distribution of sample mean, stratified random sampling.
2.   Linear Statistical Models
Scatter diagram, Linear regression and correlation, Least squares method, Rank
11
correlation, Multiple regression & multiple correlation, Analysis of variance (one
way, two way with as well as without interaction).
3.   Estimation
Point estimation, criteria for good estimates (un-biasedness, consistency),   04
Methods of estimation including maximum likelihood estimation.
4.   Sufficient Statistic   04
Concept & examples, complete sufficiency, their application in estimation.
5.   Test of hypothesis   10

Comparison with parametric inference, Use of order statistics, Sign test, Wilcoxon
signed rank test, Mann-Whitney test, Run test, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test,
Spearman’s and Kendall’s test, Tolerance region.
7.   Basics of Time Series Analysis & Forecasting   05
Stationary Models, Identification, Estimation and Forecasting.

understanding each layer of computer network architecture, and transmission systems to
network applications. It also focuses on congestion control techniques, protocols, and
application layer functions.

1. Explain the concepts of computer networks, topologies and data communication.
2. Analyze the various error detection and correction and medium access techniques.
3. Apply network layer addressing and routing techniques to different network
topologies.
4. Analyze the different protocols of the layered architecture of computer networks.

This course teaches the fundamentals of secure programming in C. Students will learn how a C

standards and design principles of secure programming are explored so that security can be built-
in the design time to avoid security vulnerabilities.

After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain the fundamentals of secure programming
2. Analyse C programs for security vulnerabilities
3. Implement security attacks

Computer Systems, Secure Programming Design Principles.

Allocation and Access, Eliminating Loop Inefficiencies, reducing Procedure
Calls, Eliminating Unneeded Memory References, Loop Unrolling, Enhancing

security.

Load-time exploitation, Basics of static and dynamic linking.

Stack layout of variadic functions, Exploit the formatted output string and
buffer overflow vulnerabilities.

Path Traversal Vulnerabilities, File I/O deadlock and Race Condition, time of
check and time of use (TOCTOU) vulnerabilities.

Pre-requisite: Basic knowledge of technology
Course Objective
We live in a technology enabled world where data is collected and process as we interact with any
technology product or service. This data is used by the companies to predict our tastes, our habits,
or future possible health problems. This use of data has created a big privacy threat. Various
governments have developed stringent privacy laws like GDPR to protect the privacy of their
citizens. Effective information privacy is very difficult. Globally organizations are approaching
privacy problem based on two concepts: Privacy by design and privacy engineering. In this course
students will be exposed to both the concepts.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Identify data privacy threats and suggest their countermeasures
2. Implement various privacy models
3. Design privacy program for an organization
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   06
Data privacy need and concepts, privacy by design principles, information
privacy requirements and guidelines, information privacy threats and
vulnerabilities, privacy risk assessment, privacy and security control
selection, privacy integration, testing and evaluation, trade-offs between
privacy and security, usable privacy.
2.   Data Privacy Attacks and Models   07
The evolving threat environment, privacy threat taxonomy, NIST threat
model, privacy attacks (Linkage Attack, re-identification Attack, Statistical
Attack), De-identification of direct identifiers,
Basic Privacy Models K- Anonymity, L-Diversity, t-closeness, Differential
Privacy, Generalisation, Suppression, Perturbation, Randomization.
3.   Online Privacy   07
The online eco-system for personal data, online privacy threats, online
privacy requirements, privacy notices and tracking, Privacy Preserving Data
Sharing and Publications, Privacy Preserving Access Control Models.
4.   Information Privacy Management   05
Information privacy governance, privacy roles, privacy program plan, key
areas of privacy management, privacy policy, NIST privacy framework,
OASIS privacy management model, privacy awareness training and
education.

Pre-requisite: Basic Probability Theory and abstract algebra
Course Objective
This course provides an introduction to the elliptic curve cryptography. The course covers the
required mathematical background to understand the ECC. The course will cover the theory of
elliptic curves and its applications.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Implement various cryptographic schemes using elliptic curves, including variants of the
Diffie-Hellman key exchange, the ElGamal public key cryptosystem, and digital signatures
2. Apply techniques of elliptic curves over finite fields to the discrete logarithm problem
3. Survey pairing based cryptosystems on elliptic curves
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to elliptic curves   06
Definition   of   elliptic   curves. Group   law. Endomorphisms and
isomorphisms. j-invariant, Weierstrass and Edwards curves.
2.   Elliptic curves over finite fields   06
Torsion points. Frobenius morphism. Group structure and group order.
Hasse's theorem. Supersingular curves. Discrete logarithm problem.
3.   Elliptic curve cryptosystems   08
Diffie-Hellman key exchange. ElGamal encryption. Schnorr identification.
ECDSA. Bit coin.
4.   Generating elliptic curves for cryptography   06
Schoof's algorithm. Complex multiplication. Pairing based cryptography,
Abstract properties of pairings. Pairing-friendly elliptic curves. Generating
pairing-friendly curves.
5.   Discrete logarithm attacks   04
Baby step-giant step. Pollard rho. Menezes-Okamoto-Vanstone and Frey-
Rück reductions. Anomalous curves.

Course Objective
DevSecOps automatically bakes in security at every phase of the software development lifecycle,
enabling development of secure software at the speed of Agile and DevOps. It is an extension of
standard DevOps practices. It integrates application and infrastructure security seamlessly into
Agile and DevOps processes and tools. It addresses security issues as they emerge, when they're
easier, faster, and less expensive to fix. The primary goal of this course is to create a theory and
practice mix that emphasizes on the core concepts of DevSecOps, Docker containers and
Kubernetes clustering from a security, monitoring, and administration perspective.

Pre-requisite: Digital Forensics Fundamentals
Course Objective
Image and video evidence is a growing concern during an investigation as more and more of our
lives are captured in some form. From cell phones to CCTV security cameras in public places to
cell phone cameras, our everyday activities are constantly being recorded. This evidence, when
properly collected and analysed, can be crucial in solving crimes. This course will introduce
students to the concepts of video and image forensics. The course will cover how to properly
identify, collect, and handle digital video and image evidence in a way that maintains evidence
integrity and is consistent with best practices in the field.
Course Outcomes
After successful completion of the course, student would be able to -
1. Forensically extract image and video evidence from given media
2. Perform image and video authentication and detect tampering
3. Create and detect deepfake
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   4
Image and Video as legal evidence and related issues, principles of forensic
analysis of digital images and video, protocols and guidelines related to
collection, recovery, enhancement, analysis, and interpretation of image and
video evidence.
2.   Fundamentals of image and video processing and analytics   8
Basic concepts, image and video formats and standards, Overview of technical
issues related to video recordings (Data losses and impairments, visual
distortions and artefacts, video quality evaluation metrics) Various categories
of digital videos, based on the kind of recording device, placement of the
camera, mode of capture, and environmental conditions at the time of
recording, video analytics algorithms.
3.   Image and Video Authentication and Tamper Detection   12
Image and Video Source and Content Authentication, basic Tamper Detection
and their limitations (Hash value analysis, Hex editor analysis, Metadata
analysis, and Error Level Analysis (ELA)), Study of various methods of digital
image and video manipulation and their detection techniques (i.e., various
kinds of forgeries such as copy paste aka splicing, object removal forgeries,
upscale-crop, and resampling, frame-based tampering, Re-compression and
transcoding detection, etc.)
4.   Deepfake Detection   6
Introduction to deepfake technology, deepfake creation process and detection
methods.
Total   30

Pre-requisite: Fundamental Knowledge of Cybersecurity
Course Objective
Technical challenges of the cybersecurity are better understood as compared to human challenges.
Cybersecurity is fundamentally a problem of human interaction with technology. This course
provides an overview of human interactions with cybersecurity technology, from users to system
designers. This course looks at application of theories from other domains like economics and
behavioural science to the cybersecurity context.
Course Outcomes
After successful completion of the course, student would be able to -
1. Apply various theories from other domains to cybersecurity decision making
2. Apply game theory to cybersecurity context
3. Design cybersecurity awareness campaign using marketing and behavioural theories
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Economics   6
Classical and Behavioural economics, asymmetric information, auction theory,
the economics of security and dependability, application of Kahneman-Tversky
approach to cybersecurity, Heuristics and biases in cybersecurity decision
making.
2. Game Theory and Cybersecurity   8
Introduction, payoff, matrix games, mixed strategy, Saddle point, dominated
strategies, applications of game theory to cybersecurity.
3.   Personality Theory and Cybersecurity   5
Personality traits and cybersecurity, Profiling in the cybersecurity context,
profiling matrices, ABCD Analysis
4.   Marketing and Communications for Cybersecurity Awareness Campaign   6
The communication conundrum,   similarity between marketing and
cybersecurity awareness campaigns, tracking   results and measuring
effectiveness.
5.   Behaviour Management for Security Awareness Leaders   5
System 1 and System 2 thinking, working with human nature, Fogg Behaviour
Model, Nudge and frames, designing and debugging behaviour, tracking
results and measuring effectiveness.
Total   30

IoT technologies, including privacy disclosure and data manipulation’s Internet of things

unique identities and are connected to the internet to facilitate intelligent applications that
make energy, logistics, industrial control, retail, agriculture and many other domains. This

IoT technologies, including privacy disclosure and data manipulation.

Pre-requisite: Basic knowledge of technology
Course Objective
We live in a technology enabled world where data is collected and process as we interact
with any technology product or service. This data is used by the companies to predict our
tastes, our habits, or future possible health problems. This use of data has created a big
privacy threat. Various governments have developed stringent privacy laws like GDPR to
protect the privacy of their citizens. Effective information privacy is very difficult. Globally
organizations are approaching privacy problem based on two concepts: Privacy by design
and privacy engineering. In this course students will be exposed to both the concepts.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Identify data privacy threats and suggest their countermeasures
2. Implement various privacy models
3. Design privacy program for an organization
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   06
Data privacy need and concepts, privacy by design principles,
information privacy requirements and guidelines, information privacy
threats and vulnerabilities, privacy risk assessment, privacy and
security control selection, privacy integration, testing and evaluation,
trade-offs between privacy and security, usable privacy.
2.   Data Privacy Attacks and Models   07
The evolving threat environment, privacy threat taxonomy, NIST threat
model, privacy attacks (Linkage Attack, re-identification Attack,
Statistical Attack), De-identification of direct identifiers,
Basic Privacy Models K- Anonymity, L-Diversity, t-closeness,
Differential Privacy, Generalisation, Suppression, Perturbation,
Randomization.
3.   Online Privacy   07
The online eco-system for personal data, online privacy threats, online
privacy requirements, privacy notices and tracking, Privacy Preserving
Data Sharing and Publications, Privacy Preserving Access Control
Models.
4.   Information Privacy Management   05
Information privacy governance, privacy roles, privacy program plan,
key areas of privacy management, privacy policy, NIST privacy
framework, OASIS privacy management model, privacy awareness
training and education.

theory of elliptic curves and its applications.

1. Implement various cryptographic schemes using elliptic curves, including variants
of the Diffie-Hellman key exchange, the ElGamal public key cryptosystem, and
digital signatures

isomorphisms. j-invariant, Weierstrass and Edwards curves.

principles. The students would have knowledge of concept of ‘State’ and interdependencies of

Course Objective:
This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus. This
course will help the students achieve sound understanding of the concepts of calculus, develop
problem solving skills and apply the concepts and techniques of calculus to solve problems within
Engineering domain. This course will equip the students with intermediate to advanced level
concepts and aligned tools to help them tackle advanced mathematics and related applications.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the fundamental concepts of differential calculus for functions of one variable,
including limits, derivatives, Mean Value Theorems, Taylor and Maclaurin series, and
LHospital’s rule. (K2)
2. Solve problems involving functions of several variables using partial differentiation, Taylor
series expansion, and techniques for finding maxima and minima, including Lagrange’s
method of undetermined multipliers. (K3)
3. Use Beta and Gamma functions to solve problems in single-variable calculus. (K2)
4. Compute and interpret double and triple integrals, including change of variables and
coordinate transformations, and apply them to determine areas and volumes. (K3)
5. Examine vector functions using gradient, divergence, curl, and scalar potential and apply
fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to
evaluate integrals. (K3)
6. Integrate concepts from differential, integral, and vector calculus to formulate and solve real-
world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences. (K3)

Pre-requisite: Linear Algebra and Ordinary Differential Equations
Course Objective
The principal objective of the course is to develop students' logical reasoning and problem-solving
skills by introducing fundamental concepts of discrete mathematics essential for computer science
and engineering applications. It provides a strong foundation in set theory, logic, combinatorics,
graph theory, and abstract algebra, enabling students to analyze and construct mathematical
arguments. Through the study of proof techniques, recurrence relations, and discrete structures,
students will gain the ability to model computational problems and prove the correctness of
algorithms. The course also highlights the practical applications of discrete mathematics in real-
world contexts, such as data structures, cryptography, network security, and algorithm design,
equipping students for advanced studies and careers in computing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Apply fundamental concepts of set theory, relations, and functions to solve mathematical
and computational problems.
2. Construct valid mathematical arguments using propositional and predicate logic, proof
techniques, and induction methods.
3. Analyze combinatorial structures and recurrence relations to model and solve discrete
problems in engineering applications.
4. Implement graph and tree algorithms to solve optimization and network-related problems.
5. Demonstrate an understanding of abstract algebraic structures and their applications in
coding theory.

Course Objective
This course provides an introduction to time series analysis. It will educate students on how to choose an
appropriate forecasting method in a particular environment and then apply it using necessary computations.

for analyzing time series data. It will also provide directions to Improve forecasting using better statistical
models based on statistical analysis
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –

autocorrelation, and visualize them using various plotting techniques.

diagnostics to identify appropriate forecasting models.

reconciliation methods and compare with alternative approaches.
5. Design advanced forecasting solutions using complex seasonality, the Prophet model, VARs,
bootstrapping, and bagging on real-world datasets using statistical software.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year
students’ learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate
with the required practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think
critically, solve challenging problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral
communication skills, teamwork and planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary
areas which will help broaden their scope and learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the
research gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design
and fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop
algorithms and verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be
required to submit a report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation,
analysis functional simulation and synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her
work carried out before examiners.

Pre-requisite: Fundamental knowledge of physics, chemistry, and mathematics.
Course Objective:
To introduce students to modern biology with an emphasis on the evolution of biology as a multi-
disciplinary field, to make them aware of the application of engineering principles in biology. This
will encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems with engineering
tools. They will also be exposed to the application of engineering principles in biology and
engineering robust solutions inspired by biological examples.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Identify the principles of biomimicry and explain their applications in engineering and
sustainable design, demonstrating an understanding of biologically inspired solutions. (K1)
2. Classify the fundamental building blocks of life (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic
acids) and describe their structural and functional roles in cellular processes and metabolism.
(K2)
3. Explain the molecular basis of genetic information transfer, including DNA replication,
transcription, and translation, and interpret Mendel's laws and their significance in genetics. (K2)
4. Describe the mechanisms of enzyme action, enzyme-substrate interactions, and enzyme
inhibition, and discuss their industrial and biological applications. (K2)
5. Explain the principles of metabolism and energy transactions, and categorize microorganisms
based on their characteristics, growth kinetics, and applications in biotechnology and drug
discovery. (K1)
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Biomimicry
Applications of biology in engineering. Biology as an independent scientific
discipline. Importance of studying biology. Various applications of biology.   06
Biologically inspired engineering. Biomimicry in engineering uses designs,
processes, and ecosystems. Sustainable engineering.
2.   The fundamental building blocks of life
Unity in diversity of life, Molecules of life. Structure and functions of   04
carbohydrates, amino acids, proteins, and lipids. Hierarchy in protein structure.

Engineering Graphics; mainly visualization & conventions of drawing, the tools of
drawing and the use of drawings in engineering applications. The course has been
structured to include sufficient simulations which would aid the student in visualization
of three-dimensional objects and developing the drawing.

planes using drawing instruments.

of solids using AutoCAD software.

orthographic views with the help of AutoCAD software

isometric drawing using AutoCAD software.

hexagon, circle), plane surface inclined to one reference plane

Introduction, types of solids; Projections of regular solids (prisms,
pyramids) covering those inclined to one reference plane
4.   Orthographic Projections   02
Principles of orthographic projections using 1st angle method of
projections, conventions used in quadrant formation, conversion of
isometric models to orthographic views, orthographic views of
geometrical solids and objects from industry.

Pre-requisite: Physics, Chemistry, Mathematics
Course Objective
The aim of this course is to foster a holistic understanding of the composition and working of the Earth
and be able to differentiate between minerals, rock types and landscape types with reference to their
genesis. Also, the course focuses on the application of plate tectonic theory to differentiate structural
features in rocks, decipher seismicity probabilities and predict geological hazards, fundamentals of
Geo-Economics and use geological principles in Civil Engineering.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Differentiate between Earth materials, Earth processes and landscapes
2. Explain structural geology and tectonics
3. Discuss natural disasters based on geological parameters
4. Test and interpret Earth Materials
5. Test and interpret Geological Maps
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Geology   01
Theories of the formation of the Earth; Compositional layering and the internal
structure of the Earth, Rock Cycle; Carbon Cycle; work of Geological Survey of
India
2   Mineralogy and Physical Geology   08
Introduction to minerals, Bowen’s Reaction Series, physical properties; common
rock forming mineral classes; introduction to crystallography, mineral
Provinces, fundamentals of economic geology, India’s mineral deposits,
weathering and Erosion, Types, factors and products of erosion and deposition;
work of running water, sea, wind, glacier, groundwater, aquifer types, recharge
3   Igneous Petrology   05
Depth-wise classification of igneous rocks, Volcanic eruption types and ejected
materials, Concept of hot springs and geysers, Magma types, Basis of expressing
Igneous texture, Types of igneous textures, Igneous intrusive and extrusive
structures, common igneous rocks like Basalt, Granite, Mantle generated rocks
Sedimentary Petrology
Modes of formation of sedimentary rocks, Mineralogical composition of
sedimentary rocks, Basis of expressing sedimentary textures, Types of
sedimentary textures, Sedimentary structures, Classification of sedimentary
rocks, Sedimentary Facies and Provenance, Common sedimentary rocks like
Sandstone, Limestone, Breccia, Fossiliferous rocks

SVKM’s Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
Metamorphic Petrology
Agents of metamorphism, Types of metamorphism, Metamorphic grades and
facies, Metamorphic textures, structures, common metamorphic rocks like schists,
gneisses, marble.
4   Structural Geology   06
Folds, Faults, Joints, Unconformities: Types, classification
Geological maps: fundamentals, symbols and basic interpretation
Introduction to cartography; Introduction to ArcGIS, QGIS
5   Plate tectonic theory   03
Evolution of the theory of plate tectonics
Types of plate movements
Plate Tectonic Theory Case Studies: Himalayas, Andes, New Zealand, Atlantic
Ocean
6   Historical Geology   02
Stratigraphy: Theories, Deccan Basalt, Cuddapah, Vidhyan, Himalayas,Theories
of mass extinction and Ice Ages
7   Geological Hazards and Exploration   05
Types, Causes, mitigation, Case Studies for landslides, Earthquakes, Tsunami,
Floods: Direct and Indirect methods of Geophysical exploration, Site selection,
geological considerations and hazards; Case Studies of dams, reservoirs and
tunnels
Total   30

Course Objectives:
The objective of this course is to teach the limitations of classical physics in explaining several
experimental facts leading to the development of quantum physics. Also, this course will
expose the students to different applications of quantum mechanics, such as quantum
tunneling and quantum computation.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Understand the need for Quantum mechanics (K2)
2. Explain the basic laws related to quantum mechanics and apply them to solve
related problems. (K3)
3. Apply the concept of quantum mechanics to real-life instrumentation and applications.
(K3)
4. Understand the requirement of quantum computation and its various aspects. (K2)
5. Gauge the theoretical principles through laboratory experimentation, enhancing problem-
solving abilities and technical proficiency in modern physics applications. (K3)

Introduction to Quantum Physics, Black body radiation, Explanation of it
using the photon concept, Photoelectric effect, Compton effect, de Broglie
hypothesis, Experiments demonstrating wave properties of electron: Electron   6
interference (double slit experiment), Electron Diffraction (Davison - Germer
experiment), Uncertainty Principle, Verification of matter waves.

interpretation of the wave function, Superposition principle of eigenstates.
Concept of collapse of wave function. Time-dependent and time-
2
independent Schrodinger Equation.
Concept of the free particle, particle in an infinite and finite potential well,
box problem. Bound vs. unbound states.

principles of justice, equality, and liberty as enshrined in the Preamble of the Constitution.

Course Objective

understanding and application of file and directory management, process management, text
manipulation, and permissions. Focuses on shell scripting for process automation, configuration
and process management, and security applications. Emphasizes hands-on experience securing
and hardening the Linux operating system.

Pre-requisite: Principles of Economics –I, II
Course Objective
This course seeks to equip students from all backgrounds with a basic understanding of the
international business environment and the fundamentals of international business strategy. In
addition, this course aims to develop the following skills in students
•   Critical thinking
•   Collaboration and teamwork
• Research and writing skills
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain how differences between countries create additional challenges for firms doing
business internationally
2. Explain how firms can create value by doing business internationally
3. Identify key decisions related to foreign market selection, market entry modes, and
international strategy that firms need to make when going international
4. Apply theoretical frameworks to make informed recommendations for such firms
5. Describe how foreign exchange markets work; derive business/economic implications
6. Evaluate arguments for and against government restrictions on trade and investment;
derive business/economic implications
7. Identify ethical challenges related to international business
8. Explain long-run trends and development in the international business environment;
derive business/economic implications.

why companies do business internationally and how this can create

face when going international. How these general principles apply to

Course Objective

bonding of elements .To introduce electromagnetic spectrum ranges converted to different
technologies used for various applications. To acquaint with concepts of electrochemistry and basic
organic reactions. To study important engineering materials and management of e-waste.

1. Explain the foundational knowledge of the subject using chemistry principles

environment

3   Electrochemistry   6

equation, Applicability of Nernst equation
4   Important Engineering Materials   6

performance of algorithms. Devise efficient algorithms in common engineering design situations.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe the importance of space-time complexity of an algorithm

3. Analyse dynamic programming and Backtracking design paradigm

shortest path Bellman Ford algorithm, All pairs shortest paths: Floyd's

completeness & NP hard problems.

Pre-requisite: Statistics and Probability, Calculus
Course Objective
Stochastic Processes and Applications refers to skills, practices and techniques used in
stochastic systems found in several real life applications. This discipline consists of an
understanding of stochastic systems and their applications in wide array of business situations
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand and apply the foundational concepts of probability theory, including
axiomatic probability, random variables, probability distributions, expectation,
convergence of random variables, and laws of large numbers. (L2-Understanding and
L3- Applying)
2. Utilize mathematical tools such as generating functions and transforms to analyze the
behavior of random variables and sequences. (L3- Applying and L4-Analyzing)
3. Classify and analyze different types of stochastic processes, including discrete-time
and continuous-time processes, based on their state and parameter spaces. (L2-
Understanding and L4-Analyzing)
4. Apply and analyse real-world phenomena using discrete-time Markov chains,
compute transition probabilities, classify states, and determine long-run behaviors
including stationary distributions. (L3- Applying and L4-Analyzing)
5. Apply and evaluate the problems involving continuous-time Markov chains, including
Poisson and birth-death processes, using Kolmogorov equations and infinitesimal
generators. (L3- Applying and L5- Evaluating)

Pre-requisite: Managing Uncertainty (SEM - III)
Course Objective
This course aims at giving the foundation knowledge Statistical Inference and regression analysis.
In particular, it gives details of theory of Estimation and testing of hypothesis. Both theoretical
aspect will be discussed and practical problems will be dealt with in great detail. In this course
the students also learn different models for categorical data such as Generalized Linear, logit,
logistic and log linear models
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Recall fundamental concepts of confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and maximum
likelihood estimation (MLE) (L1- Remembering)
2. Explain the likelihood function, maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) across various
distributions (Binomial, Multinomial, Gaussian), and apply the continuous version of
Bayes' theorem. (L2 -Understanding and L3- Applying)
3. Perform hypothesis testing using Z-tests, t-tests, and Chi-square tests for independence
and goodness of fit, including interpretation of p-values, Type I and Type II errors. (L3-
Applying and L4 – Analyzing)
4. Interpret generalized linear models (GLMs) such as logistic regression for binary outcomes,
including log-odds interpretation and model diagnostics. (L2-Understanding)
5. Perform and interpret Ridge and Lasso regression for feature selection with Python
implementations and visualizations (L4-Analyzing)
6. Evaluate and create advanced statistical models, including logistic regression for binary
outcomes and non-parametric tests (Sign Test, Rank Sum Test, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman
tests), with Python implementations and visualizations. (L5 – Evaluating and L6-Creating)

The interaction of data science and technology with the world is via signal processing: detecting,
transcoding, understanding and generating time-dependent and space-dependent signals in the
broadest sense. Data is rich and abundant. However, every data wrangler has come across most
of the time this data, which is very noisy in nature. Processing noisy signals and filtering
unwanted part from an image has been a huge concern over the last few decades. Signal and
image processing techniques developed today are very robust and effective models. The objective
is to port some processing techniques from the audio and signal field and use them to process
data. To give basic mathematical understanding of transformation for image and signal

4. List the fundamental concepts in Image representation and state basic filtering techniques

automata, closure properties of CFLs.

Context-sensitive grammars (CSG) and languages, linear bounded
automata and equivalence with CSG.

(recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages
and   their closure properties, variants of Turing machines,

diagonalization languages, reduction between languages and Rice s

Introductory ideas on Time complexity of deterministic and
nondeterministic Turing machines, P and NP, NP- completeness,

The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year students’
learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with the required
practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically, solve challenging
problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication skills, teamwork and
planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope and
learning in different domains.

research gaps (L1- Remembering)

fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and verify

Pre-requisite: Fundamental knowledge of physics, chemistry, and mathematics.

Course Objective:
To introduce students to modem biology with an emphasis on evolution of biology as a multi-disciplinary

field, to make them aware of application of engineering principles in biology. This will encourage engineering
students to think about solving biological problems with engineering tools. They will also be exposed to the
application of engineering principles in biology and engineering robust solutions, inspired by biological

examples.

Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Identify key principles of biomimicry and develop engineering solutions for different fields

2. Classify microorganisms and their molecular properties and analyze the role of DNA as genetic
material in transferring information among living organisms

3. Describe the fundamental building blocks of life, including carbohydrates, amino acids, proteins,
and lipids, and illustrate their functions in cellular processes and metabolism

Course Objective
The course would enable students to get a brief introduction of the Indian Constitution and
its principles. The students would have knowledge of concept of   ‘State’ and
interdependencies of its institutions vis a vis their relation with fundamental rights.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the historic evolution of the Indian Constitution, its drafting, nature and
to understand the principles mentioned in its Preamble
2. Inculcate fundamental rights in its true sense and also the permissible restrictions
upon it so as to enjoy these rights within permissible limits while simultaneously
performing their duties and to apply these principles into their professional lives
3. Ingrain the structure of our polity and role of Judiciary in maintaining the basic
structure of the Constitution
4. Attain knowledge of the Emergency provisions, when and how it is imposed, to know
the additional powers the bestowed upon the Government at times of Emergency and
to understand the Amendment procedure

astronomy. To enhance the student’s ability to apply the above principles of Physics in solving
engineering problems related to everyday life.

applications.

Pre-requisite: Nil
Course Objective
This course provides basic orientation towards macroeconomic principles and help them
understand the functions of economy at Macro level. To combine elements of basic variables of
macroeconomics. To familiarize with importance of macroeconomic approach in managing
economy. To understand the application of macroeconomic theories at aggregate level. To
emphasize the role of macroeconomic policies and analyse their implication for economy along
with international linkages.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Learn various macroeconomic variables, circular flow of income and their linkages to macro
economy
2. Analyze aggregates of macroeconomics and understand goods market and money market,
Indian Financial System, Business fluctuations and Stabilization Policies
3. Orient oneself towards higher levels of learning related to economic planning, international
trade, foreign exchange market and international organizations at macro level
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Macroeconomics   03
Meaning, Nature & Scope and importance   of Macroeconomics,
Interdependence   between   Microeconomics &   Macroeconomics,
macroeconomics goals, major issues and concerns of macroeconomics.
2   Structure of Macroeconomics   03
Subject matter of Macroeconomics, Structure of Macro Economy, Different
sectors of the economy, Circular Flow of Income & Product, Leakages &
Injections in the Circular Flow.
3   Keynes’s Theory of Employment   03
Principles of effective demand, aggregate demand function, aggregate supply
function, determination of equilibrium level of employment-Effective
demand.
4   Macroeconomic Aggregates   03
Aggregate Consumption- component of consumption, determinant of
consumption, consumption function, Saving function, Capital formation-
component of investment, determinant of investment, investment function
and investment multiplier.
5   Goods Market and Money Market (IS-LM Curves Model)   03
B. Tech CSE (DS) – 311 (VT)/SEM III/AY 2024-25/Page 4
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
Introduction to Goods Market and Money Market and links between them,
Goods Market equilibrium- derivation of IS Curve, Money market
equilibrium- derivation of LM Curve, Equilibrium of goods Market and
Money Market, critique of IS-LM Curves model.
6   Inflation – Unemployment Trade-off (Philips Curve)   03
Types and causes of unemployment, Unemployment situation in India,
policy measures to solve unemployment problem in India, Inflation- meaning
and types, effects of Inflation on distribution of income & wealth and on
output & growth, methods to control Inflation, Unemployment and Inflation-
The Philips Curve, causes of shift in Philips Curve, relation between short-
run Philips Curve and long-run Philips Curve.
7   Indian Financial System   03
Credit and Commercial Banking- meaning and functions, purposes, roles of
commercial banks in economic development, credit creation and limitations
on the credit creating power of the banks, Central Banking- principles and
functions of commercial banking, methods of credit control by central bank
for economic prosperity.
8   Analysis of Business Cycle   03
Phases of Business Cycle, Features of Business Cycle, Theories of Business
Cycle, Business Cycle and Indian Economy in post-liberalization era.
9   Economic Stabilization Policy- Monetary Policy   03
Tools of Monetary policy, expansionary monetary policy to cure recession,
monetary policy to control inflation, liquidity trap and effectiveness of
monetary policy, tight monetary policy, RBI’s Monetary policy in India and
its critical evaluation.
10   Economic Stabilization Policy- Fiscal policy I   03
Tools of Fiscal policy- Public Finance, Public Expenditure, Taxation.
11   Economic Stabilization Policy- Fiscal policy II   03
Introduction and importance of Budget in Economy, Indian Budgeting
System, Budget Deficit and Government Borrowing, Crowding-out effect and
effectiveness of Fiscal Policy.
12   Economic Planning and Policy   03
Rational, Features and Objectives of Economic Planning, Strategies of India’s
Developmental Plans, Assessment of India’s planning, Export-Import Policy,
Evaluation of latest Foreign Trade Policy of India.
13   International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism   03
International Trade, Reasons for International Trade, Absolute Cost Theory,
Comparative Cost Theory, Free Trade versus Protection, Cases for Protection,
Foreign Capital and Foreign Aid.
14   Foreign Exchange and Foreign Exchange Market   003
India’s Exchange Rate Policy, Foreign Exchange Reserve, Exchange Rate
Regimes, Exchange Rate Management in India, Capital Account
Convertibility.
15   International Organizations   03

linear programming and optimization techniques.

Course Objective
To develop an understanding of essential database concepts. To understand different issues

with modeling, designing and implementation To understand the need of data analytics and

Pre-requisite: Principles of Economics –I, II
Course Objective
This course seeks to equip students from all backgrounds with a basic understanding of the
international business environment and the fundamentals of international business strategy. In
addition, this course aims to develop the following skills in students
   Critical thinking
   Collaboration and teamwork
 Research and writing skills
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain how differences between countries create additional challenges for firms doing
business internationally
2. Explain how firms can create value by doing business internationally
3. Identify key decisions related to foreign market selection, market entry modes, and
international strategy that firms need to make when going international
4. Apply theoretical frameworks to make informed recommendations for such firms
5. Describe how foreign exchange markets work; derive business/economic implications
6. Evaluate arguments for and against government restrictions on trade and investment;
derive business/economic implications
7. Identify ethical challenges related to international business
8. Explain long-run trends and development in the international business environment;
derive business/economic implications.

social characteristics – and how this matters for international business.

markets,

differences, Foreign exchange rates
3   International business strategy   8
why companies do business internationally and how this can create
