foreign markets and discuss the main challenges and decisions firms
face when going international. How these general principles apply to

Pre-requisite: HSC level Chemistry
Course Objective
To familiarize with atomic structure, periodicity of elements in periodic table and chemical
bonding of elements .To introduce electromagnetic spectrum ranges converted to different
technologies used for various applications. To acquaint with concepts of electrochemistry and basic
organic reactions. To study important engineering materials and management of e-waste.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain the foundational knowledge of the subject using chemistry principles
2. Identify newer chemical materials for better product designing
3. Analyze the impact of science and its progress on society and provide solution for cleaner
environment
4. Evaluate the various aspects of chemistry to convert into useful applications.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Atomic structure and Periodic properties of elements   8
Study of atom structure with reference to Bohr’s model, wave particle
duality, Schrodinger wave equation. Concept of valency and electronic
configuration. Explanation of Aufbau principle, Hund’s rule and Pauli’s
Exclusion Principle that helps in writing electronic configuration.
Introduction to Modern periodic table, Nomenclature of s, p, d, f group
elements. Trends in physical properties: effective nuclear charge, atomic
radii, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity. Concept of
semiconductors and metalloids. Concept of acids and bases.
2   Chemical bonding   6
Intermolecular forces: Ionic, covalent, co-ordinate bonds and types of
intramolecular interactions (with one example for each type). Introduction to
co-ordination chemistry and Co-ordination number, magnetism of the co-
ordinate complexes.
3   Electrochemistry   6
Concept of electrochemical cell & electrolytic cell. Cell potential, EMF of Cell,
Relation of free energy with EMF of cell, Faraday’s law, Derivation of Nernst
equation, Applicability of Nernst equation
4   Important Engineering Materials   6
Nanomaterials: Structure, properties, applications of CNTs, Fullerenes,
Graphite.
Liquid Crystals: Definition, classification, properties with applications.

Polymers: Introduction to polymers and polymerization mechanisms, Types
of polymers, Specialty polymers like Conducting polymers, Self-healing
polymers with applications.
5   Spectroscopic techniques and Applications   6
General idea on Electromagnetic radiation, Basic Principle of Spectroscopy,
UV-Visible Spectroscopy & applications, IR Spectroscopy & applications,
Nuclear magnetic resonance & applications. MRI applications in medicine.
8   Environmental Chemistry   2
E-waste management: Definition, classification and management of e-waste
in India with reference to Environment (Protection) Act.
9   Solutions and Stoichiometry   5
Types of solutions and its characteristics, properties of aqueous solutions,
different units for expressing concentration of solutions (ppm, ppb,
normality, molarity, molality, mole fraction of solute, mass fraction of solute
and solvent), empirical and molecular formula from elemental composition,
numerical based on empirical formula, normality, molarity, molality
molarity.
10   Organic Reactions   6
Basic organic reactions like- addition reactions, elimination reactions,
substitution reactions, pericyclic reactions, rearrangement reactions,
photochemical reactions and redox reactions.
Specific Reactions of functional groups containing oxygen (-COOH, -OH, -
CHO, -C=O); Nucleophilic substitution reaction, Elimination reaction.
Organic Name Reactions E.g. Aldol & related reactions.

performance of algorithms. Devise efficient algorithms in common engineering design situations.

Course Objective
This course aims at giving the foundation knowledge Statistical Inference and regression analysis.
In particular, it gives details of theory of Estimation and testing of hypothesis. Both theoretical
aspect will be discussed and practical problems will be dealt with in great detail. In this course
the students also learn different models for categorical data such as Generalized Linear, logit,
logistic and log linear models
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Define parametric and non-parametric models
2. Interpret the notion of a parametric models, point and interval estimation of the parameters
of those models
3. Apply Linear, Logistic and Non-linear regression models and its implementation in real life
situation

Course Objective
The interaction of data science and technology with the world is via signal processing: detecting,
transcoding, understanding and generating time-dependent and space-dependent signals in the
broadest sense. Data is rich and abundant. However, every data wrangler has come across most
of the time this data, which is very noisy in nature. Processing noisy signals and filtering
unwanted part from an image has been a huge concern over the last few decades. Signal and
image processing techniques developed today are very robust and effective models. The objective
is to port some processing techniques from the audio and signal field and use them to process
data. To give basic mathematical understanding of transformation for image and signal
processing and sampling To introduce elementary concepts of LTI system, convolution.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Classify discrete and continuous data signals and learn the engineering mathematical aspect
of it and perform operations on it
2. Model finite impulse and infinite impulse response filters
3. Simplify the concepts of Convolution and Sampling to solve and support problems
4. List the fundamental concepts in Image representation and state basic filtering techniques to
facilitate noise removal

Course Objective
This course will help students learn to evaluate and apply design principles and human
factors to apparel, housing and residential technologies and other consumer products.
Exploring the use and design of products through history, in different cultures, and by
diverse users adds to the knowledge base for all consumers. This course is to sensitize the
students about the Design domain and help them collaborate with designers in their professional
practice.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Identify and discuss design principles and elements and their application to consumer
products for diverse users, such as apparel, housing and residential technologies
2. Explain the historical and cultural context of design and consumer products through pre-
industrial and industrial periods and modern era
3. Apply interpretive strategies or methodologies in design
4. Discuss the design process and the importance of diverse user needs in the creation of
consumer products

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year
students’ learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate
with the required practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think
critically, solve challenging problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral
communication skills, teamwork and planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary
areas which will help broaden their scope and learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the
research gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design
and fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop
algorithms and verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be
required to submit a report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation,
analysis functional simulation and synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her
work carried out before examiners.

Course Objective
This course provides basic orientation towards macroeconomic principles and help them
understand the functions of economy at Macro level. To combine elements of basic variables
of macroeconomics. To familiarize with importance of macroeconomic approach in
managing economy. To understand the application of macroeconomic theories at aggregate
level. To emphasize the role of macroeconomic policies and analyse their implication for
economy along with international linkages.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Learn various macroeconomic variables, circular flow of income and their linkages
to macro economy
2. Analyze aggregates of macroeconomics and understand goods market and money
market, Indian Financial System, Business fluctuations and Stabilization Policies
3. Orient oneself towards higher levels of learning related to economic planning,
international trade, foreign exchange market and international organizations at
macro level
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Macroeconomics   03
Meaning, Nature & Scope and importance of Macroeconomics,
Interdependence between Microeconomics & Macroeconomics,
macroeconomics goals, major issues and concerns of macroeconomics.
2   Structure of Macroeconomics   03
Subject matter of Macroeconomics, Structure of Macro Economy,
Different sectors of the economy, Circular Flow of Income & Product,
Leakages & Injections in the Circular Flow.
3   Keynes’s Theory of Employment   03
Principles of effective demand, aggregate demand function, aggregate
supply function, determination of equilibrium level of employment-
Effective demand.
4   Macroeconomic Aggregates   03
Aggregate Consumption- component of consumption, determinant of
consumption, consumption   function, Saving   function, Capital
formation- component of investment, determinant of investment,
investment function and investment multiplier.
5   Goods Market and Money Market (IS-LM Curves Model)   03

meaning and types, effects of Inflation on distribution of income &
wealth and on output & growth, methods to control Inflation,
Unemployment and Inflation- The Philips Curve, causes of shift in
Philips Curve, relation between short-run Philips Curve and long-run
Philips Curve.

Credit and Commercial Banking- meaning and functions, purposes,
roles of commercial banks in economic development, credit creation
and limitations on the credit creating power of the banks, Central
Banking- principles and functions of commercial banking, methods of
credit control by central bank for economic prosperity.

Business Cycle, Business Cycle and Indian Economy in post-
liberalization era.

Tools of Monetary policy, expansionary monetary policy to cure
recession, monetary policy to control inflation, liquidity trap and
effectiveness of   monetary policy, tight monetary policy, RBI’s
Monetary policy in India and its critical evaluation.

Tools of Fiscal policy- Public Finance, Public Expenditure, Taxation.

Introduction and importance of Budget in Economy, Indian Budgeting
System, Budget Deficit and Government Borrowing, Crowding-out
effect and effectiveness of Fiscal Policy.
12 Economic Planning and Policy   03
Rational, Features and Objectives of Economic Planning, Strategies of
India’s Developmental Plans, Assessment of India’s planning, Export-
Import Policy, Evaluation of latest Foreign Trade Policy of India.
13   International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism   03
International Trade, Reasons for International Trade, Absolute Cost
Theory, Comparative Cost Theory, Free Trade versus Protection, Cases
for Protection, Foreign Capital and Foreign Aid.

rapidly that is Big Data, most of the time (about 70%) is spent on data gathering, data cleaning and making

hands-on training for data cleaning and know the theory of ETL (Extract, Transform, and Load) process. To

wrangling and sharing

Pre-requisite: Basic Knowledge of Computer Network, Operating Systems and programming
Course Objective
To impart knowledge to Critically assess organisation's security and be able to apply managerial,
technical, operational security controls to improve organisation's security.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Identify and apply key elements of managerial and operational security practice
2. Analyse and evaluate a company of your choosing and compile a formal risk assessment of
your analysis, findings, and suggest actions for the company to take through interpretation
of your findings
3. Identify key elements of technical security and be able to explain how they function and
how and where they may be usefully applied
4. Use technical security software and identify how and where it may be usefully applied
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Information Security
Overview, definition, information security concepts, threats, vulnerabilities
and security controls, attack (active and passive attacks) with examples,   5
security design principles, methods of defenses, security policies and its
types, legal and ethical aspect
2   Cryptography
Cryptography basics, transposition and substitution ciphers, symmetric and
asymmetric cryptographic algorithms (AES, Diffie Hellman, and RSA),   7
stream and block ciphers, key management, digital signature, hash functions,
Attacks on cryptosystems.
3   Program Security
Secure programs, Non malicious Program Errors, malicious software,   4
database security, countermeasures.
4   User Authentication   2
Authentication   basics,   factors   of   authentication, password based
authentication, token based authentication, biometric authentication, remote
user authentication, security issues
5   Access control   3
Access control principles, discretionary access control, mandatory access
control, role based access control, identity, credential, and access
management, trust frameworks
6   Security Technologies   5
Firewalls, types of Firewalls, Filtering Services, DMZ, Implementing policies
(Default allow, Default Deny) on proxy, NAT, Intrusion Detection and

Pre-requisite: Programming for Problem Solving, Data structures
Course Objective
To develop an understanding of essential database concepts. To understand different issues
involved in the design and implementation of a database systems. To understand and use database
query languages to access and manage a database. To design and build a simple database system
with modeling, designing and implementation To understand the need of data analytics and
advanced database systems like data warehouse and data mining
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe the terminology, features and basic concepts of database systems
2. Formulate queries using structured query language and relational algebra
3. Design a model expressed in the form of an entity relationship diagram and transform it into a
relational model
4. Demonstrate an understanding of normalization theory, transactions and need for data analytics
and advanced database models
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Database Management Systems   3
Role and advantages of the DBMS, Types of Databases, Importance of database
design, Evolution of file system, Problems with file system, Database System
environment, DBMS functions, Data models, importance of data models, types
of data models, Data abstraction (Book   : “Database System Design,
Implementation, and Management”, Carlos Coronel, Steven Morris, Peter Bob)
2   Introduction to Relational Model   4
Structure of relational databases- relation, attribute, tuple, domain, Codd’s
rules, Database schema, Keys, schema diagrams, Database integrity constraints
: Domain integrity, Entity integrity, Referential integrity, Relational query
languages, Introduction to Relational Algebra, Basic Relational Algebra
Operations, Cartesian Product, Joins, Aggregate functions, Modification of the
databases
3   Introduction to SQL   5
Data Definition Commands, Data Definition Commands, Data Manipulation
Commands, Select Queries, Additional Data Definition Commands, Additional
Select Query Keywords (Book : “Database System Design, Implementation, and
Management”, Carlos Coronel, Steven Morris, Peter Bob)

Set operators, Join operators, Views, Sub-queries (Book : “Database System

Peter Bob)
5   Database Design Using the ER Model   5
Overview of the design process, Components of the ER Model, Concepts of ER
model : Mapping Cardinalities, Primary Key, Participation constraints, Weak
entity sets, Generalization, specialization, Converting ER model to Relational
Model, ER model Design issues
6   Relational Database Design   3
Features of Good Relational Designs, Problems with bad design, Decomposition
using concept of functional dependencies, Introduction to process of
normalization and de-normalization. Normal forms – 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, De-
normalization
7   Indexing   2
Introduction to indexes, Need of index in database systems, Types of indexes,
SQL implementation of index
8   Transactions   2
What is transactions? Properties of transaction, Transaction states, Issues with

9   Data Warehousing and Data Mining   3
The need for data analysis, Decision support data, Introduction to Data

Pre-requisite: Software Engineering (MCNB02003), Object Oriented Software Engineering

Course Objective
The objective of this course is to provide an understanding of the management issues and processes
during the software development project. It provides a holistic view of the different aspects of the
development process. Students will become conversant with various tools & techniques used in
project management in modern industrial environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain basic concepts of project planning, management and evaluation.
2. Demonstrate the use of software effort estimation and activity plan in a given project.
3. Discuss resource allocation and risk management in software projects.
4. Describe project tracking, project management and software quality processes.

function point analysis, object points, COCOMO model.

Pre-requisite: Discrete Mathematics (BTCS01001), Data Structures and Algorithms
(BTCS02003)
Course Objective
To introduce fundamentals of automata theory, regular sets and grammars, To design
automata for different types of languages.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain the fundamentals of Automata theory and regular sets
2. Design regular language modelling in Finite Automata and non-deterministic finite
automata
3. Describe context free and context sensitive languages and design automata for these
languages
4. Explain undecidability and complexity of problems.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit Description   Duration
1   Introduction   4
Alphabet, languages and grammars, productions and derivation,
Chomsky hierarchy of languages
2   Regular languages and finite automata   6
Regular expressions and languages, deterministic finite automata
(DFA) and equivalence with regular expressions, nondeterministic
finite automata (NFA) and equivalence with DFA, regular grammars
and equivalence with finite automata, properties of regular
languages, Kleene’s   theorem, pumping   lemma   for   regular
languages, Myhill-Nerode theorem and its uses, minimization of finite
automata.
3   Context-free languages and pushdown automata   4
Context-free grammars (CFG) and languages (CFL), Chomsky
and Greibach normal forms, nondeterministic pushdown automata
(PDA) and equivalence with CFG, parse trees, ambiguity in CFG,
pumping lemma for context-free languages, deterministic pushdown
automata, closure properties of CFLs.
4   Context-sensitive languages   4
Context-sensitive grammars (CSG) and languages, linear bounded
automata and equivalence with CSG.
5   Turing machines   4
The basic model for Turing machines (TM), Turing recognizable
(recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages
and   their closure properties, variants of Turing machines,

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
nondeterministic TMs and equivalence with deterministic TMs,
unrestricted grammars and equivalence with Turing machines, TMs as
enumerators.
6   Undecidability   4
Church-Turing thesis, universal Turing machine, the universal and
diagonalization languages, reduction between languages and Rice s
theorem, undecidable problems about languages.
7   Basic Introduction to Complexity   4
Introductory ideas on Time complexity of deterministic and
nondeterministic Turing machines, P and NP, NP- completeness,
Cook’s Theorem, other NP -Complete problems.
Total   30

The aim of the course is to introduce the concepts of statistical treatment of risk-neutral
valuation, arbitrage, options and derivatives. It will provide hands-on implementation of
various risk and pricing models that are used in the industry. The purpose of this course is to
give the students exposure to the practical applications of quantitative finance in the real world.
It will teach the students how to put their theoretical understanding into practice.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the similarities and differences in the main asset classes namely equities, fixed
income securities and commodities,
2. Apply the risk neutral probability measures and the fundamental theorems of asset
pricing in solving problems,
3. Analyze the mathematical statements about financial models and Construct counter-
examples for false statements.

Objectives
The interaction of data science and technology with the world is via signal processing: detecting,
transcoding, understanding and generating time-dependent and space-dependent signals in the
broadest sense. Data is rich and abundant. However, every data wrangler has come across most
of the time this data, which is very noisy in nature. Processing noisy signals and filtering
unwanted part from an image has been a huge concern over the last few decades. Signal and
image processing techniques developed today are very robust and effective models. The objective
is to port some processing techniques from the audio and signal field and use them to process
data. To give basic mathematical understanding of transformation for image and signal
processing and sampling To introduce elementary concepts of LTI system, convolution.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Classify discrete and continuous data signals and learn the engineering mathematical aspect
of it and perform operations on it
2. Model finite impulse and infinite impulse response filters
3. Simplify the concepts of Convolution and Sampling to solve and support problems
4. List the fundamental concepts in Image representation and state basic filtering techniques to
facilitate noise removal

design and development of database systems, with an emphasis on how to organize, maintain and retrieve
- efficiently, and effectively - information from a database management system.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, student will be able to -
1. Describe core concepts of database and model a database management system through ER
modelling
2. Apply knowledge of relational algebra and structured query language to retrieve and manage
data from relational database

Pre-requisite: Programming for Problem Solving, Data structures
Course Objective
To develop an understanding of essential database concepts. To understand different issues
involved in the design and implementation of a database systems. To understand and use
database query languages to access and manage a database. To design and build a simple
database system with modeling, designing and implementation To understand the need of
data analytics and advanced database systems like data warehouse and data mining
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe the terminology, features and basic concepts of database systems
2. Formulate queries using structured query language and relational algebra
3. Design a model expressed in the form of an entity relationship diagram and transform it
into a relational model
4. Demonstrate an understanding of normalization theory, transactions and need for data
analytics and advanced database models

Pre-requisite: Software Engineering (MCNB02003), Object Oriented Software Engineering
(MCNB03004)
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to provide an understanding of the management issues and
processes during the software development project. It provides a holistic view of the different
aspects of the development process. Students will become conversant with various tools &
techniques used in project management in modern industrial environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain basic concepts of project planning, management and evaluation.
2. Demonstrate the use of software effort estimation and activity plan in a given project.
3. Discuss resource allocation and risk management in software projects.
4. Describe project tracking, project management and software quality processes.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction   3
Software development as a project, Stakeholders in software project,
process, resources, quality and cost. Objective issues and problems
relating to software projects.
2   Project Planning and Project Evaluation   6
Steps in project planning, Defining scope and objective, project Phases
and Project Lifecycle, work breakdown structure, GANTT Chart,
Developing Project Charter, Project Management plan, Execute plans,
Social-Economic Environmental influences.
Evaluation: Strategic assessment, Technical assessment, Cost-benefit
analysis, Cash flow forecasting, Breakeven analysis, Risk Evaluation.
3   Project Management Process   3
Project processes, Process groups, Process Interaction, Customising
process interaction, Mapping of project Management processes
4   Selection of Appropriate Project Approach   3
Choosing development technology and methodology, Various Process
models.
5   Software Effort Estimation   6
Problems in software estimation, effort estimation techniques, expert
judgment, Estimation by analogy, top-down and bottom-up estimation,
function point analysis, object points, COCOMO model.
6   Activity planning   5
Network planning model, Activity-on-arrow network, PERT,
precedence network, forward pass and backward pass, critical path,
slack and float, Product Data Management (PDM)

Pre-requisite: Discrete Mathematics (BTCS01001), Data Structures and Algorithms
(BTCS02003)
Course Objective
To introduce fundamentals of automata theory, regular sets and grammars, To design
automata for different types of languages.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain the fundamentals of Automata theory and regular sets
2. Design regular language modelling in Finite Automata and non-deterministic finite
automata
3. Describe context free and context sensitive languages and design automata for these
languages
4. Explain undecidability and complexity of problems.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit Description   Duration
1   Introduction   4
Alphabet, languages and grammars, productions and derivation,
Chomsky hierarchy of languages
2   Regular languages and finite automata   6
Regular expressions and languages, deterministic finite automata
(DFA) and equivalence with regular expressions, nondeterministic
finite automata (NFA) and equivalence with DFA, regular grammars
and equivalence with finite automata, properties of regular
languages, Kleene’s   theorem, pumping   lemma   for   regular
languages, Myhill-Nerode theorem and its uses, minimization of finite
automata.
3   Context-free languages and pushdown automata   4
Context-free grammars (CFG) and languages (CFL), Chomsky
and Greibach normal forms, nondeterministic pushdown automata
(PDA) and equivalence with CFG, parse trees, ambiguity in CFG,
pumping lemma for context-free languages, deterministic pushdown
automata, closure properties of CFLs.
4   Context-sensitive languages   4
Context-sensitive grammars (CSG) and languages, linear bounded
automata and equivalence with CSG.
5   Turing machines   4
The basic model for Turing machines (TM), Turing recognizable
(recursively enumerable) and Turing-decidable (recursive) languages
and   their closure properties, variants of Turing machines,
nondeterministic TMs and equivalence with deterministic TMs,

Introductory ideas on Time complexity of deterministic and

Pre-requisite: Digital Signal Processing (BTCO05006)
Course Objective
1. To provide the fundamental knowledge of Image processing and related algorithms
involved in it.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Outline the fundamentals of image processing
2. Compute and analyse effects of various image transformation techniques in spatial and
frequency domains
3. Analyse images using image segmentation and morphological operations
4. Compress the images using basic transforms, wavelets
Detailed Syllabus
Unit Description   Duration
1.   Digital Image Processing Systems   2
Introduction, Fundamental steps of image processing, Display Image
Sampling and quantization, Basic relationships between pixels. Types of
images: Monochrome, grey, colour.
2. Image Enhancement in the Spatial domain   2
Grey level transformations, Histogram processing, Arithmetic and logic
operations, Spatial filtering: Introduction, Smoothing and sharpening
filters.
3. Image Segmentation, Representation and Description   3
Detection of discontinuities, Edge linking and Boundary detection,
Thresholding, Region based segmentation, Representation – Chain
Codes, polynomial approximations, Signatures, Boundary Descriptors,
Regional Descriptors
4.   Morphological Image Processing   2
Introduction, Dilation, Erosion, Opening, closing, Hit –or-Miss
transformation, Morphological algorithm operations on binary images
and Morphological algorithm operations on gray-scale images.
5. Image Transforms   2
Introduction to Fourier transform, Walsh transform, Hadamard
transform, Discrete Sine transform, Discrete cosine transform,.
Frequency domain filters: Smoothing and Sharpening filters,
6.   Wavelets and Multiresolution Processing   2
STFT, need of wavelets, Image pyramids, Filter Banks, Haar transform,
Application of wavelets.
7. Image Data Compression   2
Fundamentals, Redundancies: Coding, Interpixel, Pysycho-visual,
fidelity criteria, Image compression models, Error free compression,
Lossy compression methods.

Pre-requisite: Nil
Objectives:
This course provides basic orientation towards macroeconomic principles and help them
understand the functions of economy at Macro level:
 To combine elements of basic variables of macroeconomics.
 To familiarize with importance of macroeconomic approach in managing economy.
 To understand the application of macroeconomic theories at aggregate level.
 To emphasize the role of macroeconomic policies and analyze their implication for
economy along with international linkages.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Learn various macroeconomic variables, circular flow of income and their linkages
to macro economy.
2. Analyze aggregates of macroeconomics and understand goods market and money
market, Indian Financial System, Business fluctuations and Stabilization Policies.
3. Orient oneself towards higher levels of learning related to economic planning,
international trade, foreign exchange market and international organizations at
macro level.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Macroeconomics: Meaning, Nature & Scope and   3
importance   of   Macroeconomics,   Interdependence   between
Microeconomics & Macroeconomics, macroeconomics goals, major
issues and concerns of macroeconomics.
2   Structure of Macroeconomics:   Subject matter of Macroeconomics,   3
Structure of Macro Economy, Different sectors of the economy, Circular
Flow of Income & Product, Leakages & Injections in the Circular Flow.
3   Keynes’s Theory of Employment: Principles of effective demand,   3
aggregate demand function, aggregate supply function, determination
of equilibrium level of employment-Effective demand.
4   Macroeconomic Aggregates: Aggregate Consumption- component of   3
consumption, determinant of consumption, consumption function,
Saving function, Capital formation- component of investment,
determinant of investment, investment function and investment
multiplier.

Introduction to Goods Market and Money Market and links between
them, Goods Market equilibrium- derivation of IS Curve, Money
market equilibrium- derivation of LM Curve, Equilibrium of goods
Market and Money Market, critique of IS-LM Curves model.
6   Inflation – Unemployment Trade-off (Philips Curve): Types and   3
causes of unemployment, Unemployment situation in India, policy
measures to solve unemployment problem in India, Inflation- meaning
and types, effects of Inflation on distribution of income & wealth and
on output & growth, methods to control Inflation, Unemployment and
Inflation- The Philips Curve, causes of shift in Philips Curve, relation
between short-run Philips Curve and long-run Philips Curve.
7   Indian Financial System: Credit and Commercial Banking- meaning   3
and functions, purposes, roles of commercial banks in economic
development, credit creation and limitations on the credit creating
power of the banks, Central Banking- principles and functions of
commercial banking, methods of credit control by central bank for
economic prosperity.

Business Cycle, Theories of Business Cycle, Business Cycle and Indian
Economy in post-liberalization era.
9   Economic Stabilization Policy- Monetary Policy: Tools of Monetary   3
policy, expansionary monetary policy to cure recession, monetary
policy to control inflation, liquidity trap and effectiveness of monetary
policy, tight monetary policy, RBI’s Monetary policy in India and its
critical evaluation.

Public Finance, Public Expenditure, Taxation.
11 Economic Stabilization Policy- Fiscal policy II: Introduction and   3
importance of Budget in Economy, Indian Budgeting System, Budget
Deficit and Government Borrowing, Crowding-out effect and
effectiveness of Fiscal Policy.
12 Economic Planning and Policy: Rational, Features and Objectives of   3
Economic Planning, Strategies of India’s Developmental Plans,
Assessment of India’s planning, Export-Import Policy, Evaluation of
latest Foreign Trade Policy of India.
13   International Trade, Comparative Advantage, and Protectionism:   3
International Trade, Reasons for International Trade, Absolute Cost
Theory, Comparative Cost Theory, Free Trade versus Protection, Cases

Pre-requisite: Principles of Economics –I, II
Objectives: This course seeks to equip students from all backgrounds with a basic
understanding of the international business environment and the fundamentals of
international business strategy. In addition, this course aims to develop the following
skills in students:
   Critical thinking
   Collaboration and teamwork
 Research and writing skills
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Explain how differences between countries create additional challenges for firms
doing business internationally
2. Explain how firms can create value by doing business internationally
3. Identify key decisions related to foreign market selection, market entry modes, and
international strategy that firms need to make when going international
4. Apply theoretical frameworks to make informed recommendations for such firms
5. Describe how foreign exchange markets work; derive business/economic
implications
6. Evaluate arguments for and against government restrictions on trade and
investment; derive business/economic implications
7. Identify ethical challenges related to international business
8. Explain long-run trends and development in the international business
environment; derive business/economic implications.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   The environment of international business: Examine how   8
countries differ in terms of their economic, political, and social
characteristics – and how this matters for international business.
The basics of foreign exchange markets and how they affect
international business.

2   The globalization of business, Economic development and   7
emerging markets, Emerging markets: Business implications,
Foreign market analysis: The PEST framework, Political risk and
corruption, Culture and cultural differences, Foreign exchange
rates
3   International business strategy: why companies do business   8
internationally and how this can create value. Exploring the
different options available to firms for entering foreign markets
and discuss the main challenges and decisions firms face when
going international. How these general principles apply to
companies with ‘digital’ business models, such as Netflix,
Facebook, OLA, UBER, FLIPKART etc.
4   Why do firms expand internationally?, Foreign direct investment   7
(FDI), Local adaptation vs global integration, International
business in the digital age, The globalization of research &
development (R&D)
5   Current issues in international business including the role of   8
international trade policy (e.g. the “trade war” between the US
and China), the role of technology, as well as ethical challenges
associated with international business.
6   Theories of international trade, Trade barriers and “trade wars”:   7
Impact on IB, Trade agreements and international institutions,
The “dark side” of globalization? Social, environmental and other
concerns, Ethics in IB, The future of IB

Pre-requisite: HSC level Chemistry
Objectives:
1. To familiarize with atomic structure, periodicity of elements in periodic table and
chemical bonding of elements
2. To introduce electromagnetic spectrum ranges converted to different technologies used
for various applications.
3. To acquaint with concepts of electrochemistry and basic organic reactions
4. To study important engineering materials and management of e-waste.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Explain the foundational knowledge of the subject using chemistry principles
2. Identify newer chemical materials for better product designing
3. Analyze the impact of science and its progress on society and provide solution for cleaner
environment
4. Evaluate the various aspects of chemistry to convert into useful applications.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Atomic structure and Periodic properties of elements:   8
Study of atom structure with reference to Bohr’s model, wave particle
duality, Schrodinger wave equation. Concept of valency and electronic
configuration. Explanation of Aufbau principle, Hund’s rule and
Pauli’s Exclusion Principle that helps in writing electronic
configuration. Introduction to Modern periodic table, Nomenclature of
s, p, d, f group elements. Trends in physical properties: effective
nuclear charge, atomic radii, ionization energy, electron affinity,
electronegativity. Concept of semiconductors and metalloids. Concept
of acids and bases.
2   Chemical bonding:   6
Intermolecular forces: Ionic, covalent, co-ordinate bonds and types of
intramolecular interactions (with one example for each type).
Introduction to co-ordination chemistry and Co-ordination number,
magnetism of the co-ordinate complexes.
3   Electrochemistry:   6
Concept of electrochemical cell & electrolytic cell. Cell potential, EMF
of Cell, Relation of free energy with EMF of cell, Faraday’s law,
Derivation of Nernst equation, Applicability of Nernst equation

Graphite.
Liquid Crystals: Definition, classification, properties with applications.
Polymers: Introduction to polymers and polymerization mechanisms,
Types of polymers, Specialty polymers like Conducting polymers, Self-
healing polymers with applications.
5   Spectroscopic techniques and Applications:   6
General idea on Electromagnetic radiation, Basic Principle of
Spectroscopy, UV-Visible Spectroscopy & applications, IR
Spectroscopy & applications, Nuclear magnetic resonance &
applications. MRI applications in medicine.
8   Environmental Chemistry:   2
E-waste management: Definition, classification and management of e-
waste in India with reference to Environment (Protection) Act.
9   Solutions and Stoichiometry:   5
Types of solutions and its characteristics, properties of aqueous
solutions, different units for expressing concentration of solutions
(ppm, ppb, normality, molarity, molality, mole fraction of solute, mass
fraction of solute and solvent), empirical and molecular formula from
elemental composition, numerical based on empirical formula,
normality, molarity, molality molarity.
10   Organic Reactions:   6
Basic organic reactions like- addition reactions, elimination reactions,
substitution reactions, pericyclic reactions, rearrangement reactions,
photochemical reactions and redox reactions.
Specific Reactions of functional groups containing oxygen (-COOH, -
OH, -CHO, -C=O); Nucleophilic substitution reaction, Elimination
reaction. Organic Name Reactions E.g. Aldol & related reactions.

Objectives
The interaction of data science and technology with the world is via signal processing: detecting,
transcoding, understanding and generating time-dependent and space-dependent signals in the
broadest sense. Data is rich and abundant. However, every data wrangler has come across most
of the time this data, which is very noisy in nature. Processing noisy signals and filtering
unwanted part from an image has been a huge concern over the last few decades. Signal and
image processing techniques developed today are very robust and effective models. The objective
is to port some processing techniques from the audio and signal field and use them to process
data. To give basic mathematical understanding of transformation for image and signal
processing and sampling To introduce elementary concepts of LTI system, convolution.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Classify discrete and continuous data signals and learn the engineering mathematical aspect
of it and perform operations on it,
2. Model finite impulse and infinite impulse response filters,
3. Simplify the concepts of Convolution and Sampling to solve and support problems,
4. List the fundamental concepts in Image representation and state basic filtering techniques to
facilitate noise removal.

Objectives
The interaction of data science and technology with the world is via signal processing: detecting,
transcoding, understanding and generating time-dependent and space-dependent signals in the
broadest sense. Data is rich and abundant. However, every data wrangler has come across most
of the time this data, which is very noisy in nature. Processing noisy signals and filtering
unwanted part from an image has been a huge concern over the last few decades. Signal and
image processing techniques developed today are very robust and effective models. The objective
is to port some processing techniques from the audio and signal field and use them to process
data. To give basic mathematical understanding of transformation for image and signal
processing and sampling To introduce elementary concepts of LTI system, convolution.

1. Classify discrete and continuous data signals and learn the engineering mathematical aspect
of it and perform operations on it,

3. Simplify the concepts of Convolution and Sampling to solve and support problems,

facilitate noise removal.

Pre-requisite: Programming, Algorithm, CS
Objectives:
This course gives you an introduction to modeling methods and simulation tools for a wide
range of natural phenomena. The different methodologies that will be presented here can be
applied to very wide range of topics such as
 Fluid motion, stellar dynamics, population evolution etc.
 This course does not intend to go deeply into any numerical method or process and
does not provide any recipe for the resolution of a particular problem
   It is rather a basic guideline towards different methodologies that can be applied to
solve any kind of problem and help you pick the one best suited for you.
The assignments of this course will be made as practical as possible in order to allow you to
actually create from scratch short programs that will solve simple problems. Although
programming will be used extensively in this course we do not require any advanced
programming experience in order to complete it.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Sound understanding of overview and general ideas about modeling and simulation
 Dynamical systems modeling is the principal method developed to study time-space
dependent problems
 Understanding of concept of cellular automata by outlining the basic building blocks of
this method
 Understanding of introduction to the lattice Boltzmann method, a powerful tool in
computational fluid dynamics.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of vector algebra, functions, limits, differentiation and integration of
functions.
Course Objective:
This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus. This
course will help the students achieve sound understanding of the concepts of calculus, develop
problem solving skills and apply the concepts and techniques of calculus to solve problems within
Engineering domain. This course will equip the students with intermediate to advanced level
concepts and aligned tools to help them tackle advanced mathematics and related applications.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the fundamental concepts of differential calculus for functions of one variable,
including limits, derivatives, Mean Value Theorems, Taylor and Maclaurin series, and
LHospital’s rule. (K2)
2. Solve problems involving functions of several variables using partial differentiation, Taylor
series expansion, and techniques for finding maxima and minima, including Lagrange’s
method of undetermined multipliers. (K3)
3. Use Beta and Gamma functions to solve problems in single-variable calculus. (K2)
4. Compute and interpret double and triple integrals, including change of variables and
coordinate transformations, and apply them to determine areas and volumes. (K3)
5. Examine vector functions using gradient, divergence, curl, and scalar potential and apply
fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to
evaluate integrals. (K3)
6. Integrate concepts from differential, integral, and vector calculus to formulate and solve real-
world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences. (K3)

Course Objective

several methods of simplifying networks. Steady state and transient analysis will make them
understand deeper aspects of circuit behaviour. They would also be acquainted with the
fundamental principles of circuit theory and network synthesis.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -

dependent AC and DC sources. (L1- Remembering)

theorems, in analyzing electrical circuits. (L2- Understanding)

electrical networks. (L3- Applying)

responses in electrical circuits. (L3-Applying)

hybrid parameters, for analyzing circuit behavior. (L5- Evaluating)

stochastic processes. (L1- Remembering, L2-Understanding)

processes. (L3- Applying)

properties. (L4- Analyzing)

properties. (L2 -Understanding, L4- Analyzing)

undertake a project which involves application like speech recognition, speaker recognition etc.

Course Objective
This course aims to provide knowledge on information theory for data compression and
implement channel coding techniques for correcting and detecting errors in the
communication channel.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Illustrate the basic concepts of information, entropy, Shannon’s theorem and channel
capacity
2. Implement and analyse various source coding techniques
3. Apply various channel coding techniques for error correction and analyse their
performance.

capability, syndrome testing, decoding.   07

Course Objective
As the miniaturization of electronic devices enables the arrival of new gadgets, it is important
to note that the devices that we still use were invented decades ago. Over the period these
devices have improved in their construction and performance. The course here will enable the
student to understand the construction, working principle, application of basic electronic
devices, operational amplifiers, and its application.

1. Explain construction and characteristics of various types of diodes and illustrate simple
circuits with diodes

3. Explain the basic concepts of operational amplifier

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of Basic Electrical Engineering and Mathematics.
Course Objectives
This course aims to acquaint students with the fundamentals of electric and magnetic fields and
propagation of uniform plane waves. This course also helps to understand and analyze
magneto statics, magnetic flux density, relations between field due to time-varying situations
and transmission lines.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Implement vector calculus concepts to understand behavior of static electric field
2. Implement vector calculus concepts to understand behavior of static magnetic field
3. Analyze Maxwell’s equation in different forms (differential and integral) and apply them to
uniform plane wave propagation
4. Describe the concept of voltage, current impedance, and power along two-conductor
transmission lines using the solution of the wave equation and Smith chart
Unit Description   Duration
1.   Review of Vector Calculus
Vector Field, Rectangular, Cylindrical and Spherical Coordinate systems.   04
2.   Coulomb’s law and electric field intensity
Coulomb’s law, electric field intensity, calculation of electric field intensity for   08
various charge distributions.
Electric flux density and Gauss’s law
Electric flux density, Gauss’s law, vector operator and divergence theorem.
3.   Energy, potential and Capacitance
Energy expended in moving a point charge in an electric field, line integral,
potential and potential difference, calculations of electric field of both point charge   08
and system of charges, potential gradient, dipole, energy density, parallel plate
capacitance. Current and current density continuity of current, conductor
properties, dielectric material and properties.

4.   Steady magnetic field
Biot – Savart law, Ampere’s circuital law, curl of H, Stoke’s theorem, magnetic flux   04
and flux density.
5.   Time varying fields and Maxwell’s equations
Faraday’s law concept of displacement currents, Maxwell’s equations in point   04
form, Maxwell’s equations in integral form, boundary conditions and significance
of Maxwell’s equations.
6.   Uniform Plane waves
Uniform plane waves in time domain in free space, wave equation in free space   05
and conducting medium, propagation of electromagnetic waves in free space and
conducting medium and wave impedance of free space medium.
7.   Poynting vector and flow of power
Poynting vector and flow of power: Poynting theorem, power flow for a plane   02
wave, Poynting loss in a plane conductor.
8.   Introduction to Transmission Lines
Equations of Voltage and Current on TX line, Propagation constant and
characteristic impedance, and reflection coefficient and VSWR, Impedance   10
Transformation on Loss-less and Low loss Transmission line, Power transfer on TX
line, Smith Chart, Admittance Smith Chart, Applications of transmission lines:
Impedance Matching, use transmission line sections as circuit elements.
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of Engineering Mathematics, Circuits and Network Technology, Signals
and Systems.
Course Objectives
This course aims to acquaint students with the fundamentals of the Basics theory of process and
control systems and System stability. It also helps to analyse and design the system for fulfilling the
performance and stability criterion.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the modelling of linear-time-invariant systems using transfer function and state space
representations
2. Describe the concept of stability and its assessment for linear-time invariant systems
3. Design simple feedback controllers
4. Analyse the state space variable and models
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to control problem
Industrial Control examples. Mathematical models of physical systems.
Control hardware and their models. Transfer function models of linear time-   08
invariant systems.
Feedback Control: Open-Loop and Closed-loop systems. Benefits of Feedback.
Block diagram algebra.
2.   Time Response Analysis
Standard test signals. Time response of first and second order systems for
standard test inputs. Application of initial and final value theorem.   10
Design specifications for second-order systems based on the time-response.
Concept of Stability. Routh-Hurwitz Criteria. Relative Stability analysis. Root-
Locus technique. Construction of Root-loci.
3.   Frequency-response analysis
Relationship between time and frequency response, Polar plots, Bode plots.   06
Nyquist stability criterion. Relative stability using Nyquist criterion – gain and
phase margin. Closed-loop frequency response.
3

Electronics & Telecommunication (2023 – 2024)
4.   Introduction to Controller Design
Stability, steady-state accuracy, transient accuracy, disturbance rejection,
insensitivity and robustness of control systems. Root-loci method of feedback
controller design. Design specifications in frequency-domain. Frequency-
10
domain methods of design. Application of Proportional, Integral and
Derivative Controllers, Lead and Lag compensation in designs.
Analog and Digital implementation of controllers.
5.   State variable Analysis
Concepts of state variables. State space model. Diagonalization of State Matrix.
Solution of state equations. Eigenvalues and Stability Analysis. Concept of   06
Controllability and Observability. Pole-placement by state feedback. Discrete-
time systems. Difference Equations. State-space models of linear discrete-time
systems. Stability of linear discrete-time systems.
6.   Introduction to Optimal Control and Nonlinear Control
Performance Indices. Regulator problem, Tracking Problem. Nonlinear   05
system–Basic concepts.

Course Objectives
The aim of this course is to provide knowledge of the basic elements of various types of
Analog & digital modulation and demodulation techniques. This course also makes student
acquainted with different types of coding, decoding and spread spectrum techniques.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the principles and concepts of different analog & digital modulation techniques.
2. Implement different base band shaping techniques for data transmission and detection.
3. Analyze different algorithms for source and error control coding.
4. Describe the concepts and applications of spread spectrum modulation.

Course Objective

techniques. It equips the students with intermediate to advanced level concepts and tools in
probability and statistics that help them tackle relevant problems within engineering domain.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Solve problems involving random variables, probability distributions and testing of
hypothesis, correlation and regression
2. Identify suitable probability distribution and testing techniques to solve related problems
3. Apply knowledge of random variables, probability distributions, measures of central
tendency, correlation and regression to solve real life problems
4. Analyse data samples using statistical methods

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of vector algebra, functions, limits, differentiation and integration of
functions.
Course Objective:
This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus. This
course will help the students achieve sound understanding of the concepts of calculus, develop
problem solving skills and apply the concepts and techniques of calculus to solve problems within
Engineering domain. This course will equip the students with intermediate to advanced level
concepts and aligned tools to help them tackle advanced mathematics and related applications.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Demonstrate the fundamental concepts of differential calculus for functions of one variable.
2. Solve problems involving functions of several variables using partial differentiation, Taylor
series expansion, and techniques for finding maxima and minima, including Lagrange’s method
of undetermined multipliers.
3. Use Beta and Gamma functions to solve problems in single-variable calculus.
4. Compute and interpret double and triple integrals, including change of variables and coordinate
transformations, and apply them to determine areas and volumes.
5. Examine vector functions using gradient, divergence, curl, and scalar potential and apply
fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to evaluate
integrals.
6. Integrate concepts from differential, integral, and vector calculus to formulate and solve real-
world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences.

Pre-requisite: Linear Algebra and Ordinary Differential Equations
Course Objective
The principal objective of the course is to develop students' logical reasoning and problem-solving
skills by introducing fundamental concepts of discrete mathematics essential for computer science
and engineering applications. It provides a strong foundation in set theory, logic, combinatorics,
graph theory, and abstract algebra, enabling students to analyze and construct mathematical
arguments. Through the study of proof techniques, recurrence relations, and discrete structures,
students will gain the ability to model computational problems and prove the correctness of
algorithms. The course also highlights the practical applications of discrete mathematics in real-
world contexts, such as data structures, cryptography, network security, and algorithm design,
equipping students for advanced studies and careers in computing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Apply fundamental concepts of set theory, relations, and functions to solve mathematical
and computational problems.
2. Construct valid mathematical arguments using propositional and predicate logic, proof
techniques, and induction methods.
3. Analyze combinatorial structures and recurrence relations to model and solve discrete
problems in engineering applications.
4. Implement graph and tree algorithms to solve optimization and network-related problems.
5. Demonstrate an understanding of abstract algebraic structures and their applications in
coding theory.

about computer networking.

cryptographic algorithms and its application.

After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain and implement various symmetric key cryptographic algorithms
2. Explain and implement various asymmetric key cryptographic algorithms

Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration

modern cryptography, perfectly secret encryption, one time pad and

DES and AES, modes of operations.

Quadratic Congruence, Fermat’s little theorem, Euler’s theorem.
5.   Asymmetric Key Cryptography   05

Curve Cryptosystem.

Course Objective
This course is an introduction to the field of cyber forensics. This course introduces various aspects
of cyber forensics to the students. Students will learn about various methods, tools and techniques
to perform forensic operations on a given media.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to-
1. Describe Windows and Linux File systems
2. Perform various forensics operations on a given media
3. Describe various professional, ethical and legal issues related to cyber forensics
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to cybercrime and cyber forensics   6
Definition of cybercrime, type and classification of cybercrimes, Overview of
cyber forensics, forensic process, types of investigations, digital evidence,
data acquisition and forensic imaging, digital forensic tools, and Incident
Response
2   File System Analysis   6
Understanding file systems, booting process, disk drives and solid-state
devices, FAT and NTFS file systems, partition table and MFT, understanding
whole disk encryption, Windows registry, file structure of ext4.

Preparation for forensic analysis, data carving, recovering graphics files and
header analysis, email and internet activity analysis, data hiding techniques,
malware analysis
4   Network Forensics   4
Overview, analyzing network traffic, network-based evidence,
investigating routers.

Mobile phone basics, inside mobile devices, acquisition procedure for
mobile devices, mobile forensic tools.
6   Legal, Professional and Ethical issues   4

report writing

building blocks. It helps to understand the IoT hardware and various protocols used in IoT
applications for everyday life. It also provides information on associated technologies like cloud
computing and hands-on expertise in building IoT applications.

1. Describe the fundamentals of IoT

3. Distinguish the IoT data using various data analytics methods

To learn traditional testing methods applied to develop robust software products and services.
Quality and security of software products rests on early error detection and reporting throughout
the development life cycle. It will enable the students implement manual and automated testing of
software products.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, student would be able to-
1. Design and implement test cases for different levels and types of testing
2. Select appropriate manual and automatic testing for different modules of software
3. Apply test-driven development to improve testing and delivery in software development

Defects, Failures.

Graph matrices-Loop testing-Data flow testing-Mutation testing

Pre-requisite: Computer Network, Operating Systems and programming
Course Objective
This course is an introduction to vulnerability assessment and penetration testing. Students will
learn about various methods, tools and techniques to perform ethical hacking and will simulate
various attacks in the lab environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, student would be able to-
1. Demonstrate hacking in a lab environment
2. Describe various countermeasures
3. Describe various professional, ethical and legal issues related to ethical hacking
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction   6
Need for adversarial thinking and penetration testing, ethics of hacking, hacking
process, types of hackers, types of penetration testing, testing methodologies
(OSSTMM, PTES, and OWASP Testing Guide), and Rules of engagement.
2   Reconnaissance and scanning   8
Introduction, types of reconnaissance, various techniques of recon (social
engineering, web based recon, DNS based recon, network based recon, Google
hacking etc.), countermeasures, scanning, types of scanning (port scanning,
network scanning, and vulnerability scanning), Sniffers
3   Exploitation   10
Password cracking, spoofing, session hijacking, DoS / DDoS, Buffer Overflow,
malware, evading firewall and IDS, SQL Injection, OWASP top 10 web
application vulnerabilities, hacking wireless networks, metasploit, meterpreter,
AV evasion, metasploit databases and tool integration, privilege escalation,
4   Hacking Mobile platforms   2
Overview of android and iOS, OWASP mobile to 10 risks and mitigation.
5   Legal, Professional and Ethical issues   2
Cyber laws in India, various ethical dilemma, professional conduct, and
penetration testing report writing
6   Case Study   2
Total   30
Text Books
1. C. Easttom, Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) Exam Cram, 1st Edition, Pearson Education, 2023.

Pre-requisite: Software engineering.
Course Objective
To learn traditional testing methods applied to develop robust software products and services.
Quality and security of software products rests on early error detection and reporting throughout
the development life cycle. It will enable the students implement manual and automated testing of
software products.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, student would be able to-
1. Design and implement test cases for different levels and types of testing
2. Select appropriate manual and automatic testing for different modules of software
3. Apply test-driven development to improve testing and delivery in software development
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Software Testing   4
Testing objectives and activities. Traditional and Agile testing process. Errors,
Defects, Failures.
2   Testing Techniques   6
Black-Box Testing Techniques- Equivalent Partitioning-Boundary Value
Analysis (BVA)- State Transition Testing-Decision table based Testing - Cause-
Effect Graphing Based Testing - Error Guessing
White-Box Testing Techniques- Logic Coverage criteria-Basic path testing-
Graph matrices-Loop testing-Data flow testing-Mutation testing
3   Unit Testing & Integration Testing   6
Unit testing framework, Naming and structuring Test Cases, Specification-
based Testing Techniques. Integration test techniques, Data Requirement,
Planning.
4   System Testing, User acceptance Testing & Regression Testing   6
Test techniques, Data Requirement, Planning
5   Test & Behavior Driven Development   8
Classic Style, Mockist Style
Contemporary issues: Applications of Software Testing in industry
Total   30

2   2   0   3   Marks Scaled to 50   Marks Scaled to 50
Pre-requisite: Computer Networks
Course Objective
The course focuses on designing, specification, and implement a modern, large scale network
design using the latest technology and devices, while understanding how to secure the network.
Understanding the sufficient Operations, Administration, Management, Provisioning, network
resources can be learnt.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, student would be able to-
1. Explain the major application architectures and applicable standards of networks
2. Design and manage computer network systems
3. Demonstrate the logical design process for core, distribution, and access networks
4. Describe how network monitoring and alarm reporting influences the network design
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction   3
Analyzing the technical goals of network, scalability, availability, network
Performance definitions, making network design, tradeoffs characterizing the
network traffic, understanding various standards.
2   Characterizing the Existing Internetwork   6
Characterizing the network infrastructure, network map, large internetworks,
logical architecture, network addressing and naming, analyzing network
availability and network utilization, network accuracy, analyzing errors on
switched Ethernet networks, analyzing network efficiency, analyzing delay
and response time.
Characterizing Network Traffic
Terminal/host traffic flow, client/server traffic flow, peer-to-peer traffic flow,
server/server traffic flow, distributed computing traffic flow, traffic flow in
voice over IP networks, characterizing traffic load, characterizing Quality of
Service requirements.
3   Logical Network Design   6
Designing a network topology, hierarchical network design, flat WAN
Topologies, flat LAN topologies, redundant network design topologies,
Spanning tree protocol, virtual LANs, wireless LANs, redundant wireless
access points, designing the enterprise edge topology, secure network design
topologies.
4   Designing Models for Addressing and Numbering   6
Network layer addresses, IP dynamic addressing, IP version 6, zero
configuration networking, hierarchical routing, route summarization
AY 2024-25
SVKM’s Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
(aggregation), discontiguous subnets, mobile hosts, link-local addresses,
global unicast addresses
5   Selecting Switching and Routing Protocols   4
Portfast, uplinkfast and Backbonefast, Unidirectional link detection, dynamic
trunk protocol, distance-vector routing protocols, hierarchical versus Non-
hierarchical routing protocols, IP routing, border gateway protocol, integrated
routing and bridging.
6   Testing, and Optimizing the Network Design   2
Testing your network design, optimizing your network design.
7   Developing Network Security Strategies   3
Network security design, security mechanisms, modularizing security
design, securing wireless networks, authentication in wireless networks.
Total   30
Textbooks
1. Behrouz A. Forouzan, Data Communications and Networking, 5th Edition, McGraw-Hill
Education, 2017.
2. Michel Thomatis, Network Design Cookbook: Architecting Cisco Networks, Version 10.2.8, 1st
Edition, Cisco press, August 2016.
Reference Books
1. Russ White, Denise Donohue, Art of Network Architecture, The: Business-Driven Design
(Networking Technology) Cisco press, 1st Edition, 2014.
2. Priscilla Oppenheimer, Top-Down Network Design, 3rd Edition, Cisco Press, 2011.

Pre-requisite: Programming for Problem Solving, Operating Systems
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to acquire knowledge about the development of embedded system
architecture using RTOS and enable the students to understand embedded-system programming
and use it for designing and developing embedded solutions.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain embedded system architecture and RTOS
2. Identify how microprocessor, memory, peripheral components and buses interact in an
embedded system design
3. Develop solutions for various real time applications using Embedded programming
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration

Classification of Embedded System, Concept of Embedded System Design,
and Design challenges: Processor technology, IC technology, Design
technology and Trade-offs.

Development Life cycle.

Course Objective
The objective of this course is to familiarize students with advanced data structures used to solve
real world problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, student would be able to-
1. Choose appropriate data structures and algorithms, understand the ADT/libraries, and use it
to design algorithms for a specific problem.

Prerequisite: Computer Networks
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to familiarize students with the working of internetworks. This course
focus on top-down approach, the Internet and a modern treatment of computer networking, its
attention to both principles and practice, and its accessible style and approach toward learning
about computer networking.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe medium access layer protocols
2. Design IP addressing scheme, analyze packet forwarding, and compare different routing
protocols
3. Compare and analyze transport protocols and other key protocols essential for networking
4. Explain various multimedia protocols, internet security concepts and future networks
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Medium access layer   03
Channel allocation problem, hidden node and exposed node problem FDM,
TDM, CDMA, MACA.
2.   Internet protocol   05
IPv4, compare IPv4 and IPv6, IPv6 - (address, special address, transition from
IPv4 to IPv6; subnetting classless addressing).
3.   Network Layer   06
Routing tables and forwarding, Routing protocols - Open Shortest Path First
and Border Gateway Protocol, DHCP, Mobile IP, AODV.
4.   Transport layer   06
Transmission Control Protocol - Reno, SCTP, I-TCP, Snoop TCP and Mobile
TCP.
5.   Multimedia in the internet   03
SIP, QoS (flow classes, flow control to improve QoS - FIFO, Priority and WFQ).
6.   Network security   05
Introduction to Internet security - application layer security, transport layer
security (SSL and TLS), IPSec, VPN, Firewall, WPA2, WPA3.
7.   Introduction to Internet of Things and applications, software defined   02
networks and 5G.
Total   30

Course Objective
This course is an introduction to Cryptography. It introduces the concepts used in traditional as
well as modern cryptography. Students will learn various symmetric and asymmetric
cryptographic algorithms and its application.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Explain and implement various symmetric key cryptographic algorithms
2. Explain and implement various asymmetric key cryptographic algorithms
3. Describe various attacks on cryptosystems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Overview of Cryptography and Its Applications   04
Introduction, security goals (CIA triad), Goals of cryptography, principles of
modern cryptography, perfectly secret encryption, one time pad and
Shannon’s theorem, cryptographic applications.
2.   Classical cryptosystems   04
Shift Ciphers, Affine Ciphers, The Vigenère Cipher, Playfair Ciphers,
Substitution Ciphers, Transposition Ciphers, stream and block ciphers,
Cryptanalysis.
3.   Symmetric Key Cryptography   08
Integer and modular arithmetic, Extended Euclidean Algorithm, Linear
Congruence, Algebraic structures (Group, Rings, and Fields), Galois Field,
Modern Block Cipher and its components(D- Boxes and S-Boxes), product
ciphers, stream ciphers (FSR and LFSR), attacks on stream and block ciphers,
DES and AES, modes of operations.
4.   Mathematics for Asymmetric Key Cryptography   03
Primes, primality testing, factorization, Chinese remainder theorem,
Quadratic Congruence, Fermat’s little theorem, Euler’s theorem.
5.   Asymmetric Key Cryptography   05
RSA Cryptosystem, Rabin Cryptosystem, ElGamal Cryptosystem, Elliptic
Curve Cryptosystem.
6.   Key Management   03
Key Distribution Centre, Needham-Schroeder Protocol, Kerberos, Diffie,-
Hellman Key Agreement, Certification Authority, Public-Key infrastructure

broaden their scope and learning in different domains.

Objectives:

e To provide a thorough introduction to "Service Oriented Architecture" (SOA),
which refers to a design pattern made up of components and interconnections
that stress interoperability and location transparency.

e It covers both the design of SOA systems as well as practical hands-on
programming of a distributed Web Service based system and how it is
succeeding, traditional distributed architecture on a global scale.

e Making students understand as to why SOA is the next phase in the evolution of
business automation and how past technical disparities of client-server
environment, distributed solutions are blanketed by layers of abstraction of
global accepted standard for representing logic and information.

e Service-orientation establishes a universal model in which automation logic and
business logic conform, the model equally to a task, a solution, an enterprise, a
community and resources are cleanly partitioned and consistently represented.

Outcomes: Students would be able to:

1. Apply knowledge of Client-Server and distributed architectures, RPC Protocol.

2. Design and conduct experiments on Web Services by embedding distributed
components, using Java API’s & REST technology.

3. Understand all elements of SOA infrastructure and Web Services.

4. Implement the techniques, skills, through modern engineering tools like Java
Platform/ Dot Net/ Apache Axis necessary for developing effective Web Service
solutions.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of vector algebra, functions, limits, differentiation and integration of
functions.
Course Objective:
This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus. This
course will help the students achieve sound understanding of the concepts of calculus, develop
problem solving skills and apply the concepts and techniques of calculus to solve problems within
Engineering domain. This course will equip the students with intermediate to advanced level
concepts and aligned tools to help them tackle advanced mathematics and related applications.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Understand the fundamental concepts of differential calculus for functions of one variable,
including limits, derivatives, Mean Value Theorems, Taylor and Maclaurin series, and
LHospital’s rule. (K2)
2. Solve problems involving functions of several variables using partial differentiation, Taylor
series expansion, and techniques for finding maxima and minima, including Lagrange’s
method of undetermined multipliers. (K3)
3. Use Beta and Gamma functions to solve problems in single-variable calculus. (K2)
4. Compute and interpret double and triple integrals, including change of variables and
coordinate transformations, and apply them to determine areas and volumes. (K3)
5. Examine vector functions using gradient, divergence, curl, and scalar potential and apply
fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to
evaluate integrals. (K3)
6. Integrate concepts from differential, integral, and vector calculus to formulate and solve real-
world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences. (K3)

Pre-requisite: Fundamental knowledge of physics, chemistry, and mathematics.
Course Objective:
To introduce students to modern biology with an emphasis on the evolution of biology as a multi-
disciplinary field, to make them aware of the application of engineering principles in biology. This
will encourage engineering students to think about solving biological problems with engineering
tools. They will also be exposed to the application of engineering principles in biology and
engineering robust solutions inspired by biological examples.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Identify the principles of biomimicry and explain their applications in engineering and
sustainable design, demonstrating an understanding of biologically inspired solutions. (K1)
2. Classify the fundamental building blocks of life (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic
acids) and describe their structural and functional roles in cellular processes and metabolism.
(K2)
3. Explain the molecular basis of genetic information transfer, including DNA replication,
transcription, and translation, and interpret Mendel's laws and their significance in genetics. (K2)
4. Describe the mechanisms of enzyme action, enzyme-substrate interactions, and enzyme
inhibition, and discuss their industrial and biological applications. (K2)
5. Explain the principles of metabolism and energy transactions, and categorize microorganisms
based on their characteristics, growth kinetics, and applications in biotechnology and drug
discovery. (K1)

processes, and ecosystems. Sustainable engineering.
