Pre-requisite: Nil
Course Objective
In this course students will get acquainted with the various systems of forces. It is designed for the
students to understand the concept of static equilibrium and apply the equations of motion to rigid
bodies.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Identify and solve force systems using fundamental principles of mechanics to understand
their effects on engineering structures and components
2. Apply equilibrium conditions to determine support reactions, internal forces, and assess the
stability of various structures
3. Identify centroids and moments of inertia of engineering components, utilizing the parallel
and perpendicular axis theorems for structural analysis
4. Analyze particle motion using velocity, acceleration, and different coordinate systems
5. Apply Newton’s laws, D'Alembert's principle under translational motion, rotational motion
to solve particle motion problems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1. System of Forces   05
Rectangular components of forces in space, moment, couple, Varignon’s theorem,
resolution of forces, resultant of force system (coplanar, non-coplanar), concept
of virtual work, principle of virtual work.
2. Application of System of Forces and Equilibrium   08
Conditions of equilibrium, types of support, loads and beams, free body
diagrams, support reactions.
Friction
Laws of friction, angle of friction, angle of repose, cone of friction, equilibrium of
bodies on rough horizontal and inclined plane, application to inclined planes,
wedges, ladder & screw jack.
Analysis of Pin Jointed Plane Trusses
Perfect truss, analysis using method of joints and method of sections.
3. Centroid and Moment of Inertia   03
Centroid, moment of inertia, polar moment of inertia, and product of inertia,
parallel and perpendicular axis theorem.

Velocity and acceleration in terms of rectangular coordinate system, rectilinear
motion, curvilinear motion, projectile motion, tangential and normal component
of acceleration, acceleration - time, velocity- time graphs and their uses, relative
velocity
Kinematics of Rigid Bodies
Translation, pure rotation and plane motion of rigid bodies, instantaneous centre
of rotation for the velocity for bodies in plane motion, link mechanisms (up to
two links).
5. Kinetics of Particles   07
Newton’s laws of motion, D’Alembert’s principle, equation of dynamic
equilibrium, linear motion, curvilinear motion.
Kinetics of Rigid Bodies
D’Alembert’s principle for bodies under translational motion, rotational motion
about a fixed axis and plane motion.

Course Objective
This course is aimed at detailed introduction of various key manufacturing processes such as casting,
welding, forging, rolling, extrusion, drawing and machining. The course has been structured to impart the
in-depth understanding of industrial applications of various processes and equipment used in
manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Identify different types of patterns, moulding sands, and casting techniques
2. Explain the principles and applications of rolling, forging, and extrusion processes
3. Classify various welding techniques and their applications in manufacturing
4. Apply suitable metal forming and joining techniques based on material and process requirements
5. Analyze the working principles and machining operations of a lathe machine
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Metal Casting   09
Pattern Making
Types of patterns, allowances, colour coding.
Moulding sands
Types, properties, preparation and testing of sand. Core boxes, core making, types of
cores and their manufacturing; Gating system – runner and risers.
Moulding processes
Shell moulding, CO2 moulding, investment casting, die casting, centrifugal casting
and continuous casting; Study of various defects in castings.
2   Forming processes   08
Cold and hot working.
Rolling
Principle and mechanism, types of rolling mills, various rolling processes and their
applications, defects in rolling.
Forging
Classification of forging processes, basic categories and methods of forging.
Extrusion
Hot and cold extrusion, Extrusion equipment, defects in extruded parts.
Wire and tube Drawing
Metal stamping and embossing, blanking, piercing, bending, deep drawing.

processes, Arc welding - Types, submerged arc welding, gas metal arc welding,
shielded metal arc welding, tungsten arc welding – theory and their applications;
electron beam welding, laser beam welding, Solid state welding processes - ultrasonic
welding, friction welding, resistance welding and its types - spot, seam and projection

Pre-requisite: Physics, Chemistry
Course Objective
The course is aimed at imparting basic knowledge of science of materials and physical metallurgy. This
course introduces and cements the concept of structure property correlations. It is designed to lay the
foundation for the detailed understanding of mechanical behavior of materials, phase diagrams, heat
treatment and failure of materials. The students are also introduced to certain applications of ferrous,
non-ferrous and new age materials.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Relate mechanical properties with the mechanical processing of materials
2. Demonstrate the mechanical behaviour of metals using destructive and non-destructive testing
3. Analyze the root cause of failure in different types of materials
4. Interpret Phase Transformations in Iron-Iron Carbon Alloys
5. Recommend suitable heat treatment processes with the help of phase diagrams.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Mechanical Behavior of Metals   05
Deformation
Crystal structures and imperfections, elastic and plastic deformation.
Deformation in single crystal and polycrystalline materials. Cold and Hot
working of materials and Strain hardening of metals. Recrystallization
annealing, recovery and grain growth.
2   Testing of Materials   04
Destructive Testing
Basic mechanical properties, tensile testing, hardness testing, Impact testing.
Non-Destructive Testing
Dye Penetrant, Magnetic Particle and Ultrasonic testing.
3   Failure of Metals   05
Fracture: Definition and types of fracture.
Fatigue: Definition and significance of cyclic stress, mechanism of fatigue
failure. S-N curve and its interpretation, Notch effect, surface effect, Corrosion
and thermal fatigue.
Creep: Definition and significance of creep, analysis of classical creep curve,
creep resistant materials.
4   Phase Diagrams   05
Concept of solidification of metals, Solidification of pure metals, solid
solutions. Hume Rothery rules, Phase rule, Cooling curves, Important binary

Course Objective
This course is designed to introduce the fundamentals of automation and its importance in mechanical
engineering industries. This course helps the students to understand the basic concepts of automated
systems, including sensors, actuators, mechanisms, and fluid power elements used in manufacturing and
material handling. Students also develop an understanding of the integration of mechanical systems with
automation components and the role of experimentation and simulation in realizing automated
processes.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain fundamentals, applications, and types of automation drives in manufacturing
2. Identify sensors and actuators used in automated mechanical systems.
3. Analyze mechanisms and motion transfer used in mechanical automation systems.
4. Illustrate fluid power components and their role in automation systems.
5. Demonstrate automation concepts through experimentation and simulations.
Detailed Syllabus

automation, advantages and limitations of automation.

mechanical, electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, comparison of automation drives.

proximity sensors – inductive, capacitive, photoelectric, magnetic.

3   Mechanical Automation and Mechanisms

follower mechanism, Geneva mechanism, four-bar linkage.

Applications of mechanisms in assembly, packaging and indexing systems,   03
sequencing of mechanical operations using mechanisms.

1. Explain fundamental fluid properties and differentiate between various types of fluids and flow
behaviour
2. Analyze the principles of fluid statics, buoyancy, and flotation, and apply them to real-world
engineering problems
3. Apply fluid kinematics and dynamics principles to characterize fluid motion and solve engineering
problems
4. Analyze laminar and turbulent flows in pipes, including velocity distribution, shear stress, and
pressure losses
5. Estimate energy losses in pipes and pipe network performance for different flow configurations
6. Analyze boundary layer formation, thickness, separation, and drag forces in external flow
applications
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1. Fluid Properties   03
Concept of continuum, fluid properties, Classification of fluid, Newton’s law of
viscosity, stress-strain relationship.
2. Fluid Statics   10
Basic hydrostatic equation, Pascal’s Law, application to Manometers and mechanical
gauges, hydrostatic forces on plane and curved submerged surfaces.
Buoyancy and Floatation
Archimedes’ Principle, buoyancy force and centre of buoyancy, metacentre,
metacentric height, analytical method to find metacentric height, condition of
equilibrium of submerged bodies, oscillation of a floating body
3. Fluid Kinematics   08
Description of fluid motion-Lagrangian method and Euler’s method, classification of
flow types- steady and unsteady, uniform and non-uniform, laminar and turbulent,
one two and three- dimensional flow, rotational and irrotational, laminar and
turbulent, compressible and incompressible.
Flow patterns- stream lines, path lines, stream tubes and streak lines. Continuity
equation (Cartesian and polar co-ordinates), circulation and vorticity, velocity
potential and stream function.
B Tech/Mechanical/Sem-V/2026-27/Page 5
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
4. Fluid Dynamics   09
Euler’s equation of motion, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications-venturimeter,
orificemeter, rotameter, pitot tube, Impulse-Momentum equation and its applications,
Reynolds Transport Theorem and its application.
Dimensional Analysis
Secondary or derived quantities, Reyleigh method, Buckingham−𝜋theorem,
dimensionless numbers, Theory of similarity, Model laws.
5. Laminar Flow   10
Navier-Stokes equation of motion, developing expression for flow rate, pressure drop,
shear stress, friction factor. Flow of viscous fluid in circular pipes- Hagen Poiseuille
law, Couette flow.
Turbulent Flow
Shear stresses in turbulent flow, theories of turbulent shear stress, hydro-dynamically
smooth and rough surface, modeling of turbulence, Moody’s chart.
Flow Through Pipes
Energy losses in pipes: Minor and Major losses, Darcy-Weisbatch equation for head
loss in pipes, hydraulic gradient lines, and total energy lines, pipes in series and
parallel, Equivalent pipe.
6. Boundary Layer Theory   05
Concept of Boundary layer, Boundary layer over flat plate, Boundary Layer thickness,
momentum thickness, displacement thickness and energy thickness. Boundary layer
equations and their solutions. Blasius solution (without derivation), Von-Karman
momentum integral equation. Laminar boundary layer and turbulent boundary layer.
Separation and control and Concept of drag.
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Materials Engineering
Course Objective
The main objective of this course is to provide basic understanding of composite materials used in
various engineering applications. The course also explains mechanical properties, micromechanics
and manufacturing methods of composite materials.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Relate processing, characterization and applications of various composite materials
2. Apply failure criteria and evaluate the results of composite materials
3. Evaluate the relative merits of using alternatives (corresponding to various simple and composite
materials) for important engineering and other applications
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   03
Definition, history, characteristics, concept of composite materials, comparison
with metals, composite materials in engineering, industrial scenario, advantages
and limitations of composites
2.   Types of Matrix Materials and Reinforcements   06
Functions of a matrix, desired properties of a matrix, polymer matrix
(thermosets and thermoplastics), metal matrix, ceramic matrix, carbon matrix,
glass matrix etc., role and selection of reinforcement materials, types of fibers -
glass fibers, boron fibers, carbon fibers, organic fibers - aramid fibers, ceramic
fibers - oxide fibers and nonoxide fibers, alumina fibers, silicon carbide fibers,
tungsten carbide fibers, multiphase fibers, whiskers, flakes etc.
3.   Types of Composites   14
Based on matrix materials, polymer matrix composites (PMC), metal matrix
composites (MMC), ceramic matrix composites (CMC), carbon fiber composites;
based on reinforcements, fiber reinforced composites, fiber reinforced polymer
(FRP) composites, laminated composites, particulate composites, polymer
matrix composites (PMC) – processing, structure and properties, applications,
metal matrix composites (MMC) – types, processing, properties, applications,
ceramic matrix composites (CMC) - processing, properties, applications, carbon
fiber composites - processing, properties, applications.
4.   Micromechanics and Macromechanics of Composites   06
Density, mechanical properties - prediction of elastic constants, elastic constants
of an isotropic material, elastic constants of a lamina.
5.   Monotonic Strength and Fracture   08
Tensile strength of unidirectional fiber composites, compressive strength of
unidirectional fiber composites, fracture modes in composites - single and
multiple fractures, deboning and delamination fracture.

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering

Nanocomposites, hybrid composites, self-healing composites, self-reinforced
composites, in-situ composites, smart composites, industrial applications of
composite materials - aerospace industries, automobile and other surface
transport industries, packaging industries, house hold and sports components
etc., recycling of composites
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics
Course Objective
This course focusses on the application of classical mechanics to various biological problems by
combining the fields of biology and physiology. This course is concerned with the application of
principles of mechanics to the conceptualization, design, development and analysis of equipment
and systems as applied to human body.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Correlate mechanics, biomechanics and kinesiology and differentiate between their uses in the
analysis of human movement
2. Relate the reference positions, planes, and axes associated with the human body
3. Evaluate the skeletal considerations for movement and the different mechanics involved in
bones
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Basic Terminology   05
Biomechanics, kinesiology, anatomy, functional anatomy
linear motion, angular motion, kinematics, kinetics, statics and dynamics.
2.   Kinematic Concepts for Analyzing Human Motion   05
Linear, angular and general motion, anatomical reference position, planes
and axes, joint movement terminology, spatial reference systems, analyzing
human movement and tools for measuring kinematic quantities.
3.   Applications of Statics to Biomechanics   10
Skeletal joints, skeletal muscles, mechanics of the elbow, mechanics of the
shoulder, mechanics of the spinal column, mechanics of the hip, mechanics
of the knee and mechanics of the ankle.
4.   Skeletal Considerations for Movement   10
Bone tissue function, composition of bone tissue, macroscopic structure of
bone, bone formation, strength and stiffness of bone, loads applied to bone,
stress fractures, articular cartilage, fibrocartilage and ligaments.
Total   30

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes I and II, Machine Drawing
Course Objective
The objective of the course is to impart introductory knowledge of Additive Manufacturing (AM)
and its capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industries. The course is structured to
acquaint the students with the operating principles and applications of most prominent
technologies in the field of additive manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Compare the fundamental principles of various additive manufacturing technologies in terms
of material requirements, manufacturing technologies and applications
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the product
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Additive Manufacturing   06
Introduction to AM, history of AM, definition, distinction between AM, CNC
& other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications
of AM processes, design for additive manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry:
present and future, AM process chain, AM file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF, PLY,
VRML, and LEO), part orientation, support generation, model slicing,
contour generation, machine set-up, build file preparation.
2.   Classification of Additive Manufacturing Techniques   12
Material Extrusion:
Process mechanism, process parameters, extrusion of: ceramics, metals,
biomaterials, composites, contour crafting, concrete printing
Vat Polymerization:
Process mechanism, process parameters, advantages, disadvantages,
applications, Digital Light Processing (DLP), recent advances, Large-Scale
Rapid Liquid Printing.
Binder & material jetting processes:
Binder jetting process workflow, material requirements, binder-powder
interaction, binder properties.
Material Jetting process workflow, thermal and piezoelectric inkjet, material
jetting fluid mechanics, drop-on-demand and continuous methods of MJ.
Powder bed fusion AM process:

Selective laser sintering (SLS), process mechanism, process parameters,
selective laser melting (SLM), process workflow and material requirements,
powder melting mechanisms, electron beam melting (EBM) process.
Sheet Lamination AM Processes:
Process mechanism, process parameters, ultrasonic additive manufacturing
(UAM), ultrasonic welding fundamentals, UAM process parameters
Directed Energy Deposition (DED) Processes:
Process workflow, materials feeding for DED: powder (Laser Engineered Net
Shaping) and wire, process parameters, cold spray.
3.   Post- Processing   04
Product quality evaluation, need for post-processing, support material
removal, surface finish improvement, aesthetic improvement, property
enhancements using non-thermal and thermal techniques.
4.   Design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM)   04
Design guidelines: part orientation, support, geometry considerations, layer
thickness, part size, material consideration, residual stress, topology
optimization, case studies on design for AM.
5.   Applications of AM & Industry 4.0   04

engineering, economic consideration, Industry 4.0 for AM, case studies on
application of AM in various industries.

Course Objective
The objective of this course is to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of industrial design
principles and their application in modern manufacturing and engineering systems. It aims to develop

enhance safety, comfort, and operational efficiency. The course also emphasizes aesthetic concepts,

Pre-requisite: Mathematics I, Mathematics II, Engineering Mechanics, Strength of Materials, Heat
Transfer
Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to the finite element methods. The guidelines for selecting
displacement functions and the concepts that should be considered when modeling are discussed as
the course progresses. This course describes how to treat different types of forces for two-dimensional
elements and to solve one-dimensional heat transfer problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Understanding the basic principles of FEA, including discretization, element types and shape
functions
2. Derive the stiffness matrix for the beam and Constant-Strain Triangular element
3. Illustrate FEA characteristic equations to analyze plain stress, plain strain and derive element
matrices for CST elements
4. Develop FEA Characteristic equations for Isoparamteric problems and heat transfer problem
5. Analyze solution accuracy by performing error estimation, mesh refinement studies, and
convergence analysis to improve simulation reliability
6. Use ANSYS in real-world mechanical, thermal, and structural engineering problems to analyze
their behavior
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   07
Brief history, matrix notation, general steps, applications and advantages of the
FEM, computer programs for the FEM, stiffness matrix for a spring element,
spring assemblage, direct stiffness method, boundary conditions.
2.   Truss   08
Stiffness matrix for a bar element, displacement function, transformation of
vectors in two dimensions, global stiffness matrix for bar arbitrarily oriented in
the plane, computation of stress for a bar in the x – y plane, solution of a plane
truss, use of symmetry in structures, inclined supports.
3.   Beam and Frame   10
Beam stiffness, assemblage of beam stiffness matrices, direct stiffness method,
distributed loading, beam element with nodal hinge, two-dimensional arbitrarily
oriented beam element, rigid plane frame, skewed supports, beam element
arbitrarily oriented in space, concept of substructure analysis

Stiffness Matrix, Body and Surface Forces, Plane Stress Problem, Bilinear
Rectangle, Comparison of Elements
5.   Practical Considerations in Modeling   05
Finite Element Modeling, Equilibrium and Compatibility of Finite Element
Results, Convergence of Solution and Mesh Refinement.
6.   Heat Transfer and Mass Transport   08
Basic Differential Equation, Heat Transfer with Convection, Thermal

Pre-requisite: Engineering Physics
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to develop awareness and basic skills necessary for the reliable
measurements and measuring instruments and impart knowledge on methods of measurement of
different engineering parameters such as pressure, temperature, displacement, etc. and different
metrological instruments for linear, angular, taper and surface finish measurements.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Describe various terminologies associated with measurement and metrology
2. Understand the objectives of metrology, methods of measurement, standards of measurement
& various measurement parameters
3. Choose sensors, devices and methods for measurement of specific parameters with required
accuracy
4. Demonstrate the ability to apply precision measurement techniques to ensure accuracy and
quality control in mechanical systems
5. Measure and derive important dimensions of thread forms and gears
6. Analyze the impact of various factors on the measurement process

measurement, resistance thermometry, pyrometer.

Piezo-electric pressure gauge, Low vacuum gauges - McLeod gauge, thermal
conductivity gauge, Pirani gauge, ionization gauge, comparison of different
pressure measuring instruments.
3.   Strain Gauges   04
Classification, electrical strain gauge: working principle and types, gauge factor
(analytical treatment), analysis of Wheatstone’s network using strain gauges,
mounting of strain gauges.

and perpendicular axis theorems for structural analysis

Course Objective
This course is aimed at detailed introduction of various key manufacturing processes such as casting,
welding, forging, rolling, extrusion, drawing and machining. The course has been structured to impart the
in-depth understanding of industrial applications of various processes and equipment used in
manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Identify different types of patterns, moulding sands, and casting techniques
2. Explain the principles and applications of rolling, forging, and extrusion processes
3. Classify various welding techniques and their applications in manufacturing
4. Apply suitable metal forming and joining techniques based on material and process requirements
5. Analyze the working principles and machining operations of a lathe machine

Pre-requisite: Physics, Chemistry
Course Objective
The course is aimed at imparting basic knowledge of science of materials and physical metallurgy.
This course introduces and cements the concept of structure property correlations. It is designed to lay
the foundation for the detailed understanding of mechanical behavior of materials, phase diagrams,
heat treatment and failure of materials. The students are also introduced to certain applications of
ferrous, non-ferrous and new age materials.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Relate mechanical properties with the mechanical processing of materials
2. Demonstrate the mechanical behaviour of metals using destructive and non-destructive
testing
3. Analyse the root cause of failure in different types of materials
4. Interpret Phase Transformations in Iron-Iron Carbon Alloys
5. Recommend heat treatment processes with the help of phase diagrams
6. Select appropriate materials for various applications depending on the structural requirements

1   Mechanical Behavior of Metals   05

working of materials and Strain hardening of metals. Recrystallization annealing,
recovery and grain growth.

resistant materials.

Course Objective
The course provide basic orientation towards microeconomic principles and help them understand the
functions of management. This course also aims to understand issues dealing with small-scale economic
phenomena and concepts such as prices and output of firms, industries and resource owners along with
examining market impact of technological change with regards to understand broader aspects of the
economy and its environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand Fundamental Economic Concepts - Explain the basic concepts of economics,
including scarcity of resources, economic systems, and demand-supply analysis. (K1, K2)
2. Demonstrate Consumer and Producer Behavior - Apply utility analysis and production
theories to understand consumer decision-making and cost structures in different market
conditions (K2, K3)
3. Illustrate Market Structures and Pricing Mechanisms - Differentiate between market
structures such as monopoly, oligopoly, perfect and imperfect competition, and explain
price and output determination. (K2, K3)
4. Apply Management Principles in Decision-Making - Demonstrate an understanding of
management functions such as planning, organizing, decision-making, and leadership
based on classical and modern theories. (K2, K3)
5. Understand the Role of Business Functions in Organizational Success - Examine the
significance of key business functions such as finance, marketing, human resources, and
operations, and their interdependence in achieving organizational objectives. (K1, K2)

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics
Course Objective
The course is aimed at providing adequate understanding of the fundamentals of stresses and strains
in deformable bodies subjected to various types of static loads. It is designed to impart the knowledge
of basic concepts of deformation & deflection, identifying the relevant tests to be performed on beams
and power transmitting shafts. It develops the ability to assess the strength of engineering materials and
subsequently examine the failure criteria of structural members using relevant analysis.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain fundamental concepts of stress, strain and material properties in structural analysis
2. Construct shear force and bending moment diagrams for statically determinate beams under
various loading conditions
3. Analyze beam bending stresses, shear stresses, and deflections using beam theory
4. Analyze torsional stresses in solid and hollow circular shafts used in power transmission
5. Determine principal stresses, maximum shear stress, and stress transformation using Mohr’s circle
6. Determine mechanical properties and access failure characteristics by material testing using UTM
or similar equipment.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Stress and Strain   06
Strain, modulus of elasticity, modulus of rigidity, bulk modulus, yield stress,
ultimate stress, factor of safety, shear stress, Poisson’s ratio, analysis of members
made of composite materials.

beams for different types of loading.
Simple Theory of Bending

flexure formula, section modulus, moment of resistance of a section.
Shear Stress in Beams
Distribution of shear stress across plane sections used commonly for structural
purposes.
3   Simple Theory of Torsion   04
Torsion of circular shafts – solid and hollow, stresses in power transmission shafts
(including shafts in series and parallel).
4   Bending Moment Combined with Axial Loads   05

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics
Course Objective
The course is aimed at developing the detailed understanding of various mechanism used in devices or
machines. This course focuses on analysis of the motion of mechanisms and to design mechanisms that
yield the desired motion. The course is designed for the students to understand and master the concepts
of displacement, velocity and acceleration of simple mechanisms and machine components. These
include cam profile and its analysis, gear kinematics with gear train calculations, belt drives and chain
drives, and friction clutches and brakes.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the fundamentals of links, mechanisms, machines, brakes and clutches
2. Analyse planar mechanism for displacement, velocity and acceleration graphically and analytically
3. Construct various type of Cam profiles and analyze the standard motion of the follower
4. Illustrate the machine components like belt, ropes and chains for required mechanisms
5. Estimate the performance and efficiency of brakes and clutches, considering frictional forces and
their impact on machine operation
6. Evaluate simple, compound, reverted, and epicyclic gear trains to determine velocity ratios

Spatial Mechanisms, Kinematic Pairs, Kinematic Chains, Kinematic Diagrams,
Kinematic Inversion, four bar chain, single and double Slider Crank Mechanisms
and their Inversions, Degrees of Freedom, Mobility and range of movement -
Kutzbach and Grubler’s criterion, Number Synthesis, Grashof’s criterion, straight
line mechanisms.

method for four bar pin jointed linkages and four bar slider crank linkages.
Velocity and Acceleration analysis - relative method four bar pin jointed linkages
and four bar slider crank linkages.

Pre-requisite: Engineering Thermodynamics
Course Objective
This course describes the application of Engineering Thermodynamics to model the energy
conversion phenomenon. With this course one can impart knowledge of air compressors and
components of steam power system. This course provides basics of I.C engines, refrigeration
systems and air conditioning systems and also build a bridge for these courses.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Analyse the working principles and performance parameters of reciprocating and rotary air
compressors
2. Evaluate the design, efficiency, and critical pressure conditions in nozzles and diffusers
3. Apply thermodynamic principles to assess the performance of steam generators and turbines
4. Examine the performance and working conditions of condensers and cooling towers
5. Assess different refrigeration and air-conditioning systems, including refrigerants, cycles,
and working principles
6. Evaluate the performance of internal combustion (IC) engines, including heat balance
calculations and valve/port timing diagrams

1.   Reciprocating Air Compressors   09
Working principle, work done, Effect of clearance volume, Single and
multistage compressors, Volumetric efficiency, Intercooling in multistage
compressors, calculation of power requirement, Rotary compressors.
Review of Thermodynamics, Vapour Power cycles, Binary Vapour Cycle,
Combined Cycle and Co-generation.
2.   Steam Generators   08
Fire Tube Boilers, Water Tube Boilers, Boiler Mountings and Accessories,
High Pressure Boilers. Draught, Performance of Boilers, Combustion of Fuel.
3.   Nozzles and Diffusers   09

and supersaturated Flow.
Steam Turbines

diagrams for simple and multistage turbines - Speed regulations –
Governors.

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics, Partial Differential Equations and Laplace transforms
Course Objective
The course is aimed at delivering detailed understanding of fluid properties and their static - dynamic
nature. This course teaches the analytical techniques necessary for grasping fundamental behavior of
incompressible fluids. It is designed for the students to learn the principles of laminar flow, turbulent
flow, and boundary layer theory to solve important practical problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain fundamental fluid properties and differentiate between various types of fluids and flow
behavior
2. Analyze the principles of fluid statics, buoyancy, and flotation, and apply them to real-world
engineering problems
3. Apply fluid kinematics and dynamics principles to characterize fluid motion and solve
engineering problems
4. Analyze laminar and turbulent flows in pipes, including velocity distribution, shear stress, and
pressure losses
5. Estimate energy losses in pipes and pipe network performance for different flow configurations
6. Analyze boundary layer formation, thickness, separation, and drag forces in external flow
applications
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1. Fluid Properties   03
Concept of continuum, fluid properties, Classification of fluid, Newton’s law of
viscosity, stress-strain relationship.
2. Fluid Statics   10
Basic hydrostatic equation, Pascal’s Law, application to Manometers and mechanical
gauges, hydrostatic forces on plane and curved submerged surfaces.
Buoyancy and Floatation
Archimedes’ Principle, buoyancy force and centre of buoyancy, metacentre,
metacentric height, analytical method to find metacentric height, condition of
equilibrium of submerged bodies, oscillation of a floating body
3. Fluid Kinematics   08
Description of fluid motion-Lagrangian method and Euler’s method, classification of
flow types- steady and unsteady, uniform and non-uniform, laminar and turbulent,
one two and three- dimensional flow, rotational and irrotational, laminar and
turbulent, compressible and incompressible.
Flow patterns- stream lines, path lines, stream tubes and streak lines. Continuity
equation (Cartesian and polar co-ordinates), circulation and vorticity, velocity
potential and stream function.
B Tech/Mechanical/Sem-V/2025-26/Page 5
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
4. Fluid Dynamics   09
Euler’s equation of motion, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications-venturimeter,
orificemeter, rotameter, pitot tube, Impulse-Momentum equation and its applications,
Reynolds Transport Theorem and its application.
Dimensional Analysis
Secondary or derived quantities, Reyleigh method, Buckingham−𝜋theorem,
dimensionless numbers, Theory of similarity, Model laws.
5. Laminar Flow   10
Navier-Stokes equation of motion, developing expression for flow rate, pressure drop,
shear stress, friction factor. Flow of viscous fluid in circular pipes- Hagen Poiseuille
law, Couette flow.
Turbulent Flow
Shear stresses in turbulent flow, theories of turbulent shear stress, hydro-dynamically
smooth and rough surface, modeling of turbulence, Moody’s chart.
Flow Through Pipes
Energy losses in pipes: Minor and Major losses, Darcy-Weisbatch equation for head
loss in pipes, hydraulic gradient lines, and total energy lines, pipes in series and
parallel, Equivalent pipe.
6. Boundary Layer Theory   05
Concept of Boundary layer, Boundary layer over flat plate, Boundary Layer thickness,
momentum thickness, displacement thickness and energy thickness. Boundary layer
equations and their solutions. Blasius solution (without derivation), Von-Karman
momentum integral equation. Laminar boundary layer and turbulent boundary layer.
Separation and control and Concept of drag.
Total   45

1. Frank M. White, Fluid Mechanics, 7th Edition, McGraw Hill, 2011.
2. S.K. Som, G.Biswas, S. Chakraborty, Introduction to Fluid Mechanics and Fluid Machines, 3rd
Edition (revised), TMH Delhi, 2015.

2. K.L. Kumar, Engineering Fluid Mechanics, 3rd Edition, S. Chand, 2016.
3. P.N. Modi, S.M. Seth, Hydraulics and Fluid Mechanics including Hydraulic Machines, 19th Edition,
Rajsons Publications, 2015.
4. K. Subrmanyan, Fluid Mechanics and Hydraulic Machines: Problems and Solutions, 2nd Edition, Tata
McGraw Hill, 2019.
5. R.V. Giles, J.B. Evett, Cheng Liu, Fluid Mechanics and Hydraulics, 4th Edition, Schaum Outline
Series, McGraw Hill, 2013.

The main objective of this course is to provide basic understanding of composite materials used in
various engineering applications. The course also explains mechanical properties, micromechanics

Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Relate processing, characterization and applications of various composite materials
2. Apply failure criteria and evaluate the results of composite materials
3. Evaluate the relative merits of using alternatives (corresponding to various simple and composite
materials) for important engineering and other applications

Course Objective
This course focusses on the application of classical mechanics to various biological problems by
combining the fields of biology and physiology. This course is concerned with the application of
principles of mechanics to the conceptualization, design, development and analysis of equipment
and systems as applied to human body.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Correlate mechanics, biomechanics and kinesiology and differentiate between their uses in the
analysis of human movement
2. Relate the reference positions, planes, and axes associated with the human body
3. Evaluate the skeletal considerations for movement and the different mechanics involved in
bones
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Basic Terminology   05
Biomechanics, kinesiology, anatomy, functional anatomy
linear motion, angular motion, kinematics, kinetics, statics and dynamics.
2.   Kinematic Concepts for Analyzing Human Motion   05
Linear, angular and general motion, anatomical reference position, planes
and axes, joint movement terminology, spatial reference systems, analyzing
human movement and tools for measuring kinematic quantities.
3.   Applications of Statics to Biomechanics   10
Skeletal joints, skeletal muscles, mechanics of the elbow, mechanics of the
shoulder, mechanics of the spinal column, mechanics of the hip, mechanics
of the knee and mechanics of the ankle.
4.   Skeletal Considerations for Movement   10
Bone tissue function, composition of bone tissue, macroscopic structure of
bone, bone formation, strength and stiffness of bone, loads applied to bone,
stress fractures, articular cartilage, fibrocartilage and ligaments.

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes I and II, Machine Drawing
Course Objective
The objective of the course is to impart introductory knowledge of Additive Manufacturing (AM)
and its capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industries. The course is structured to
acquaint the students with the operating principles and applications of most prominent
technologies in the field of additive manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Compare the fundamental principles of various additive manufacturing technologies in terms
of material requirements, manufacturing technologies and applications
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the product
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Additive Manufacturing   06
Introduction to AM, history of AM, definition, distinction between AM, CNC
& other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications
of AM processes, design for additive manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry:
present and future, AM process chain, AM file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF, PLY,
VRML, and LEO), part orientation, support generation, model slicing,
contour generation, machine set-up, build file preparation.
2.   Classification of Additive Manufacturing Techniques   12
Material Extrusion:
Process mechanism, process parameters, extrusion of: ceramics, metals,
biomaterials, composites, contour crafting, concrete printing
Vat Polymerization:
Process mechanism, process parameters, advantages, disadvantages,
applications, Digital Light Processing (DLP), recent advances, Large-Scale
Rapid Liquid Printing.
Binder & material jetting processes:
Binder jettng process workflow, material requirements, binder-powder
interaction, binder properties.
Material Jetting process workflow, thermal and piezoelectric inkjet, material
jetting fluid mechanics, drop-on-demand and continuous methods of MJ.
Powder bed fusion AM process:

Process mechanism, process parameters, ultrasonic additive manufacturing
(UAM), ultrasonic welding fundamentals, UAM process parameters

Process workflow, materials feeding for DED: powder (Laser Engineered Net
Shaping) and wire, process parameters, cold spray.

Product quality evaluation, need for post-processing, support material
removal, surface finish improvement, aesthetic improvement, property
enhancements using non-thermal and thermal techniques.

Course Objective
This course is designed to provide knowledge of different modes of heat transfer with different laws
of conduction, convection and radiation. It also helps to provide understanding of different
applications of conduction, convection and radiation.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Identify and explain different modes of heat transfer
2. Applying heat transfer principles to calculate heat transfer rates in steady and transient state
conditions in different geometries and fins
3. Analysing forced and natural convection heat transfer, including the use of empirical
correlations to determine convection heat transfer
4. Apply radiation heat transfer principles to calculate heat exchange between surfaces with
different emissivity and geometries
5. Apply basic principles of heat transfer to design heat transfer devices
6. Analyze real-world engineering problems using heat transfer principles

1.   Basic Concepts   15
Modes of Heat Transfer, its mechanism and mathematical models.

ordinates (for cylindrical and spherical walls derivation of Fourier’s three-
dimensional equation is not included), thermal resistance, solution of Fourier’s
equation for one dimensional steady state heat conduction through various
configurations such as plane, cylindrical, spherical wall, composite medium.
Critical thickness of insulation and its importance.
Heat Transfer from Extended Surfaces
Types of fins, Governing equation, fin effectiveness, efficiency of fins, concept of
corrected fin length, application of fins.
Unsteady State Heat Conduction
Lumped System Analysis
2.   Convection Heat Transfer   15
Forced and natural convection, hydrodynamic and thermal boundary layer,
Convection heat transfer coefficient, Momentum and energy equation for laminar
boundary layer, Laminar and Turbulent flow, principles of dimensional analysis,
physical significance of dimensionless numbers, Nusselt number, Prandtl
number, Reynolds number, Grashof number.

radiation properties. Microwave Heating.
Basic laws of radiation; Planck’s law, Kirchoff’s law, Stefan-Boltzman law, Wein’s-

shape factor for simple geometries, heat exchange between non-black

This course provides the understanding of the development and design aspects of products, impart
knowledge of business and technical concerns about the different methodologies of product
development. This course also discusses the concept of product life cycle and product data
management.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1.   Identify the different stages of product development and design with modern approaches
2. Apply the knowledge of Technology Forecasting using S-Curve in product development as
per customers need
3. Describe the process of benchmarking of products, technologies & techniques product design

concept selection process, Pugh’s concept, selection charts, numerical concept
scoring, process of concept embodiment, system modeling, Failure Mode Effect
Analysis (FMEA), functional modeling and decomposition, fast method, subtract

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics and Strength of Materials
Course Objective
To provide an understanding of the basics of aerodynamics in aircraft. To impart knowledge of
boundary layer theory. To introduce the aerospace vehicle and space vehicle design. To introduce wind
tunnel testing
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Analyse the basic flight mathematical aspects and potential flows
2. Discuss structural design of aircraft and space vehicles
3. Classify types of wind tunnel and describe wind tunnel testing technique
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Aerodynamics   05
Importance of Aerodynamic, four principles of aerodynamics, three laws of
aerodynamics, six fundamentals of flight.
2.   Applied Aerodynamics   10
Panel methods, pressure distribution, Kutta conditions, flow around airfoil
(unsteady potential flow, compressible flow, axisymmetric flow) and slender
body theories. Flight vehicle aerodynamics, rotor aerodynamics – low Reynolds
number aerodynamics
3.   Aircraft Vehicle Design   10
Design considerations for civilian and military aircraft, weight estimation, airfoil
and geometry selection, thrust to weight ratio and wing loading, initial sizing,
propulsion, landing gear and subsystems, aerodynamics, stability, control, and
handling qualities, flight mechanics and performance issues, aircraft layout and
configuration, structural aspects and constraint analysis.
4.   Space Vehicle Design   10
History of rocketry & launch vehicles, Current & future launch vehicles.
Orbit/trajectory requirements and missions. Launch vehicle sizing, launch into an
orbit, rocket propulsion (configuration and structural design), design for re-entry
5.   Wind Tunnel Techniques   10
Introduction to wind tunnel, Classification of wind tunnels, Elements of wind
tunnel, Conventional measurement techniques, wind tunnel testing technique.

This course is designed to impart knowledge of an IC engine and the ignition systems. It also
introduces the modern developments in internal combustion engines with optical measurement

After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain advanced engine technologies and emission norms
2. Apply concepts of different alternate fuels used for SI and CI engines
3. Analyze environmental, social, and technological issues related to the future widespread use
of internal combustion engines

Unit   Description   Duration

Compression ratio, energy supply to an engine, power developed by engine,

relative merits.

Types of cooling, cooling of critical engine components, re-cooling the coolant,
comparison of air cooled and liquid cooled engines.

Classification of fuel delivery systems, fuel transfer pumps, fixed jet carburetor,

Battery ignition system, requirements for satisfactory operation of the ignition

electronic ignition system.

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics, Fluid Mechanics and Strength of Materials
Course Objective
This course introduces the basic concepts of vibrations and discusses free vibration of an undamped
single-degree of-freedom system. This course also deals with two-degree-of-freedom systems, which
require two independent coordinates to describe their motion. The modeling of continuous
systems as multidegree-of-freedom systems is also presented in this course.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Derive the equation of motion of a single-degree-of-freedom system
2. Solve two-degree-of-freedom free- and forced-vibration problems
3. Formulate the equations of motion of multidegree-of-freedom systems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Fundamentals of Vibration   07
Basic Concepts of Vibration, Classification of Vibration, Vibration Analysis
Procedure, Spring Elements, Mass or Inertia Elements, Damping Elements,
Harmonic Motion, Harmonic Analysis
2.   Single-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   08
Free Vibration of an Undamped Translational System, Free Vibration of an
Undamped Torsional System, Free Vibration with Viscous Damping, Free
Vibration with Coulomb Damping.
3.   Two-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   06
Equations of Motion for Forced Vibration, Free Vibration Analysis of an
Undamped System, Torsional System, Forced-Vibration Analysis.
4.   Multidegree-of-Freedom Systems   09
Modeling of Continuous Systems as Multi degree of Freedom Systems, Equations
of Motion, Influence Coefficients, Generalized Coordinates and Generalized
Forces, Lagrange s Equations, Equations of Motion of Undamped Systems in
Matrix Form, Eigenvalue Problem
Total   30

1. S. S. Rao, Mechanical Vibration, Addison Wesley, 2004.
2. Michel Géradin and Daniel J. Rixen, Mechanical Vibrations Theory and Application to Structural

and its capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industries. It teaches about various
additive manufacturing techniques.

relevant to the planning, design, and operations of manufacturing or service firms. This course
also develops an understanding about quality management practices in organizations that
facilitate organizational effectiveness.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -

subject and outline the strategic concerns involved in operations decisions

in-time and MRP systems along with their limitations

Course Objective
This course focusses on a critical understanding and strategic importance of operations management.
The students can get familiar with interactions between firms based on parameters such as
information sharing, contracting and coordination in supply chain management.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Evaluate the application of operations management policies and techniques to the service
sector as well as manufacturing firms

procurement

Pre-requisite: Mathematics I, Mathematics II, Engineering Mechanics, Strength of Materials, Heat

Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to the finite element methods. The guidelines for selecting
displacement functions and the concepts that should be considered when modeling are discussed as
the course progresses. This course describes how to treat different types of forces for two-dimensional
elements and to solve one-dimensional heat transfer problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Understanding the basic principles of FEA, including discretization, element types and shape
functions
2. Derive the stiffness matrix for the beam and Constant-Strain Triangular element
3. Illustrate FEA characteristic equations to analyze plain stress, plain strain and derive element
matrices for CST elements
4. Develop FEA Characteristic equations for Isoparamteric problems and heat transfer problem
5. Analyze solution accuracy by performing error estimation, mesh refinement studies, and
convergence analysis to improve simulation reliability
6. Use ANSYS in real-world mechanical, thermal, and structural engineering problems to analyze
their behavior
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   07
Brief history, matrix notation, general steps, applications and advantages of the
FEM, computer programs for the FEM, stiffness matrix for a spring element,
spring assemblage, direct stiffness method, boundary conditions.
2.   Truss   08
Stiffness matrix for a bar element, displacement function, transformation of
vectors in two dimensions, global stiffness matrix for bar arbitrarily oriented in
the plane, computation of stress for a bar in the x – y plane, solution of a plane
truss, use of symmetry in structures, inclined supports.
3.   Beam and Frame   10
Beam stiffness, assemblage of beam stiffness matrices, direct stiffness method,
distributed loading, beam element with nodal hinge, two-dimensional arbitrarily
oriented beam element, rigid plane frame, skewed supports, beam element
arbitrarily oriented in space, concept of substructure analysis

Stiffness Matrix, Body and Surface Forces, Plane Stress Problem, Bilinear
Rectangle, Comparison of Elements
5.   Practical Considerations in Modeling   05
Finite Element Modeling, Equilibrium and Compatibility of Finite Element
Results, Convergence of Solution and Mesh Refinement.
6.   Heat Transfer and Mass Transport   08
Basic Differential Equation, Heat Transfer with Convection, Thermal
Conductivities, Heat Transfer Coefficients, One-Dimensional and Two-
Dimensional Finite Element Formulation, Line or Point Sources,   One-
Dimensional Heat Transfer with Mass Transport

Course Objective
The objective of this course is to develop awareness and basic skills necessary for the reliable
measurements and measuring instruments and impart knowledge on methods of measurement of
different engineering parameters such as pressure, temperature, displacement, etc. and different
metrological instruments for linear, angular, taper and surface finish measurements.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Describe various terminologies associated with measurement and metrology
2. Understand the objectives of metrology, methods of measurement, standards of measurement
& various measurement parameters
3. Choose sensors, devices and methods for measurement of specific parameters with required
accuracy
4. Demonstrate the ability to apply precision measurement techniques to ensure accuracy and
quality control in mechanical systems
5. Measure and derive important dimensions of thread forms and gears
6. Analyze the impact of various factors on the measurement process
Detailed Syllabus

1.   Introduction to Measurement   04
Need of measurement, Study of instruments, measurement methods, generalized
measurement system & its functional elements, instrument characteristics - static
& dynamic characteristics, calibration.
2.   Temperature and Pressure Measurement   10
Thermometry
Overview   of thermometry, thermometers,   thermo-electric temperature
measurement, resistance thermometry, pyrometer.
Pressure Measurement
Bourdon tubes, dead weight pressure gauge tester, diaphragm gauge, LVDT,
Piezo-electric pressure gauge, Low vacuum gauges - McLeod gauge, thermal
conductivity gauge, Pirani gauge, ionization gauge, comparison of different
pressure measuring instruments.

4.   Measurement Standards, Comparators and Angular Measurement   10
Definition and concept of metrology, measurement standards, types and sources
of errors, accuracy and precision, introduction to uncertainty in measurement,

Concept and procedure.

Line and end standards, slip gauges and linear measuring instruments.
Angular Measurement
Angle standards, sine bar, angle gauges, autocollimator, angle dekkor, optical
square, taper measurement, universal bevel protractor.
Interferometry
Basic principles, source of light, optical flats, fringe pattern and their
interpretation.

Types, construction and working of Mechanical, Optical, Electrical, Pneumatic
comparators.

and profile projector.

Pre-requisite: Basic Electrical Engineering, Engineering Mechanics and Strength of Materials
Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to wind energy and wind turbines. It introduces the current
challenges in modern wind turbine analysis, design, and development and provides a comprehensive
examination of state-of-the-art technologies.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Categorize various types of wind turbines and its principal components
2. Determine the mechanical power, types of stresses and the control parameters
3. Analyze the economics, effects on the environment, safety in operation and the potential hazards
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   10
Importance of renewable, technical issues, wind farm development, wind turbine
siting, new and future technologies, energy in a moving object and moving fluid,
power in the wind, power absorption by a turbine, wind speed variation, force
from wind, aerodynamic force, lift and drag coefficients, airfoils.
2.   Types and Components of Wind Turbine   10
Turbine classification, propeller wind turbine, The H-rotor, Darrieus turbine,
Savonius rotor, mechanical components - tower, foundation, rotor, nacelle,
gearbox, turbine brake, electrical components - generators, transformers and
anemometer.
3.   Propeller   05
Mechanical power, diagrams, mechanical power in a turbine, turbine power
variation with angular speed, daily energy production by a turbine, annual energy
production.
4.   Wind Turbine Design   10
Power accord with the wind speed, wind speed measurement, power calculations,
output power quality and requirement, blade pitch control, turbine operating
power curve, yaw control, parking brake, fault control, various operational states
of a turbine, loads on the rotor, aerodynamic loads on the blade, other blade loads,
vibrations, blade fatigue, blade construction.

comparison with other energy sources, cost per unit, onshore wind farms, noise,
view, landscape, effects on birds, RF interference and effect on communications,
offshore wind farms, effects on birds and marine animals, safety and working
with wind turbines, effect of temperature and environmental changes, protection
from lightning, ice forming on the blades, wind energy in urban areas, working
environment, possible hazards, commonsense safety rules, standardized safety
rules, and official regulations, climbing gear, minimizing the risk .
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics
Course Objective
The course is aimed at providing adequate understanding of the fundamentals of stresses and strains
in deformable bodies subjected to various types of static loads. It is designed to impart the knowledge
of basic concepts of deformation & deflection, identifying the relevant tests to be performed on beams
and power transmitting shafts. It develops the ability to assess the strength of engineering materials and
subsequently examine the failure criteria of structural members using relevant analysis.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand the resultant stresses induced in beams and other structural members
2. Evaluate the deformations of various determinate beams
3. Analyse stress on thin shells due to internal pressure
4. Calculate the stresses in circular torsion members
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Stress and Strain   06
Strain, modulus of elasticity, modulus of rigidity, bulk modulus, yield stress,
ultimate stress, factor of safety, shear stress, Poisson’s ratio, analysis of members
made of composite materials.
2   Stresses in Beams due to transverse loading   17
Shear Force and Bending Moment
Axial force, shear force and bending moment diagrams for statically determinate
beams for different types of loading.
Simple Theory of Bending
Flexure formula for straight beams, simple problems involving application of
flexure formula, section modulus, moment of resistance of a section.
Shear Stress in Beams
Distribution of shear stress across plane sections used commonly for structural
purposes.
3   Simple Theory of Torsion   04
Torsion of circular shafts – solid and hollow, stresses in power transmission shafts
(including shafts in series and parallel).
4   Bending Moment Combined with Axial Loads   05
Application to members subjected to eccentric loads, core of a section, problems
on chimneys involving lateral loads.

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics
Course Objective
The course is aimed at developing the detailed understanding of various mechanism used in
devices or machines. This course focuses on analysis of the motion of mechanisms and to design
mechanisms that yield the desired motion. The course is designed for the students to understand
and master the concepts of displacement, velocity and acceleration of simple mechanisms and
machine components. These include cam profile and its analysis, gear kinematics with gear train
calculations, belt drives and chain drives, and friction clutches and brakes.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand the fundamentals of links, mechanisms, machines, brakes, clutches and
gyroscope
2. Analyse planar mechanism for displacement, velocity and acceleration graphically and
analytically
3. Construct various type of Cam profiles and analyze the standard motion of the follower
4. Compare different type of gears, gear-trains and its applications
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction of Mechanisms and Machines   08
Concepts of Kinematics and Dynamics, Mechanisms and Machines, Planar
and Spatial Mechanisms, Kinematic Pairs, Kinematic Chains, Kinematic
Diagrams, Kinematic Inversion, four bar chain, single and double Slider
Crank Mechanisms and their Inversions, Degrees of Freedom, Mobility and
range of movement - Kutzbach and Grubler’s criterion, Number Synthesis,
Grashof’s criterion, straight line mechanisms.
2.   Velocity and Acceleration Analysis   07
Velocity and Acceleration analysis: (Graphical approach)
Velocity analysis: instantaneous centre of rotation method, relative velocity
method for four bar pin jointed linkages and four bar slider crank linkages.
Velocity and Acceleration analysis - relative method four bar pin jointed
linkages and four bar slider crank linkages.
3. CAM   06
Types of cams, Types of followers, Follower displacement programming,
Derivatives of follower Motion, Motions of follower, Layout of cam profiles.

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
4.   Belt, Ropes and Chains   07
Types of belt drive, Velocity ratio, Slip, Pulley arrangement, Length of belt,
Law of belting, Ratio of friction tension, Power transmitted, Centrifugal
effects on belts, Maximum power transmitted, Creep, Chains, Chain length,
Angular speed ratio, Classification of chains.
5.   Friction Clutches and Brakes   07
Introduction to friction clutches, Rolling Friction, Types of Clutches, Types
of brakes, Block and Shoe brakes, Differential band brake, Internal
expanding shoe brake.
6.   Gears and Gear Trains   10
Terminology, Law of Gearing, Characteristics of involute and cycloidal
action, Interference and undercutting, centre distance variation, minimum
number of teeth, contact ratio, spur, helical, spiral bevel and worm gears,
problems.
Gear Trains: Synthesis of Simple, compound & reverted gear trains,
Analysis of epicyclic gear trains

conversion phenomenon. With this course one can impart knowledge of air compressors and
components of steam power system. This course provides basics of I.C engines, refrigeration
systems and air conditioning systems and also build a bridge for these courses.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain the fundamental concepts of applied thermodynamics
2. Analyze the components of steam power systems
3. Investigate the concept of I.C. Engines, air compressors and refrigeration and air
conditioning systems

Review of Thermodynamics, Vapour Power cycles, Binary Vapour Cycle,

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics , Partial Differential Equations and Laplace transforms
Course Objective
The course is aimed at delivering detailed understanding of fluid properties and their static - dynamic
nature. This course teaches the analytical techniques necessary for grasping fundamental behavior of
incompressible fluids. It is designed for the students to learn the principles of laminar flow, turbulent
flow, and boundary layer theory to solve important practical problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Differentiate fluid properties and their static- dynamic nature
2. Analyze fundamental behavior of incompressible fluid
3. Evaluate the fundamental behaviour of laminar and turbulent flow and boundary layer theory to
solve real life problems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1. Fluid Properties   03
Concept of continuum, fluid properties, Classification of fluid, Newton’s law of
viscosity, stress-strain relationship.
2. Fluid Statics   10
Basic hydrostatic equation, Pascal’s Law, application to Manometers and mechanical
gauges, hydrostatic forces on plane and curved submerged surfaces.
Buoyancy and Floatation
Archimedes’ Principle, buoyancy force and centre of buoyancy, metacentre,
metacentric height, analytical method to find metacentric height, condition of
equilibrium of submerged bodies, oscillation of a floating body
3. Fluid Kinematics   08
Description of fluid motion-Lagrangian method and Euler’s method, classification
of flow types- steady and unsteady, uniform and non-uniform, laminar and
turbulent, one two and three- dimensional flow, rotational and irrotational, laminar
and turbulent, compressible and incompressible.
Flow patterns- stream lines, path lines, stream tubes and streak lines. Continuity
equation (Cartesian and polar co-ordinates), circulation and vorticity, velocity
potential and stream function.
B Tech/Mechanical/Sem-V/2024-25/Page 5
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
4. Fluid Dynamics   09
Euler’s equation of motion, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications-venturimeter,
orificemeter, rotameter, pitot tube, Impulse-Momentum equation and   its
applications, Reynolds Transport Theorem and its application.
Dimensional Analysis
Secondary or derived quantities, Reyleigh method, Buckingham−𝜋theorem,
dimensionless numbers, Theory of similarity, Model laws.
5. Laminar Flow   10
Navier-Stokes equation of motion, developing expression for flow rate, pressure
drop, shear stress, friction factor. Flow of viscous fluid in circular pipes- Hagen
Poiseuille law, Couette flow.
Turbulent Flow
Shear stresses in turbulent flow, theories of turbulent shear stress, hydro-
dynamically smooth and rough surface, modeling of turbulence, Moody’s chart.
Flow Through Pipes
Energy losses in pipes: Minor and Major losses, Darcy-Weisbatch equation for head
loss in pipes, hydraulic gradient lines, and total energy lines, pipes in series and
parallel, Equivalent pipe.
6. Boundary Layer Theory   05
Concept of Boundary layer, Boundary layer over flat plate, Boundary Layer
thickness, momentum thickness, displacement thickness and energy thickness.
Boundary layer equations and their solutions. Blasius solution (without derivation),
Von-Karman momentum integral equation. Laminar boundary layer and turbulent
boundary layer. Separation and control and Concept of drag.
Total   45

Edition (revised), TMH Delhi, 2015.

Series, McGraw Hill, 2013.

The main objective of this course is to provide basic understanding of composite materials used in
various engineering applications. The course also explains mechanical properties, micromechanics

After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Relate processing, characterization and applications of various composite materials

3. Evaluate the relative merits of using alternatives (corresponding to various simple and composite
materials) for important engineering and other applications

Course Objective
This course focusses on the application of classical mechanics to various biological problems by
combining the fields of biology and physiology. This course is concerned with the application of
principles of mechanics to the conceptualization, design, development and analysis of equipment
and systems as applied to human body.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Correlate mechanics, biomechanics and kinesiology and differentiate between their uses in the
analysis of human movement
2. Relate the reference positions, planes, and axes associated with the human body
3. Evaluate the skeletal considerations for movement and the different mechanics involved in
bones

Biomechanics, kinesiology, anatomy, functional anatomy
linear motion, angular motion, kinematics, kinetics, statics and dynamics.

Linear, angular and general motion, anatomical reference position, planes
and axes, joint movement terminology, spatial reference systems, analyzing
human movement and tools for measuring kinematic quantities.
3.   Applications of Statics to Biomechanics   10
Skeletal joints, skeletal muscles, mechanics of the elbow, mechanics of the
shoulder, mechanics of the spinal column, mechanics of the hip, mechanics
of the knee and mechanics of the ankle.
4.   Skeletal Considerations for Movement   10
Bone tissue function, composition of bone tissue, macroscopic structure of
bone, bone formation, strength and stiffness of bone, loads applied to bone,
stress fractures, articular cartilage, fibrocartilage and ligaments.

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes I and II, Machine Drawing
Course Objective
The objective of the course is to impart introductory knowledge of Additive Manufacturing (AM)
and its capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industries. The course is structured to
acquaint the students with the operating principles and applications of most prominent
technologies in the field of additive manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Compare the fundamental principles of various additive manufacturing technologies in terms
of material requirements, manufacturing technologies and applications
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the product
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Additive Manufacturing   06
Introduction to AM, history of AM, definition, distinction between AM, CNC
& other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications
of AM processes, design for additive manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry:
present and future, AM process chain, AM file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF, PLY,
VRML, and LEO), part orientation, support generation, model slicing,
contour generation, machine set-up, build file preparation.
2.   Classification of Additive Manufacturing Techniques   12
Material Extrusion:
Process mechanism, process parameters, extrusion of: ceramics, metals,
biomaterials, composites, contour crafting, concrete printing
Vat Polymerization:
Process mechanism, process parameters, advantages, disadvantages,
applications, Digital Light Processing (DLP), recent advances, Large-Scale
Rapid Liquid Printing.
Binder & material jetting processes:
Binder jettng process workflow, material requirements, binder-powder
interaction, binder properties.
Material Jetting process workflow, thermal and piezoelectric inkjet, material
jetting fluid mechanics, drop-on-demand and continuous methods of MJ.
Powder bed fusion AM process:

Selective laser sintering (SLS), process mechanism, process parameters,
selective laser melting (SLM), process workflow and material requirements,
powder melting mechanisms, electron beam melting (EBM) process.
Sheet Lamination AM Processes:
Process mechanism, process parameters, ultrasonic additive manufacturing
(UAM), ultrasonic welding fundamentals, UAM process parameters
Directed Energy Deposition (DED) Processes:
Process workflow, materials feeding for DED: powder (Laser Engineered Net
Shaping) and wire, process parameters, cold spray.
3.   Post- Processing   04
Product quality evaluation, need for post-processing, support material
removal, surface finish improvement, aesthetic improvement, property
enhancements using non-thermal and thermal techniques.
4.   Design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM)   04
Design guidelines: part orientation, support, geometry considerations, layer
thickness, part size, material consideration, residual stress, topology
optimization, case studies on design for AM.
5.   Applications of AM & Industry 4.0   04

engineering, economic consideration, Industry 4.0 for AM, case studies on

This course is designed to provide knowledge of different modes of heat transfer with different laws
of conduction, convection and radiation. It also helps to provide understanding of different
applications of conduction, convection and radiation.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the basic laws of heat transfer
2. Analyse realistic problems involving different modes of heat transfer
3. Apply basic principles of heat transfer to design heat transfer devices

Unit   Description   Duration

Modes of Heat Transfer, its mechanism and mathematical models.
Conduction Heat Transfer
Fourier’s general conduction equation in Cartesian, Cylindrical and Spherical co-
ordinates (for cylindrical and spherical walls derivation of Fourier’s three-
dimensional equation is not included), thermal resistance, solution of Fourier’s
equation for one dimensional steady state heat conduction through various
configurations such as plane, cylindrical, spherical wall, composite medium.

corrected fin length, application of fins.

Lumped System Analysis

Convection heat transfer coefficient, Momentum and energy equation for laminar

number, Reynolds number, Grashof number.
Empirical relations and their use for forced internal and external convection for
circular and non-circular ducts.
Empirical relations and their use for free convection on vertical, horizontal flat
plate and cylinders.

Physical phenomenon and Pool boiling curve.

It helps them to identify the various components of an automation system and design circuits to
control the physical output work.

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes – I and II
Course Objective
This course provides the understanding of the development and design aspects of products, impart
knowledge of business and technical concerns about the different methodologies of product
development. This course also discusses the concept of product life cycle and product data
management.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1.   Identify the different stages of product development and design with modern approaches
2. Apply the knowledge of Technology Forecasting using S-Curve in product development as
per customers need
3. Describe the process of benchmarking of products, technologies & techniques product design
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Product Design and Development   10
Definition of product design, product development versus product design, types
of design and redesign, design by evolution and innovation, factors in product
design, morphology of product design (seven phases), standardization,
simplification and specialization in product design, product life cycle and its
various phases, modern approaches- concurrent design in product development,
product development team and product development planning with reference to
ISO standard, new product development process/stages, difference between
product verification and production validation.
2.   Product Development – Technical and Business Concerns   09
Technology forecasting and Technology S-curve, Kano model, Mission statement
and technical questioning. Economic analysis of product, customer needs and
satisfaction, customer population and market segmentation, gathering customer
needs information, analysis of gathered information.
3.   Product Development from Concept to Product Function   12
Generating concepts, information gathering and brainstorming, morphological
analysis, concept selection-design evaluation, estimation of technical feasibility,
concept selection process, Pugh’s concept, selection charts, numerical concept
scoring, process of concept embodiment, system modeling, Failure Mode Effect
Analysis (FMEA), functional modeling and decomposition, fast method, subtract
and operate procedure, establishing system functionality.

Engineering; Managing Competitiveness- benchmarking, outsourcing and mass
customization.

Course Objective
This course is designed to impart knowledge of an IC engine and the ignition systems. It also
introduces the modern developments in internal combustion engines with optical measurement
techniques and emission control.
Course Outcome
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Explain advanced engine technologies and emission norms
2. Apply concepts of different alternate fuels used for SI and CI engines
3. Analyze environmental, social, and technological issues related to the future widespread use
of internal combustion engines
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Basic Characteristics of Engines   05
Compression ratio, energy supply to an engine, power developed by engine,
specific weight and specific volume, cylinder pressures, indicated mean effective
pressure determination, torque characteristics, cylinder arrangement and their
relative merits.
Engine Cooling Systems
Types of cooling, cooling of critical engine components, re-cooling the coolant,
comparison of air cooled and liquid cooled engines.
2.   Fuel Delivery in Spark Ignition Engines   06
Classification of fuel delivery systems, fuel transfer pumps, fixed jet carburetor,
computer controlled carburetor, gasoline injection systems.
Ignition Systems in Spark Ignition Engines
Battery ignition system, requirements for satisfactory operation of the ignition
system, ignition timing and advancing mechanisms, magneto ignition system,
electronic ignition system.
3.   Combustion and Combustion Systems in Compression Ignition Engines   06
Air motion in compression ignition engines, delay period in compression ignition
engines, types of diesel combustion systems.
Scavenging and Super Charging in Compression Ignition Engines
Types of scavenging systems, improved and modified scavenging systems, super
charging and engine performance, methods of super charging.

phase doppler interferometry for spray characterization, optical engines and

Need for emission control, classification/ categories of emissions, major
