Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics, Fluid Mechanics and Strength of Materials
Course Objective
This course introduces the basic concepts of vibrations and discusses free vibration of an undamped
single-degree of-freedom system. This course also deals with two-degree-of-freedom systems, which
require two independent coordinates to describe their motion. The modeling of continuous
systems as multidegree-of-freedom systems is also presented in this course.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Derive the equation of motion of a single-degree-of-freedom system
2. Solve two-degree-of-freedom free- and forced-vibration problems
3. Formulate the equations of motion of multidegree-of-freedom systems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Fundamentals of Vibration   07
Basic Concepts of Vibration, Classification of Vibration, Vibration Analysis
Procedure, Spring Elements, Mass or Inertia Elements, Damping Elements,
Harmonic Motion, Harmonic Analysis
2.   Single-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   08
Free Vibration of an Undamped Translational System, Free Vibration of an
Undamped Torsional System, Free Vibration with Viscous Damping, Free
Vibration with Coulomb Damping.
3.   Two-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   06
Equations of Motion for Forced Vibration, Free Vibration Analysis of an
Undamped System, Torsional System, Forced-Vibration Analysis.
4.   Multidegree-of-Freedom Systems   09
Modeling of Continuous Systems as Multi degree of Freedom Systems, Equations
of Motion, Influence Coefficients, Generalized Coordinates and Generalized
Forces, Lagrange s Equations, Equations of Motion of Undamped Systems in
Matrix Form, Eigenvalue Problem
Total   30
Text Books
1. S. S. Rao, Mechanical Vibration, Addison Wesley, 2004.
2. Michel Géradin and Daniel J. Rixen, Mechanical Vibrations Theory and Application to Structural
Dynamics, John Wiley & Sons, 2015.

Pre-requisite: Mathematics I, Mathematics II, Engineering Mechanics, Strength of Materials, Heat

Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to the finite element methods. The guidelines for selecting
displacement functions and the concepts that should be considered when modeling are discussed as
the course progresses. This course describes how to treat different types of forces for two-dimensional
elements and to solve one-dimensional heat transfer problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Derive the stiffness matrix for the beam and Constant-Strain Triangular element
2. Describe some of the approximations essential in finite element solutions
3. Solve a heat transfer problem by the finite element method
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   07
Brief history, matrix notation, general steps, applications and advantages of the
FEM, computer programs for the FEM, stiffness matrix for a spring element,
spring assemblage, direct stiffness method, boundary conditions.
2.   Truss   08
Stiffness matrix for a bar element, displacement function, transformation of
vectors in two dimensions, global stiffness matrix for bar arbitrarily oriented in
the plane, computation of stress for a bar in the x – y plane, solution of a plane
truss, use of symmetry in structures, inclined supports.
3.   Beam and Frame   10
Beam stiffness, assemblage of beam stiffness matrices, direct stiffness method,
distributed loading, beam element with nodal hinge, two-dimensional arbitrarily
oriented beam element, rigid plane frame, skewed supports, beam element
arbitrarily oriented in space, concept of substructure analysis
4.   Plane Stress and Plane Strain   07
Concepts of Plane Stress and Plane Strain, Constant-Strain Triangular Element
Stiffness Matrix, Body and Surface Forces, Plane Stress Problem, Bilinear
Rectangle, Comparison of Elements

6.   Heat Transfer and Mass Transport   08
Basic Differential Equation, Heat Transfer with Convection, Thermal
Conductivities, Heat Transfer Coefficients, One-Dimensional and Two-
Dimensional Finite Element Formulation, Line or Point Sources,   One-
Dimensional Heat Transfer with Mass Transport

Pre-requisite: Engineering Physics
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to develop awareness and basic skills necessary for the reliable
measurements and measuring instruments and impart knowledge on methods of measurement of
different engineering parameters such as pressure, temperature, displacement, etc. and different
metrological instruments for linear, angular, taper and surface finish measurements.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Describe the measurement terminologies and the concept of generalized measurement
systems.
2. Select sensors, devices and methods for measurement of specific parameters with required
accuracy.
3. Analyze the impact of various factors on the measurement process.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Measurement   04
Need of measurement, Study of instruments, measurement methods, generalized
measurement system & its functional elements, instrument characteristics - static
& dynamic characteristics, calibration.
2.   Temperature and Pressure Measurement   10
Thermometry
Overview   of thermometry, thermometers,   thermo-electric temperature
measurement, resistance thermometry, pyrometer.
Pressure Measurement
Bourdon tubes, dead weight pressure gauge tester, diaphragm gauge, LVDT,
Piezo-electric pressure gauge, Low vacuum gauges - McLeod gauge, thermal
conductivity gauge, Pirani gauge, ionization gauge, comparison of different
pressure measuring instruments.
3.   Strain Gauges   04
Classification, electrical strain gauge: working principle and types, gauge factor
(analytical treatment), analysis of Wheatstone’s network using strain gauges,
mounting of strain gauges.

Definition and concept of metrology, measurement standards, types and sources
of errors, accuracy and precision, introduction to uncertainty in measurement,
Calibration
Concept and procedure.
Length Standards
Line and end standards, slip gauges and linear measuring instruments.
Angular Measurement
Angle standards, sine bar, angle gauges, autocollimator, angle dekkor, optical
square, taper measurement, universal bevel protractor.
Interferometry
Basic principles, source of light, optical flats, fringe pattern and their
interpretation.
5.   Comparators, Thread and Gear Metrology, Surface Roughness Measurement   10
Comparators
Types, construction and working of Mechanical, Optical, Electrical, Pneumatic
comparators.
Screw Thread Metrology
Screw thread terminology, measurement of thread parameters, study of thread
gauges, floating carriage micrometer.
Gear Metrology
Gear profile and measurement of parameters, study of tool maker’s microscope
and profile projector.
Surface Roughness Measurement
Surface texture, assessment of surface roughness, Tomlinson surface meter, and
other surface measuring devices.
6.   Advances in Metrology   07
Coordinate measuring machine (CMM)
Fundamental features of CMM, role of CMMs, types of CMM and applications,
types of probe.
Laser Metrology
Basic concepts of lasers, advantages of lasers, laser interferometers, types,
applications.

Vision system measurement, multisensory systems.

Introduction to nano metrology.

learning in different domains.

fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and
verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a
report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and

Pre-requisite: Basic Electrical Engineering, Engineering Mechanics and Strength of Materials
Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to wind energy and wind turbines. It introduces the current
challenges in modern wind turbine analysis, design, and development and provides a comprehensive
examination of state-of-the-art technologies.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Categorize various types of wind turbines and its principal components
2. Determine the mechanical power, types of stresses and the control parameters
3. Analyze the economics, effects on the environment, safety in operation and the potential hazards
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   10
Importance of renewable, technical issues, wind farm development, wind turbine
siting, new and future technologies, energy in a moving object and moving fluid,
power in the wind, power absorption by a turbine, wind speed variation, force
from wind, aerodynamic force, lift and drag coefficients, airfoils.
2.   Types and Components of Wind Turbine   10
Turbine classification, propeller wind turbine, The H-rotor, Darrieus turbine,
Savonius rotor, mechanical components - tower, foundation, rotor, nacelle,
gearbox, turbine brake, electrical components - generators, transformers and
anemometer.

Mechanical power, diagrams, mechanical power in a turbine, turbine power
variation with angular speed, daily energy production by a turbine, annual energy
production.
4.   Wind Turbine Design   10
Power accord with the wind speed, wind speed measurement, power calculations,
output power quality and requirement, blade pitch control, turbine operating
power curve, yaw control, parking brake, fault control, various operational states
of a turbine, loads on the rotor, aerodynamic loads on the blade, other blade loads,
vibrations, blade fatigue, blade construction.

Course Objective

improve product quality and process efficiency by identifying and measuring production process
variability, which, if not successfully addressed can lead to inconsistent product quality, costly
wastage, and other reliability and productivity problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Explain quality management concepts and diagnose quality problems
2. Apply the tool and techniques of quality management as a means to diagnose, reduce and
eliminate causes of variation
3. Analyze the sources of variation for improving quality and desired performance

Course Objective
The course is aimed at imparting basic knowledge of science of materials and physical metallurgy.
This course introduces and cements the concept of structure property correlations. It is designed to lay
the foundation for the detailed understanding of mechanical behavior of materials, phase diagrams,
heat treatment and failure of materials. The students are also introduced to certain applications of
ferrous, non-ferrous and new age materials.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Relate mechanical properties with the mechanical processing of materials
2. Analyze the root cause of failure in different types of materials
3. Recommend heat treatment processes with the help of phase diagrams
4. Select appropriate materials for various applications depending on the structural requirements

Course Objective
The course is aimed at providing adequate understanding of the fundamentals of stresses and strains
in deformable bodies subjected to various types of static loads. It is designed to impart the knowledge
of basic concepts of deformation & deflection, identifying the relevant tests to be performed on beams
and power transmitting shafts. It develops the ability to assess the strength of engineering materials and
subsequently examine the failure criteria of structural members using relevant analysis.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand the resultant stresses induced in beams and other structural members
2. Evaluate the deformations of various determinate beams
3. Analyse stress on thin shells due to internal pressure
4. Calculate the stresses in circular torsion members

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics
Course Objective
The course is aimed at developing the detailed understanding of various mechanism used in
devices or machines. This course focuses on analysis of the motion of mechanisms and to design
mechanisms that yield the desired motion. The course is designed for the students to understand
and master the concepts of displacement, velocity and acceleration of simple mechanisms and
machine components. These include cam profile and its analysis, gear kinematics with gear train
calculations, belt drives and chain drives, and friction clutches and brakes.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand the fundamentals of links, mechanisms, machines, brakes, clutches and
gyroscope
2. Analyse planar mechanism for displacement, velocity and acceleration graphically and
analytically
3. Construct various type of Cam profiles and analyze the standard motion of the follower
4. Compare different type of gears, gear-trains and its applications

and Spatial Mechanisms, Kinematic Pairs, Kinematic Chains, Kinematic
Diagrams, Kinematic Inversion, four bar chain, single and double Slider
Crank Mechanisms and their Inversions, Degrees of Freedom, Mobility and
range of movement - Kutzbach and Grubler’s criterion, Number Synthesis,
Grashof’s criterion, straight line mechanisms.

Velocity and Acceleration analysis - relative method four bar pin jointed

Course Objective
This course aims to instill in students a sound knowledge of probability theory and statistical
techniques. It equips the students with intermediate to advanced level concepts and tools in
probability and statistics that help them tackle relevant problems within engineering domain.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Solve problems involving random variables, probability distributions and testing of
hypothesis, correlation and regression
2. Identify suitable probability distribution and testing techniques to solve related problems
3. Apply knowledge of random variables, probability distributions, measures of central
tendency, correlation and regression to solve real life problems
4. Analyse data samples using statistical methods
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Basic Probability   03
Probability spaces, conditional probability, independence; Bayes theorem.
2 Random variables and Probability Distributions   06
Discrete random variables, probability mass function, cumulative distribution
function, Independent random variables, Continuous random variables,
distribution functions and densities, expectation, variance, raw and central
moments of random variables, Binomial distribution, Poisson approximation
to the binomial distribution, Normal distribution.
3   Bivariate Distributions   02
Definition of Bivariate Distribution and their properties, Conditional densities.
4   Basic Statistics   02
Measures of Central tendency; Moments, Moment generating function,
skewness, kurtosis.
Mean and variance of Binomial distribution & Poisson distribution, Moments,
skewness & kurtosis for Normal distribution.

errors, One-tailed and two-tailed test, Critical region, Large sample statistical
test for mean, Large sample statistical test for proportion, t-test for small
samples, Test for variance- F test, Chi-square test for Goodness of fit and

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics , Partial Differential Equations and Laplace transforms
Course Objective
The course is aimed at delivering detailed understanding of fluid properties and their static - dynamic
nature. This course teaches the analytical techniques necessary for grasping fundamental behavior of
incompressible fluids. It is designed for the students to learn the principles of laminar flow, turbulent
flow, and boundary layer theory to solve important practical problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Differentiate fluid properties and their static- dynamic nature
2. Analyze fundamental behavior of incompressible fluid
3. Evaluate the fundamental behaviour of laminar and turbulent flow and boundary layer theory to
solve real life problems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1. Fluid Properties   03
Concept of continuum, fluid properties, Classification of fluid, Newton’s law of
viscosity, stress-strain relationship.
2. Fluid Statics   10
Basic hydrostatic equation, Pascal’s Law, application to Manometers and mechanical
gauges, hydrostatic forces on plane and curved submerged surfaces.
Buoyancy and Floatation
Archimedes’ Principle, buoyancy force and centre of buoyancy, metacentre,
metacentric height, analytical method to find metacentric height, condition of
equilibrium of submerged bodies, oscillation of a floating body
3. Fluid Kinematics   08
Description of fluid motion-Lagrangian method and Euler’s method, classification
of flow types- steady and unsteady, uniform and non-uniform, laminar and
turbulent, one two and three- dimensional flow, rotational and irrotational, laminar
and turbulent, compressible and incompressible.
Flow patterns- stream lines, path lines, stream tubes and streak lines. Continuity
equation (Cartesian and polar co-ordinates), circulation and vorticity, velocity
potential and stream function.
B Tech/Mechanical/Sem-V/2023-24/Page 5
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
4. Fluid Dynamics   09
Euler’s equation of motion, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications-venturimeter,
orificemeter, rotameter, pitot tube, Impulse-Momentum equation and   its
applications, Reynolds Transport Theorem and its application.
Dimensional Analysis
Secondary or derived quantities, Reyleigh method, Buckingham−𝜋theorem,
dimensionless numbers, Theory of similarity, Model laws.
5. Laminar Flow   10
Navier-Stokes equation of motion, developing expression for flow rate, pressure
drop, shear stress, friction factor. Flow of viscous fluid in circular pipes- Hagen
Poiseuille law, Couette flow.
Turbulent Flow
Shear stresses in turbulent flow, theories of turbulent shear stress, hydro-
dynamically smooth and rough surface, modeling of turbulence, Moody’s chart.
Flow Through Pipes
Energy losses in pipes: Minor and Major losses, Darcy-Weisbatch equation for head
loss in pipes, hydraulic gradient lines, and total energy lines, pipes in series and
parallel, Equivalent pipe.
6. Boundary Layer Theory   05
Concept of Boundary layer, Boundary layer over flat plate, Boundary Layer
thickness, momentum thickness, displacement thickness and energy thickness.
Boundary layer equations and their solutions. Blasius solution (without derivation),
Von-Karman momentum integral equation. Laminar boundary layer and turbulent
boundary layer. Separation and control and Concept of drag.
Total   45

Course Objective
This course covers alternative fuels and the analysis of their properties. The course also provides a
comprehensive overview of the recent advances in the production and utilization aspects of different
types of liquid and gaseous alternative fuels.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Classify different alternate fuels used for spark ignition and compression ignition engines
2. Compare different alternate fuels and energy system in terms of their characteristics
3. Analyze environmental, social, and technological issues related to the future widespread use of
alternative fuels
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   04
Estimation of petroleum reserve, need for alternate fuels, availability and
properties of alternate fuels, American Society for Testing of Materials (ASTM)
standards.

Petroleum based liquid fuels and refining.
Liquid Alternative Fuels
Alcohols, general use of alcohols, properties as engine fuel, gasoline and alcohol
blends, performance in spark ignition engine, methanol and gasoline blend,
combustion characteristics in engine, emission characteristics. algae as a source
for fuels.
Vegetable Oils
Soybean oil, jatropha, pongamia, rice bran, mahua etc. as alternate fuel and their
properties, esterification of oils, biodiesel and emulsified fuels, lubricating oils
composition and effect of alternate fuels.
3.   Gaseous Alternative Fuels   07
Hydrogen production, hydrogen as an alternative fuel, fuel cell, availability of
compressed natural gas, properties and modification required to use in engines,
performance and emission characteristics of compressed natural and liquefied
natural gas in spark ignition and compression ignition engines, dimethyl ether,
and hythane as an alternative fuel.

Course Objective
This course focusses on the application of classical mechanics to various biological problems by
combining the fields of biology and physiology. This course is concerned with the application of
principles of mechanics to the conceptualization, design, development and analysis of equipment
and systems as applied to human body.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Correlate mechanics, biomechanics and kinesiology and differentiate between their uses in the
analysis of human movement
2. Relate the reference positions, planes, and axes associated with the human body
3. Evaluate the skeletal considerations for movement and the different mechanics involved in
bones

Biomechanics, kinesiology, anatomy, functional anatomy
linear motion, angular motion, kinematics, kinetics, statics and dynamics.

Linear, angular and general motion, anatomical reference position, planes
and axes, joint movement terminology, spatial reference systems, analyzing
human movement and tools for measuring kinematic quantities.
3.   Applications of Statics to Biomechanics   10
Skeletal joints, skeletal muscles, mechanics of the elbow, mechanics of the
shoulder, mechanics of the spinal column, mechanics of the hip, mechanics
of the knee and mechanics of the ankle.

Bone tissue function, composition of bone tissue, macroscopic structure of
bone, bone formation, strength and stiffness of bone, loads applied to bone,
stress fractures, articular cartilage, fibrocartilage and ligaments.

Course Objective
The objective of the course is to impart introductory knowledge of Additive Manufacturing (AM)
and its capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industries. The course is structured to
acquaint the students with the operating principles and applications of most prominent
technologies in the field of additive manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Compare the fundamental principles of various additive manufacturing technologies in terms
of material requirements, manufacturing technologies and applications
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the product
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application

& other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications
of AM processes, design for additive manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry:
present and future, AM process chain, AM file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF, PLY,
VRML, and LEO), part orientation, support generation, model slicing,
contour generation, machine set-up, build file preparation.

management.

This course is designed to impart knowledge of an IC engine and the ignition systems. It also

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics, Fluid Mechanics and Strength of Materials
Course Objective
This course introduces the basic concepts of vibrations and discusses free vibration of an undamped
single-degree of-freedom system. This course also deals with two-degree-of-freedom systems, which
require two independent coordinates to describe their motion. The modeling of continuous
systems as multidegree-of-freedom systems is also presented in this course.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Derive the equation of motion of a single-degree-of-freedom system
2. Solve two-degree-of-freedom free- and forced-vibration problems
3. Formulate the equations of motion of multidegree-of-freedom systems
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Fundamentals of Vibration   07
Basic Concepts of Vibration, Classification of Vibration, Vibration Analysis
Procedure, Spring Elements, Mass or Inertia Elements, Damping Elements,
Harmonic Motion, Harmonic Analysis
2.   Single-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   08
Free Vibration of an Undamped Translational System, Free Vibration of an
Undamped Torsional System, Free Vibration with Viscous Damping, Free
Vibration with Coulomb Damping.
3.   Two-Degree-of-Freedom Systems   06
Equations of Motion for Forced Vibration, Free Vibration Analysis of an
Undamped System, Torsional System, Forced-Vibration Analysis.
4.   Multidegree-of-Freedom Systems   09
Modeling of Continuous Systems as Multi degree of Freedom Systems, Equations
of Motion, Influence Coefficients, Generalized Coordinates and Generalized
Forces, Lagrange s Equations, Equations of Motion of Undamped Systems in
Matrix Form, Eigenvalue Problem
Total   30

1. S. S. Rao, Mechanical Vibration, Addison Wesley, 2004.

Pre-requisite: Mathematics I, Mathematics II, Engineering Mechanics, Strength of Materials, Heat

Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to the finite element methods. The guidelines for selecting
displacement functions and the concepts that should be considered when modeling are discussed as
the course progresses. This course describes how to treat different types of forces for two-dimensional
elements and to solve one-dimensional heat transfer problems.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Derive the stiffness matrix for the beam and Constant-Strain Triangular element
2. Describe some of the approximations essential in finite element solutions
3. Solve a heat transfer problem by the finite element method
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   07
Brief history, matrix notation, general steps, applications and advantages of the
FEM, computer programs for the FEM, stiffness matrix for a spring element,
spring assemblage, direct stiffness method, boundary conditions.
2.   Truss   08
Stiffness matrix for a bar element, displacement function, transformation of
vectors in two dimensions, global stiffness matrix for bar arbitrarily oriented in
the plane, computation of stress for a bar in the x – y plane, solution of a plane
truss, use of symmetry in structures, inclined supports.
3.   Beam and Frame   10
Beam stiffness, assemblage of beam stiffness matrices, direct stiffness method,
distributed loading, beam element with nodal hinge, two-dimensional arbitrarily
oriented beam element, rigid plane frame, skewed supports, beam element
arbitrarily oriented in space, concept of substructure analysis
4.   Plane Stress and Plane Strain   07
Concepts of Plane Stress and Plane Strain, Constant-Strain Triangular Element
Stiffness Matrix, Body and Surface Forces, Plane Stress Problem, Bilinear
Rectangle, Comparison of Elements

6.   Heat Transfer and Mass Transport   08

Dimensional Heat Transfer with Mass Transport

Pre-requisite: Engineering Physics
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to develop awareness and basic skills necessary for the reliable
measurements and measuring instruments and impart knowledge on methods of measurement of
different engineering parameters such as pressure, temperature, displacement, etc. and different
metrological instruments for linear, angular, taper and surface finish measurements.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Describe the measurement terminologies and the concept of generalized measurement
systems.
2. Select sensors, devices and methods for measurement of specific parameters with required
accuracy.
3. Analyze the impact of various factors on the measurement process.
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Measurement   04
Need of measurement, Study of instruments, measurement methods, generalized
measurement system & its functional elements, instrument characteristics - static
& dynamic characteristics, calibration.
2.   Temperature and Pressure Measurement   10
Thermometry
Overview   of thermometry, thermometers,   thermo-electric temperature
measurement, resistance thermometry, pyrometer.
Pressure Measurement
Bourdon tubes, dead weight pressure gauge tester, diaphragm gauge, LVDT,
Piezo-electric pressure gauge, Low vacuum gauges - McLeod gauge, thermal
conductivity gauge, Pirani gauge, ionization gauge, comparison of different
pressure measuring instruments.
3.   Strain Gauges   04
Classification, electrical strain gauge: working principle and types, gauge factor
(analytical treatment), analysis of Wheatstone’s network using strain gauges,
mounting of strain gauges.

4.   Measurement Standards, Comparators and Angular Measurement   10
Definition and concept of metrology, measurement standards, types and sources
of errors, accuracy and precision, introduction to uncertainty in measurement,
Calibration
Concept and procedure.
Length Standards
Line and end standards, slip gauges and linear measuring instruments.
Angular Measurement
Angle standards, sine bar, angle gauges, autocollimator, angle dekkor, optical
square, taper measurement, universal bevel protractor.
Interferometry
Basic principles, source of light, optical flats, fringe pattern and their
interpretation.
5.   Comparators, Thread and Gear Metrology, Surface Roughness Measurement   10
Comparators
Types, construction and working of Mechanical, Optical, Electrical, Pneumatic
comparators.
Screw Thread Metrology
Screw thread terminology, measurement of thread parameters, study of thread
gauges, floating carriage micrometer.
Gear Metrology
Gear profile and measurement of parameters, study of tool maker’s microscope
and profile projector.
Surface Roughness Measurement
Surface texture, assessment of surface roughness, Tomlinson surface meter, and
other surface measuring devices.
6.   Advances in Metrology   07
Coordinate measuring machine (CMM)
Fundamental features of CMM, role of CMMs, types of CMM and applications,
types of probe.
Laser Metrology
Basic concepts of lasers, advantages of lasers, laser interferometers, types,
applications.
Machine Vision Systems
Vision system measurement, multisensory systems.
Nano Metrology
Introduction to nano metrology.

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year students’
learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with the required
practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically, solve challenging
problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication skills, teamwork and
planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope and
learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the research
gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design and
fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and
verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a
report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and
synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her work carried out before examiners.

Course Objective
This course presents an introduction to wind energy and wind turbines. It introduces the current
challenges in modern wind turbine analysis, design, and development and provides a comprehensive
examination of state-of-the-art technologies.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Categorize various types of wind turbines and its principal components
2. Determine the mechanical power, types of stresses and the control parameters
3. Analyze the economics, effects on the environment, safety in operation and the potential hazards

Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction   10
Importance of renewable, technical issues, wind farm development, wind turbine
siting, new and future technologies, energy in a moving object and moving fluid,
power in the wind, power absorption by a turbine, wind speed variation, force
from wind, aerodynamic force, lift and drag coefficients, airfoils.

Savonius rotor, mechanical components - tower, foundation, rotor, nacelle,
gearbox, turbine brake, electrical components - generators, transformers and
anemometer.

Mechanical power, diagrams, mechanical power in a turbine, turbine power
variation with angular speed, daily energy production by a turbine, annual energy
production.

Power accord with the wind speed, wind speed measurement, power calculations,
output power quality and requirement, blade pitch control, turbine operating
power curve, yaw control, parking brake, fault control, various operational states
of a turbine, loads on the rotor, aerodynamic loads on the blade, other blade loads,
vibrations, blade fatigue, blade construction.

Objective
The objective of this course is to help the students understand the principles and applications
relevant to the planning, design, and operations of manufacturing or service firms. This course
also develops an understanding about quality management practices in organizations that facilitate
organizational effectiveness.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Develop an understanding of manufacturing and service operations management as a
subject and outline the strategic concerns involved in operations decisions
2. Apply the principles, philosophy underpinning inventory management techniques, just-
in-time and MRP systems along with their limitations
3. Analyze the economic aspects related to production management
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Concept of Production Management   07
Meaning of production, production process system, scope of production
management, objectives of production management, functions and scopes
of production management, scope of production management, brief history
of production management, responsibilities of production manager.
2.   Productivity   04
Introduction, meaning of productivity, factors affecting on productivity,
productivity improvement, measurement of productivity.
3.   Economic Analysis   06
Factors to be considered in product design. production cost concepts;
fixed cost, variable cost, break even analysis,
P-V chart, and make-buy decision.
4.   Plant Location and Plant Layout   06
Meaning of plant layout, objective of a good plant layout, factors to be
considered in plant location, types of plant layout, process layout.
techniques of plant layout, concept of group technology, group layout.
5.   Production Planning and Control (PPC)   08
Objective of PPC, functions of PPC, capacity planning, manufacturing
resource planning and scheduling, JIT system, Kanban pull system of
scheduling, line balancing.

Bill of materials, quantity planning, inventory control, economic order
quantity (EOQ), lead time, consumption rate, different ordering systems, Q
system, P system, the store’s function and ABC analysis.

Introduction to quality control, quality management, function of quality,

Course Objective
This course focusses on a critical understanding and strategic importance of operations management.
The students can get familiar with interactions between firms based on parameters such as
information sharing, contracting and coordination in supply chain management.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Evaluate the application of operations management policies and techniques to the service
sector as well as manufacturing firms
2. Analyze and organize Global Network Logistics for trade and transport systems, sourcing and
procurement
3. Apply the latest developments in information technology to supply chain management in
order to generate greater benefit

IT framework, Customer Relationship Management (CRM), Internal supply chain

understanding of Physics also helps engineers understand the working and the limitations of existing
devices and techniques, which eventually leads to new innovations and improvements. This course
aims to make students understand the basic concepts of Physics thoroughly with a view to lay
foundations for the various engineering courses.

a scientific outlook,

and technological sectors,

experimental, observational, manipulative, investigatory and decision making etc.

Course Objectives
The main objective of this course is to equip the students with the ability to solve, assemble and test
simple AC and DC electrical circuits. Further, the course also enables the student to obtain a basic
understanding of the working principle and applications of electronics devices.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. interpret DC circuits, theorems and time domain analysis of first order RL circuit,
2. solve series and parallel AC circuits and compare star/delta configurations,
3. explain the principles of transformer and electrical machines,
4. understand the construction, working principle and applications of electronics devices and
logic circuits
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1. DC Circuits   6
Electrical circuit elements (R, L and C), voltage and current sources, Kirchhoff’s
current law, Kirchhoff’s voltage laws, Analysis of simple circuits with dc
excitation, Superposition Theorem, Thevenin’s Theorems, Norton’s Theorems.
Time-domain analysis of first-order RL circuits.
2.   AC Circuits   8
Generation of alternating emf, instantaneous, rms, peak, average values and
related other terms, vector representation of AC quantities, Steady state analysis
of R, L, C series and parallel circuits, resonance. Generation of three-phase emf,
star connection, delta connection, relationship between line and phase quantities.

Construction and working of single-phase transformer Ideal and practical
transformer, equivalent circuit, Losses in transformers, Generation of rotating
magnetic fields, Construction and working of a three-phase induction motor,
Single-phase induction motor, construction and working, DC motor construction,
working and types.
4.   Analog Electronics (no mathematical treatment and design)   5
Half and full wave rectifiers, special purpose diodes -zener regulator, BJT and its
applications, amplifier, oscillator, overview of opto-electronics devices, opto-
couplers, concepts of transducer, Operational amplifier (IC-741), Inverting and
Non-Inverting, Comparator, Timer (IC-555) and multivibrators.
5.   Digital Electronics   5
Logic gates, concept of universal logic; implementation of Boolean expressions
using logic gates, application of digital circuits: e.g., adder, subtractor,
multiplexer, de-multiplexer, Analog to Digital Converter, Digital to Analog
Converter.

Course Objectives
The course would enable students to get a brief introduction of the Indian Constitution and its
principles. The students would have knowledge of concept of ‘State’ and interdependencies of its
institutions vis a vis their relation with fundamental rights.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to
1. Understand the historic evolution of the Indian Constitution, its drafting, nature and to
understand the principles mentioned in its Preamble,
2. Inculcate fundamental rights in its true sense and also the permissible restrictions upon it so
as to enjoy these rights within permissible limits while simultaneously performing their
duties and to apply these principles into their professional lives,
3. Ingrain the structure of our polity and role of Judiciary in maintaining the basic structure of
the Constitution,
4. Attain knowledge of the Emergency provisions, when and how it is imposed, to know the
additional powers the bestowed upon the Government at times of Emergency and to
understand the Amendment procedure.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Nature, Characteristics and Sources of Indian Constitution   2
2.   Fundamental rights and Fundamental duties – Concept of State, Right to   6
Equality under Articles 14 and 15, Right to certain freedoms under Article 19,
Right to Life and liberty under Article 21, Right to religion under Article 25
and 26, Right to remedy under Article 32 and Fundamental duties
3.   Indian Judiciary – Concept of Supreme Court and High Courts, Appointment   3
of Judges, Independence of Judiciary, Jurisdictions of Supreme Court and
High Courts
4.   Emergency Provisions – Concept of National Emergency under Article 352,   4
Financial Emergency under Article 360 and President rule under Article 356 of
the Constitution
Total   15

 To provide the understanding of detailed design of mechanical systems and their
uses in different application under different load conditions and safety limits.
 To impart knowledge of the fundamentals of design of some important
mechanical systems.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Understand design of pressure vessels and belt conveyor.
 Design of Design of mechanical systems like pressure vessel and conveyor.

crank shaft, end bearings and end caps, valve gear mechanism.

including rope selection, sheave, hook, bearing for hook, cross piece,
axle for sheave and shackle plate.

design of tension take up unit, idler pulley

Course: Refrigeration and Air Conditioning   Code: BTME07002
Teaching Scheme   Evaluation Scheme

Credit

3   2   0   4   Scaled to 30 marks   Scaled to 70 marks
Pre-requisite: Engineering Thermodynamics (BTME03002), Thermal Engineering
(BTME05001), Heat Transfer (BTME06001)
Objectives:
 To impart the knowledge of working of vapour compression and vapour
absorption refrigeration systems.
 To provide the understanding of different processes in psychrometry used in air-
conditioning, and introduce cooling load calculations
 To introduce duct design methods.
 To introduce the applications of refrigeration and air conditioning.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Understand the working and applications of different refrigeration systems.
 Understand the properties of refrigerants used for different cooling applications.
 Estimate the designing   criterion for Air- Conditioning systems using
psychrometry.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1   Introduction To Refrigeration:   05
Methods of refrigeration, Carnot refrigerator, Carnot heat pump, co-
efficient of performance(COP), unit of refrigeration(TR), Energy
efficiency ratio(EER)
Air-craft refrigeration systems; Need for air-craft refrigeration and
Simple air-cooling system.
2   Vapor Compression Refrigeration System:   08
Simple vapor compression cycle (VCC); T-s, h-s and p-h diagrams for
VCC, COP calculation from T-s and h-s charts for different conditions,
Theoretical and actual cycle, Wet versus dry compression, pressure
losses and their effects on the VCC, Effect of suction and delivery
pressure on VCC.
Vapor compression refrigeration (VCR) systems with multiple
evaporators and compressors.
______________

3   Absorption Refrigeration System:   05
Ammonia-water vapor absorption refrigeration (VAR) system.
Enthalpy- concentration, analysis of the system. Lithium bromide-
water absorption refrigeration system, Introduction to Electrolux
refrigeration system.
4   Refrigerants:   03
Desirable   properties   of   refrigerants, designation system   for
refrigerants, thermodynamic, chemical and physical properties,
secondary refrigerants, selection of refrigerants, ODP, GWP and TEWI
5   Psychrometry:   05
Psychrometric properties, Dalton’s law of partial pressure, chart and
processes, psychrometer, By-pass factor, Apparatus dew point
temperature
6   Air – Conditioning:   10
Human comfort-   Requirement of comfort   air conditioning,
thermodynamics of human body, effective temperature, comfort chart,
comfort zone, economic considerations for selecting the comfort points
Mixing process, basic processes in conditioning of air, psychrometric
processes in air conditioning equipment,
Different classes of air conditioning system, summer air-conditioning,
winter air conditioning.
Cooling load calculations.
7   Duct Design   06
Friction chart for circular ducts. Equivalent diameter of a circular duct
for rectangular ducts. Static pressure regain and equal pressure drop
methods of duct design. Fans and blowers. Introduction to AHU-
design/selection.
8   Applications of Refrigeration:   03
Food processing and preservation, typical examples of food processing
by refrigeration and storage, transport refrigeration.
Applications of Air Conditioning:
Industrial, commercial,   residential   hospital requirement and
transport.
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of Integral and Vector Calculus (BTAB01001), Differential

Objectives:
 To provide the understanding of basics of finite element methods and analysis.
 To impart knowledge of one dimensional and two dimensional Finite element
analysis
 To introduce the applications of FEA in structural and thermal domains.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Understand the basics and mathematical aspect of FEA.
 Apply concept of nodes and elements on structural one dimensional and two
dimensional engineering problems.
 Implement FEM procedures to analyse heat conduction and fluid flow
problems using a general purpose software ANSYS.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Finite Element Analysis: Introduction to FEA,   05
history of FEM, general FEM procedures, applications of FEM in
various fields, advantages and disadvantages of FEM and software
packages of FEA.
2   Mathematical aspects of FEA: Newton Cotes formula, Gauss   10
quadrature formula in one and two dimensional, non-Weak form
Galerkin approach, Sub domain method, finite difference method,
Weak form–Rayleigh-Ritz Method.
3   Finite Element Types: One dimensional element such as two   10
nodded and three nodded bars and beams, discretization, element
shape, interpolation function, shape function and application of
boundary conditions.

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics (BTAB01005 and BTME02004), Materials
Engineering (BTME04004) and Design of Machine Elements – I & II (BTME05003 and
BTME06003).
Objective:
 To introduce the fundamental physical principles of the classical theory of
friction, wear and lubrication.
 To demonstrate basic understanding of friction, lubrication and wear processes
 To understand the fundamental principles of high contact stresses (Hertz
stresses), fatigue-failure, and Elasto-hydrodynamic (EHD) lubrication in rolling
bearings and gears.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
 Understand the principles for selecting compatible materials for minimizing
friction and wear in machinery.
 Understand the principles of bearing selection and bearing arrangement in
machines.
 Analyze the requirements for selecting bearings in machines.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Tribology:   Tribology in design and industry,   08
economic considerations of tribology.
Lubrication: Lubrication types, lubricants and its properties, types
of additives, Lubricating oils, Sliding contact bearings, classification
and comparison
2   Friction and wear:   16
Friction: Laws of friction, friction types and causes, friction
measurement, theories of friction.
Wear: Wear types, major and minor modes of wear. Theories of
wear and influencing factors, control methods, wear measurements.

Technical communication is one of the courses that is essential for engineering

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of vector algebra, functions, limits, differentiation and integration of
functions.
Course Objective:
This course aims at providing adequate exposure to the theory and applications of Calculus. This
course will help the students achieve sound understanding of the concepts of calculus, develop
problem solving skills and apply the concepts and techniques of calculus to solve problems within
Engineering domain. This course will equip the students with intermediate to advanced level
concepts and aligned tools to help them tackle advanced mathematics and related applications.
Course Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students will be able to-
1. Demonstrate the fundamental concepts of differential calculus for functions of one variable.
2. Solve problems involving functions of several variables using partial differentiation, Taylor
series expansion, and techniques for finding maxima and minima, including Lagrange’s method
of undetermined multipliers.
3. Use Beta and Gamma functions to solve problems in single-variable calculus.
4. Compute and interpret double and triple integrals, including change of variables and coordinate
transformations, and apply them to determine areas and volumes.
5. Examine vector functions using gradient, divergence, curl, and scalar potential and apply
fundamental vector calculus theorems such as Green’s, Stokes’, and Gauss’ theorems to evaluate
integrals.
6. Integrate concepts from differential, integral, and vector calculus to formulate and solve real-
world problems in physics, engineering, and applied sciences.

Pre-requisite: Engineering Mechanics
Course Objective
The course is aimed at developing the detailed understanding of various mechanism used in devices or
machines. This course focuses on analysis of the motion of mechanisms and to design mechanisms that
yield the desired motion. The course is designed for the students to understand and master the concepts
of displacement, velocity and acceleration of simple mechanisms and machine components. These
include cam profile and its analysis, gear kinematics with gear train calculations, belt drives and chain
drives, and friction clutches and brakes.
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Describe the fundamentals of links, mechanisms, machines, brakes and clutches
2. Analyse planar mechanism for displacement, velocity and acceleration graphically and analytically
3. Construct various type of Cam profiles and analyze the standard motion of the follower
4. Illustrate the machine components like belt, ropes and chains for required mechanisms
5. Estimate the performance and efficiency of brakes and clutches, considering frictional forces and
their impact on machine operation
6. Evaluate simple, compound, reverted, and epicyclic gear trains to determine velocity ratios
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction of Mechanisms and Machines   08
Concepts of Kinematics and Dynamics, Mechanisms and Machines, Planar and
Spatial Mechanisms, Kinematic Pairs, Kinematic Chains, Kinematic Diagrams,
Kinematic Inversion, four bar chain, single and double Slider Crank Mechanisms
and their Inversions, Degrees of Freedom, Mobility and range of movement -
Kutzbach and Grubler’s criterion, Number Synthesis, Grashof’s criterion, straight
line mechanisms.
2.   Velocity and Acceleration Analysis   07
Velocity and Acceleration analysis: (Graphical approach)
Velocity analysis: instantaneous centre of rotation method, relative velocity
method for four bar pin jointed linkages and four bar slider crank linkages.
Velocity and Acceleration analysis - relative method four bar pin jointed linkages
and four bar slider crank linkages.
3.   CAM   06
Types of cams, Types of followers, Follower displacement programming,
Derivatives of follower Motion, Motions of follower, Layout of cam profiles.

effects on belts, Maximum power transmitted, Creep, Chains, Chain length,
Angular speed ratio, Classification of chains.
5.   Friction Clutches and Brakes   07
Introduction to friction clutches, Rolling Friction, Types of Clutches, Types
of brakes, Block and Shoe brakes, Differential band brake, Internal
expanding shoe brake.
6.   Gears and Gear Trains   10

Course: Industrial Engineering   Code: 702ME0E009
Teaching Scheme   Evaluation Scheme
Lecture   Practical   Tutorials   Internal Continuous   Term End
(Hours per   (Hours per   (Hours per Credit Assessment (ICA)   Examinations (TEE)
week)   week)   week)   (Marks-50)   (Marks -100)
3   0   0   3   Marks Scaled to 50   Marks Scaled to 50
Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes-I and Manufacturing Processes-II
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to give the students a systematic and comprehensive understanding
of various aspects related to industrial engineering and its relevance in the industrial
environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe the concepts of productivity and methods to improve efficiency
2. Apply the methods to measure parameters such as time and magnitude of activities
performed
3. Analyze the cost effectiveness of each function of the product in terms of usefulness to the
customer
Detailed Syllabus
Unit Description   Duration
1.   Productivity   06
Productivity concepts. Analysing the work content of a job to identify and
reduce/eliminate the excess work content. Interdependence between
working conditions and productivity.
Significance of theory of Scientific Management. Improving Efficiency and
Productivity through Work-study, Work-study components. Relationship
between Method Study and Time Study.
2.   Method Study   08
Basic procedure of method study. Factors in selecting a job to a studied.
Recording the facts with charts and diagrams. Questioning technique for
development of new method. Role of Management and workers in
implementation.
3.   Facilities & Workplace Design   05
Aligning the physical facilities- plant layout, equipment and work flow as per
the production processes. Principles of Motion Economy. Standardization of
the process.
4.   Work Measurement   10
Significance of work measurement. Techniques of work measurement. Need
of work sampling technique. Conducting work sampling study. Analytical
estimation of work. Concept of rating factor. Consideration of various
allowances. Standard time for work. Predetermined time standards. Use
standard data. MOST for work measurement. Use of time standards.
A.Y. 2024-25
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
5.   Ergonomics   7
Field of Ergonomics. Physical and cognitive issues of ergonomics. Aims of
ergonomics considerations. Working postures of operatives. Design of
objects, facilities and environment. Anthropometrical details. Database of
human factors. Ergonomic improvement of physical and cognitive issues.
Ergonomics principals. Information input and human control of systems.
Work space and arrangement. Living environment. Visual displays
6.   Value Engineering   9
Definition of Value Engineering, Uses of Value Engineering, Reasons for
unnecessary costs, Difference between Value Engineering and other cost
reduction techniques. Case studies
Total   45
Text Books
1. International Labour Office, Introduction to Work Study, 3rd edition, Oxford & I. B. H.
Publishing Co. Ltd, 2015.
2. R. Barnes, Motion and Time Study Design and Measurement of Work, 7th edition, Asia
Publishing, 2009.
Reference Books
1. M. S. Sanders & E J McCormick, Human factors in Engineering & Design, Tata McGraw Hill,
2020.
2. Merton E. Davis, William D. Falcon, Value Engineering: The Implications for Managers, American
Management Association, 2002.

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes I and II, Machine Drawing
Course Objective
The objective of the course is to impart introductory knowledge of Additive Manufacturing (AM)
and its capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industries. The course is structured to
acquaint the students with the operating principles and applications of most prominent
technologies in the field of additive manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Compare the fundamental principles of various additive manufacturing technologies in terms
of material requirements, manufacturing technologies and applications
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the product
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Additive Manufacturing   06
Introduction to AM, history of AM, definition, distinction between AM, CNC
& other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications
of AM processes, design for additive manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry:
present and future, AM process chain, AM file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF, PLY,
VRML, and LEO), part orientation, support generation, model slicing,
contour generation, machine set-up, build file preparation.
2.   Classification of Additive Manufacturing Techniques   12
Material Extrusion:
Process mechanism, process parameters, extrusion of: ceramics, metals,
biomaterials, composites, contour crafting, concrete printing
Vat Polymerization:
Process mechanism, process parameters, advantages, disadvantages,
applications, Digital Light Processing (DLP), recent advances, Large-Scale
Rapid Liquid Printing.
Binder & material jetting processes:
Binder jettng process workflow, material requirements, binder-powder
interaction, binder properties.
Material Jetting process workflow, thermal and piezoelectric inkjet, material
jetting fluid mechanics, drop-on-demand and continuous methods of MJ.
Powder bed fusion AM process:

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
Selective laser sintering (SLS), process mechanism, process parameters,
selective laser melting (SLM), process workflow and material requirements,
powder melting mechanisms, electron beam melting (EBM) process.
Sheet Lamination AM Processes:
Process mechanism, process parameters, ultrasonic additive manufacturing
(UAM), ultrasonic welding fundamentals, UAM process parameters
Directed Energy Deposition (DED) Processes:
Process workflow, materials feeding for DED: powder (Laser Engineered Net
Shaping) and wire, process parameters, cold spray.
3.   Post- Processing   04
Product quality evaluation, need for post-processing, support material
removal, surface finish improvement, aesthetic improvement, property
enhancements using non-thermal and thermal techniques.
4.   Design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM)   04
Design guidelines: part orientation, support, geometry considerations, layer
thickness, part size, material consideration, residual stress, topology
optimization, case studies on design for AM.
5.   Applications of AM & Industry 4.0   04
Aerospace, biomedical, defence, automobile, rapid tooling, reverse
engineering, economic consideration, Industry 4.0 for AM, case studies on
application of AM in various industries.
Total   30

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year students’
learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with the required
practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically, solve challenging
problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication skills, teamwork and
planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope
and learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the
research gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design and
fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and
verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a
report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and
synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her work carried out before examiners.

covering its foundational concepts and advanced applications. Students will gain insight into the
historical development and evolution of RPA, along with a deep appreciation for the benefits and

harness workflow automation, create apps, grasp the distinctions between attended and unattended
bots, and comprehend the symbiotic relationship between RPA and Artificial Intelligence (AI).

process analysis and selection

optimized automation processes

workflows, and deploy applications within operational frameworks

implementations, and making informed decisions regarding automation practices.

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes-I and Manufacturing Processes-II
Course Objective
The objective of this course is to give the students a systematic and comprehensive understanding
of various aspects related to industrial engineering and its relevance in the industrial
environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Describe the concepts of productivity and methods to improve efficiency
2. Apply the methods to measure parameters such as time and magnitude of activities
performed
3. Analyze the cost effectiveness of each function of the product in terms of usefulness to the
customer
Detailed Syllabus
Unit Description   Duration
1.   Productivity   06
Productivity concepts. Analysing the work content of a job to identify and
reduce/eliminate the excess work content. Interdependence between
working conditions and productivity.
Significance of theory of Scientific Management. Improving Efficiency and
Productivity through Work-study, Work-study components. Relationship
between Method Study and Time Study.
2.   Method Study   08
Basic procedure of method study. Factors in selecting a job to a studied.
Recording the facts with charts and diagrams. Questioning technique for
development of new method. Role of Management and workers in
implementation.
3.   Facilities & Workplace Design   05
Aligning the physical facilities- plant layout, equipment and work flow as per
the production processes. Principles of Motion Economy. Standardization of
the process.
4.   Work Measurement   10
Significance of work measurement. Techniques of work measurement. Need
of work sampling technique. Conducting work sampling study. Analytical
estimation of work. Concept of rating factor. Consideration of various
allowances. Standard time for work. Predetermined time standards. Use
standard data. MOST for work measurement. Use of time standards.
A.Y. 2023-24
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
5.   Ergonomics   7
Field of Ergonomics. Physical and cognitive issues of ergonomics. Aims of
ergonomics considerations. Working postures of operatives. Design of
objects, facilities and environment. Anthropometrical details. Database of
human factors. Ergonomic improvement of physical and cognitive issues.
Ergonomics principals. Information input and human control of systems.
Work space and arrangement. Living environment. Visual displays
6.   Value Engineering   9
Definition of Value Engineering, Uses of Value Engineering, Reasons for
unnecessary costs, Difference between Value Engineering and other cost
reduction techniques. Case studies
Total   45
Text Books
1. International Labour Office, Introduction to Work Study, 3rd edition, Oxford & I. B. H.
Publishing Co. Ltd, 2015.
2. R. Barnes, Motion and Time Study Design and Measurement of Work, 7th edition, Asia
Publishing, 2009.

2020.

Management Association, 2002.

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes I and II, Machine Drawing
Course Objective
The objective of the course is to impart introductory knowledge of Additive Manufacturing (AM)
and its capabilities in the modern digital manufacturing industries. The course is structured to
acquaint the students with the operating principles and applications of most prominent
technologies in the field of additive manufacturing.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, the student will be able to -
1. Compare the fundamental principles of various additive manufacturing technologies in terms
of material requirements, manufacturing technologies and applications
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the product
3. Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right AM process for a given application
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Additive Manufacturing   06
Introduction to AM, history of AM, definition, distinction between AM, CNC
& other digital manufacturing techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications
of AM processes, design for additive manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry:
present and future, AM process chain, AM file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF, PLY,
VRML, and LEO), part orientation, support generation, model slicing,
contour generation, machine set-up, build file preparation.
2.   Classification of Additive Manufacturing Techniques   12
Material Extrusion:
Process mechanism, process parameters, extrusion of: ceramics, metals,
biomaterials, composites, contour crafting, concrete printing
Vat Polymerization:
Process mechanism, process parameters, advantages, disadvantages,
applications, Digital Light Processing (DLP), recent advances, Large-Scale
Rapid Liquid Printing.
Binder & material jetting processes:
Binder jettng process workflow, material requirements, binder-powder
interaction, binder properties.
Material Jetting process workflow, thermal and piezoelectric inkjet, material
jetting fluid mechanics, drop-on-demand and continuous methods of MJ.
Powder bed fusion AM process:
A.Y. 2023-24
SVKM’s NMIMS Deemed-to-be University
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
Selective laser sintering (SLS), process mechanism, process parameters,
selective laser melting (SLM), process workflow and material requirements,
powder melting mechanisms, electron beam melting (EBM) process.
Sheet Lamination AM Processes:
Process mechanism, process parameters, ultrasonic additive manufacturing
(UAM), ultrasonic welding fundamentals, UAM process parameters
Directed Energy Deposition (DED) Processes:
Process workflow, materials feeding for DED: powder (Laser Engineered Net
Shaping) and wire, process parameters, cold spray.
3.   Post- Processing   04
Product quality evaluation, need for post-processing, support material
removal, surface finish improvement, aesthetic improvement, property
enhancements using non-thermal and thermal techniques.
4.   Design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM)   04
Design guidelines: part orientation, support, geometry considerations, layer
thickness, part size, material consideration, residual stress, topology
optimization, case studies on design for AM.
5.   Applications of AM & Industry 4.0   04
Aerospace, biomedical, defence, automobile, rapid tooling, reverse
engineering, economic consideration, Industry 4.0 for AM, case studies on
application of AM in various industries.
Total   30

Pre-requisite: Knowledge of all core and elective courses completed till 3rd year.
Course Objective
The capstone project is designed to provide a culminating design experience to the final-year students’
learning with essentially required hands-on experience to ensure that they graduate with the required
practical and soft skills. The course aims to encourage students to think critically, solve challenging
problems, do a feasibility study and develop written and oral communication skills, teamwork and
planning. The students may also work in interdisciplinary areas which will help broaden their scope
and learning in different domains.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Select an appropriate problem statement after reviewing the literature and identifying the
research gaps.
2. Formulate the different use cases/feasible design model.
3. Implement the prototype/proof of concept, test and validate the results.
4. Manage a team project.
5. Summarize the topic into a technical report.
Syllabus
A student is required to carry out elaborated project work. The project may be either design and
fabrication work or a simulation and synthesis of a problem/system, and develop algorithms and
verify feasibility of implementation. At the end of the semester students will be required to submit a
report detailing the literature review, design problem formulation, analysis functional simulation and
synthesis, work plan and work done and present his/her work carried out before examiners.

Objectives
This course provides basic orientation towards economic (micro and macroeconomics)
principles and help them understand the functions of management. This course also aims to
understand issues dealing with small-scale economic phenomena and concepts such as prices
and output of firms, industries and resource owners along with examining market impact of
technological change with regards to understand broader aspects of the economy and its
environment.
Course Outcomes
After completion of this course, students will be able to-
1. Illustrate basic concepts of economics (demand, supply, elasticity, scarcity) and
explain behaviour on individual, households and firm and Handle economic data
and write economic report,
2. Analyse and evaluate the impact of Economic Policies and its implication on the
Business Environment,
3. Demonstrate and determine the students towards basic management principles and
act as foundation for higher levels of learning and to be able to handle basic functions
of management (planning, organizing, coordination, and control).

Pre-requisite: Manufacturing Processes(BTMA03011), Materials Engineering (BTMA5013)
Objectives:
1. Acquire introductory knowledge of Additive Manufacturing (AM) and its capabilities in the
modern digital manufacturing industry.
2. To get acquainted with the operating principles and applications of most prominent
technologies in the field of Additive Manufacturing.
3. Explore the Design for Additive Manufacturing capabilities of each AM process and to
identify and create complex and novel designs.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Understand the fundamental principles of various Additive Manufacturing (AM)
technologies, material requirements and cost considerations with regards to each AM process.
2. Identify critical areas where AM can be applied to create value for the entire product life-
cycle.
3. Select the right AM process for a given application.
4. Develop an enterprising perspective concerning the application of AM in the design of a
product, either entirely or partly.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Additive Manufacturing: Introduction to AM, history of AM,   04
definition, distinction between AM, CNC & other digital manufacturing
techniques, reasons to use AM, classifications of AM processes, design for
Additive Manufacturing (DfAM), AM industry: present and future, AM
process chain, CAD and file formats for AM. Introduction to Metal Additive
Manufacturing. Laser Cutting vs Water jet cutting.
2.   Extrusion based AM processes: Fused deposition Modeling(FDM), history of   05
FDM, material requirements, workflow: material loading, liquefaction,
bonding, solidification, support generation, nozzle dynamics, applications,
benefits and limitations, post-processing, material characterization, extrusion
of: ceramics, metals, biomaterials, composites, non-planer systems, contour
crafting, concrete printing.
3.   Vat Polymerization AM process: Stereolithography apparatus(SLA), history   05
of SLA, material requirements, workflow: SLA chemistry, reaction mechanism,
scan patterns, applications, benefits and limitations, other liquid polymer-
based systems: Solid Ground Curing (SGC), Microstreolithography, Digital
Light Processing (DLP), Continuous Liquid Interface Production (CLIP),
Large-Scale Rapid Liquid Printing.

Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering
4.   Sheet Lamination AM Processes: Laminated Object Manufacturing (LOM),   04
LOM of paper, polymer and composite sheets, LOM mechanism: gluing,
adhesive bonding, bond then from, from then bond, thermal bonding, sheet
metal clamping, Ultrasonic Additive Manufacturing(UAM), ultrasonic
welding fundamentals, UAM process parameters, material characterization.
5.   Powder Bed Fusion AM Process: Selective Laser Sintering (SLS): process   11
workflow and material requirements, powder production methods, powder
fusion mechanism, polymer ageing and recycling, High Speed Sintering(HSS),
Multi-Jet Fusion(MJF), polymer powder characterization and selection,
Selective Laser Melting (SLM): process workflow and material requirements,
powder melting mechanism, melt pool dynamics, laser scan patterns, post-
processing, powder production, handling and recycling, Electron Beam
Melting (EBM) Process.
6.   Binder Jetting (BJ) & Material Jetting AM Process: workflow, thermal and   06
piezoelectric inkjet, material requirements, material jetting fluid mechanics,
drop-on-demand and continuous methods of MJ, material jetting of metals,
ceramics, nanomaterial, BJ AM Process: process workflow, material
requirements, powder characterization for BJ process, binder-powder
interaction, binder properties.
7.   Directed Energy Deposition (DED) Processes: Process workflow, materials   04
feeding for DED: powder (Laser Engineered Net Shaping) & wire, process
parameters and optimization, Electron Beam Additive Manufacturing (EBAM)
plasma-based DED, Cold Spray.
8.   Design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM): Key process-specific DfAM   06
guidelines, AM file formats (STL, 3MF, AMF, PLY, VRML, LEO): processing,
conversion and repair algorithms, tool path generation, topology optimization,
generative design, slicing and support generation.

Pre-requisite: Theory of structures, Concrete technology
Course Objective
This course aims to bring the students to such a level so as to enable them to take the appropriate
decision in respect of choice of prestressed section over R. C. C. as a civil engineer. Also to make the
candidate to understand the analysis of Prestressed Concrete sections and losses in prestress. This
course focuses to make the candidate able to understand and implement the guidelines of Indian
Standard code for analysis and design sections using limit state philosophy.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to -
1. Understand the concept of pre-stressing its casting techniques and applications, behaviour of the
pre-stressed structures vis-à-vis that of the RCC structure
2. Apply the concept to take the decision with respect to the choice of pre-stressed section over RCC
3. Analyse the various pre-stressed components of the structure and design the same using relevant
IS Code

Introduction, Prestressing Systems and Material Properties

materials. Definitions, advantages of prestressing, limitations of prestressing, types
1   of prestressing, source of prestressing force. External or internal prestressing, pre-
07

prestressing, uniaxial, biaxial or multiaxial prestressing. Prestressing systems and

provisions.

4   design, final design for Type – I and Type – II members. Choice of sections,   07
determination of limiting zone, post-tensioning in stages, Magnel’s graphical method,

Prerequisite: Student should have 10+2 level knowledge in chemistry, biology and physics.
Course Objective
The course introduces students to forensic investigation. It will enable students to understand and
appreciate various analytical techniques such as fingerprint analysis, digital forensic techniques,
chemical and instrumental methodologies. This will help students understand the procedures of
crime scene investigation. Overall, the course will allow students to appreciate above techniques
which are reliable and sensitive tools for detailed investigation. It will also help students in
developing strong analytical skill development, keen observation skills and patience.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to
1. Recognise the fundamentals of forensic science and its importance to human civilization
2. Develop technical skills that can be used for proper analysis of the evidence found in the
crime scene to give a lead to the investigators
3. Connect the importance of forensic science for perseverance of the society

Definitions and concepts in forensic science. Need of forensic science in various
fields. Basic principles of forensic science. Branches of forensic science.   05
Forensic science in international perspectives, including set up of INTERPOL
and FBI.
2.   Forensic Psychology
Basics of Forensic Psychology: Definition and fundamental concepts of forensic   06
psychology and forensic psychiatry. Mental disorders and forensic psychology.
Psychological assessment and its importance.
3.
Forensic Dermatoglyphics
Biological basis of fingerprints. Formation of ridges. Fundamental principles of
fingerprinting. Types of fingerprints. Fingerprint patterns. Latent prints. Latent   06
fingerprints’ detection by physical and chemical techniques. Importance of foot
prints, palm prints, and lip prints.

explosives. Blasting agents. Detection of hidden explosives. Narcotics and toxicology
Serology and DNA Typing: Forensic characterization of bloodstains. Collection
and preservation of blood evidence. Typing of dried stains. Crime scene   10
reconstruction with the aid of bloodstain pattern analysis. Composition,
functions and forensic significance of saliva, semen, sweat, milk and urine. Tests

Chromatographic methods. Fundamentals and forensic applications of various analytical

atomic absorption spectroscopy, atomic emission spectroscopy, and mass spectroscopy,
X-ray spectrometry.   10
Forensic photography- Basic principles and applications of photography in
forensic science. 3D photography. Photographic evidence. IR and UV
photography. Digital photography. Videography. Crime scene and laboratory
photography.
6   Digital Forensics
Definition and types of computer crimes. Distinction between computer crimes and
conventional crimes. Reasons for commission of computer crimes. Breaching security
and operation of digital systems. Computer virus, and computer worm – Trojan horse,
08
trap door, super zapping, logic bombs. Types of computer crimes –hacking, crimes
