Course Objective
This course will enable the students to appreciate the essential complementarity between 'VALUES' and
'SKILLS’ to ensure sustained happiness and prosperity, which are the core aspirations of all human beings. It
will facilitate the development of a Holistic perspective among students towards life and profession as well
as towards happiness and prosperity based on a correct understanding of the Human reality and the rest of
existence. Such a holistic perspective forms the basis of Universal Human Values and its movement towards
value-based living in a natural way. Moreover, it will highlight plausible implications of such a Holistic
understanding in terms of ethical human conduct, trustful and mutually fulfilling human behavior and
mutually enriching interaction with Nature. Finally, this course is intended to provide a much-needed
orientation in value education to the young minds.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to –
1. Appraise that technical education without study of human values can generate more problems than
solutions.
2. Cultivate that natural acceptance (intention) and ‘respect’ is right evaluation, and only right
evaluation leads to fulfilment in relationship and living in harmony.
3. Design sustainable solutions to the problems in society and nature.
4. Integrate utilization of knowledge in streams of Technology/Engineering/Management/any other
area of study to ensure mutual fulfilment e.g. mutually enriching production system with rest of
nature, which needs to be nurtured, protected utilized in the right manner.

Prerequisite: Student should have 10+2 level knowledge in chemistry, biology and physics.
Course Objective
The course introduces students to forensic investigation. It will enable students to understand and
appreciate various analytical techniques such as fingerprint analysis, digital forensic techniques,
chemical and instrumental methodologies. This will help students understand the procedures of crime
scene investigation. Overall, the course will allow students to appreciate above techniques which are
reliable and sensitive tools for detailed investigation. It will also help students in developing strong
analytical skill development, keen observation skills and patience.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to
1. Recognise the fundamentals of forensic science and its importance to human civilization
2. Develop technical skills that can be used for proper analysis of the evidence found in the crime
scene to give a lead to the investigators
3. Connect the importance of forensic science for perseverance of the society
Detailed Syllabus
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Forensic science
Definitions and concepts in forensic science. Need of forensic science in various
05
fields. Basic principles of forensic science. Branches of forensic science. Forensic
science in international perspectives, including set up of INTERPOL and FBI.
2.   Forensic Psychology
Basics of Forensic Psychology: Definition and fundamental concepts of forensic
06
psychology and forensic psychiatry. Mental disorders and forensic psychology.
Psychological assessment and its importance.
3.   Forensic Dermatoglyphics
Biological basis of fingerprints. Formation of ridges. Fundamental principles of
fingerprinting. Types of fingerprints. Fingerprint patterns. Latent prints. Latent   06
fingerprints’ detection by physical and chemical techniques. Importance of foot
prints, palm prints, and lip prints.
4.   Forensic Biochemistry
Arson and explosives: Chemistry of fire. Analysis of fire debris. Information from
smoke staining. Classification of explosives – low explosives and high explosives,   10
Military explosives. Blasting agents. Detection of hidden explosives. Narcotics
and toxicology
SVKM’s Narsee Monjee Institute of Management Studies
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management & Engineering
Serology and DNA Typing: Forensic characterization of bloodstains. Collection
and preservation of blood evidence. Typing of dried stains. Crime scene
reconstruction with the aid of bloodstain pattern analysis. Composition,
functions and forensic significance of saliva, semen, sweat, milk and urine. Tests
for their identifications. Genetic Marker Analysis. ABO blood groups,
significance of genetic marker typing data, sexual assault investigations.
Parentage Testing
5.   Instrumental methods in forensics
Chromatographic methods. Fundamentals and forensic applications of various
analytical techniques such as thin layer chromatography, gas chromatography
and liquid chromatography. Spectroscopic methods- UV-visible spectroscopy, IR
spectroscopy, atomic absorption spectroscopy, atomic emission spectroscopy,
and mass spectroscopy, X-ray spectrometry.   10
Forensic photography- Basic principles and applications of photography in
forensic science. 3D photography. Photographic evidence. IR and UV
photography. Digital photography. Videography. Crime scene and laboratory
photography.
6   Digital Forensics
Definition and types of computer crimes. Distinction between computer crimes
and conventional crimes. Reasons for commission of computer crimes.
Breaching security and operation of digital systems. Computer virus, and
computer worm – Trojan horse, trap door, super zapping, logic bombs. Types   08
of computer crimes –hacking, crimes related to intellectual property rights,
computer terrorism, hate speech, private and national security in cyber space.
An overview of spamming, phishing, catfishing and stalking. Extraction of
information from the hard disk.
Total   45

Prerequisite: Student should have 10+2 level knowledge in chemistry, biology and physics.
Course Objective
The course introduces students to forensic investigation. It will enable students to understand and
appreciate various analytical techniques such as fingerprint analysis, digital forensic techniques,
chemical and instrumental methodologies. This will help students understand the procedures of crime
scene investigation. Overall, the course will allow students to appreciate above techniques which are
reliable and sensitive tools for detailed investigation. It will also help students in developing strong
analytical skill development, keen observation skills and patience.
Course Outcomes
After completion of the course, students will be able to
1. Recognise the fundamentals of forensic science and its importance to human civilization
2. Develop technical skills that can be used for proper analysis of the evidence found in the crime
scene to give a lead to the investigators
3. Connect the importance of forensic science for perseverance of the society

Unit   Description   Duration

Definitions and concepts in forensic science. Need of forensic science in various
05
fields. Basic principles of forensic science. Branches of forensic science. Forensic
science in international perspectives, including set up of INTERPOL and FBI.
2.   Forensic Psychology
Basics of Forensic Psychology: Definition and fundamental concepts of forensic
06
psychology and forensic psychiatry. Mental disorders and forensic psychology.
Psychological assessment and its importance.
3.   Forensic Dermatoglyphics
Biological basis of fingerprints. Formation of ridges. Fundamental principles of
fingerprinting. Types of fingerprints. Fingerprint patterns. Latent prints. Latent   06
fingerprints’ detection by physical and chemical techniques. Importance of foot
prints, palm prints, and lip prints.
4.   Forensic Biochemistry
Arson and explosives: Chemistry of fire. Analysis of fire debris. Information from
smoke staining. Classification of explosives – low explosives and high explosives,   10
Military explosives. Blasting agents. Detection of hidden explosives. Narcotics
and toxicology

Serology and DNA Typing: Forensic characterization of bloodstains. Collection
and preservation of blood evidence. Typing of dried stains. Crime scene
reconstruction with the aid of bloodstain pattern analysis. Composition,
functions and forensic significance of saliva, semen, sweat, milk and urine. Tests
for their identifications. Genetic Marker Analysis. ABO blood groups,
significance of genetic marker typing data, sexual assault investigations.
Parentage Testing
5.   Instrumental methods in forensics
Chromatographic methods. Fundamentals and forensic applications of various
analytical techniques such as thin layer chromatography, gas chromatography
and liquid chromatography. Spectroscopic methods- UV-visible spectroscopy, IR
spectroscopy, atomic absorption spectroscopy, atomic emission spectroscopy,
and mass spectroscopy, X-ray spectrometry.   10
Forensic photography- Basic principles and applications of photography in
forensic science. 3D photography. Photographic evidence. IR and UV
photography. Digital photography. Videography. Crime scene and laboratory
photography.
6   Digital Forensics
Definition and types of computer crimes. Distinction between computer crimes
and conventional crimes. Reasons for commission of computer crimes.
Breaching security and operation of digital systems. Computer virus, and
computer worm – Trojan horse, trap door, super zapping, logic bombs. Types   08
of computer crimes –hacking, crimes related to intellectual property rights,
computer terrorism, hate speech, private and national security in cyber space.
An overview of spamming, phishing, catfishing and stalking. Extraction of
information from the hard disk.

Objectives:
1. To provide the basic understanding of measurement and instrumentation systems and
the insight of the resistive sensors and its applications in real life.
2. To introduce the concept of the reactive sensors and self-generating sensors and its
applications in real life.
3. To familiarize the characteristics, working principle and application of special purpose
transducers.
4. To impart the importance of smart sensors, sensor interface standards for wearable
device applications and to provide a brief overview of the wearable technology and its
impact on social life
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Understand the basic idea of measurements, characteristics and the errors associated
with measurements.
2. Demonstrate and realize the concept of resistive and reactive sensors to be employed
for real life applications
3. Understand the working principle of special purpose sensors and the need for
developing smart sensors.
4. Describe the taxonomy of the wearable devices and its design constraints for measuring
physical and biological signals.

Objectives:
1. To offer students the tools and techniques of film appreciation so that they will be able to actively
engage with cinema as a form of art, expression, history and culture.
2. To expose students to different genres of world cinema so as to make them avid, critical and
active viewers.
3. Through their exposure to arts and humanities, to broaden their horizons and deepen their
sensibilities so that they may respond and engage with the world with increased awareness and
competence.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. to understand the way that content, form, and contexts work together to create meaning in film.
2. to actively engage with cinema and develop an informed personal response to films.
3. view and appreciate films through an informed understanding of their technique of production,
grammar, cultural and historical context.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1.   What is cinema?   5
   Definition of cinema.
 The concept of persistence of vision.
   Film’s relationship to each of the arts: music, dance, literature, theatre,
architecture, photography and painting.
 The relationship between film and 20th-century art movements:
impressionism, cubism, surrealism.
2.   Visual literacy   5
 The vocabulary of film: shot, scene, sequence, frame, composition in depth,
 point of view, transitions, Mise-en-scène etc.

 The tools of expression- frequency and number of shots, the size of the subject
in the frame, the angle of view, composition and balance, the use of lighting
and
   color, the movement of camera and lens, how images come to express
meanings and its relation with the word-meanings. Film formats: celluloid and
digital
 Element of sound: dialogues, background score, music, silence, ambience.
3.   Film styles and Genres   5
 Image and editing. To what extent does film manipulate reality?
   Different genres. Analysis of recurrent themes, images, and narrative
structures. Action, adventure, comedy, drama, epic/historical, horror, Sci-fi,
war etc. Other formats i.e. short films: fiction & nonfiction
4.   Film appreciation and history   25
 Development of film in Europe, US and India. Important directors and their
   contribution to world cinema, film companies and films.
 World cinema: D. W. Griffith, Sergie Enstine, Robert Flaharty, Vittorio De Sica,
Walt Disney, Charles Chaplin, Franscois Trufautt, Jean Luc Godard, Ingmar
Bergmen, Andrei Tarkovsky, Sergei Eisenstein, Alfred Hitchcock, Jean Renoir,
Federico Fellini, Akira Kurosowa, Andre Wajda, Yashizoro Ozu, Steven
Speilberg, Majid Majidi, etc.
 Indian cinema: V. Shantaram, Satyajit Ray, Shyam Benegal, Ritwik Ghatak,
Girish Karnad, Rajkapoor, Guru Dutt, Adoor Gopalkrishnan, Mrinal Sen,
Bimal Roy, Basu Bhattacharya, Maniratnam, and contemporary trend-setting
directors.
5.   Film Studies   5
 Film appreciation, analysis, criticism etc.
 Reviewing films for various media.
 Censorship: need, relevance, Censor Board. Influence of cinema on society,
culture, arts.
 Film institutions: NFDC, NFAI, FTII, Film Festivals Authority of India,
Children Film Society.
 Film Society movement, International film festivals.
 Films as an industry.
   Interrelationship of film industry with other media.

1. understand the scope of AI in chemometrics and chemical data processing.

3. interpret spectroscopic data obtained from various analytical techniques.
4. apply AI in vaccine development and delivery systems during the pandemic.

analytical techniques (chromatography, UV-Visible, IR, NMR, MS), unifying AI

methods.

machines learn chemical patterns, expert systems, dendritic algorithms.

molecular descriptors, automated chemical lab bench.

Objectives:
This course intends to build a deep understanding of the Smart City concept and the technology
that underpins it. The course is designed to help the students develop innovative concepts and
prototypes for a sustainable smart city
Outcomes
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Decode the Smart City concept & different models of Smart cities in the world
2. Application of technological innovations for smart city enablement
3. Identify and measure requirements of a smart city.
4. Project work: Generate innovative solutions for smart city as projects outcome
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1. “Smart City” – Various perspectives and definitions, Characteristics of a   3
smart city: What makes a city Smart? What are the different models of Smart
city development – existing city into Smart city, New green field project,
enhancing a “town” into a Smart City.
2. Components of a smart city: Pillars of a smart city – Institutional, Physical,   3
Social, Economic, Infrastructure, Factors that make smart cities possible, Use
of technology and automation.
3.   Identification of smart cities: Framework and KPI for smart city   3
development – 1: Conditions precedent for smart city development,
Benchmarks for smart cities, Government policies, Mapping of smart cities
through Transport, Infrastructure, Water Management, energy, health,
hygiene & sanitation, education, governance, social & cultural fabric and
disaster management. Measurement of key parameters (KPI) for smart cities

6. Understanding Financial sustainability of Smart cities, the PPP model   3
for smart city development
7. Case Studies of Existing best practices in cities in India   3
8. Case Studies of Existing Smart cities of the world   3
Like Singapore, London – UK, Barcelona etc.
9.   Project work begins : Students get divided into teams, each team will study   3
one of the ten aspects of Smart city- Transport, Infrastructure, Water
Management , energy, health, hygiene & sanitation, education, governance,
social & cultural fabric and disaster management: Project work begins -
Briefing to students on the sub-themes and allotted projects related to any one
area for an in- depth study by each team. The stage gates and timelines for the
project defined along with the evaluation criteria at each deliverable.
10. Sector analysis - Project wise: Presentation of secondary research on the   3

Pre-requisite: Introductory course in Environmental Studies, physics, chemistry, geography
Objectives:
1. Interpret multidisciplinary scientific bases of climatic change: basic mechanisms that govern the
climate system and its responses to drivers of change
2. Analyse paleo-climatic change and assess recent historical variability to project future climate
projections
3. Investigate the impact of climate change on communities of human population and global
economy
4. Gain insight into legal and Financial aspects of Climate change
5. Investigate fundamentals of the fields of Geo-engineering
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
1. Explain how the climate system works and understand the physical basis of climate change
2. Investigate climate projections from the past and predict possible future climate change on Earth
3. Analyse how human activities are influencing Climate Change and Global Warming
4. Evaluate global climate change policy and its implementation, options for mitigation and
adaptation
5. Evaluate aspects of Climate change finance
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit   Description   Duration
1   Introduction to Climate Change Science:   08
 Human contribution to climate change; units of temperature, energy and
light;
 Overview of important greenhouse gases and their main sources, Earth
Energy Budget and Energy balance model, Radiative transfer, Naked planet
climate model, Nuclear winter
 Anthropogenic Drivers of Climate Change: Main observed changes in the
climate since the industrial revolution.
 Future trends and Impacts of Climate Change: Projected future trends and
impacts of climate change on surface temperature, precipitation, ocean pH
2   Paleo-Climate:   03
   Principles of Paleo-climate studies: Polar Regions and Sea level rise, Ice Ages
   Paleoclimate and Proxy Measurements
 Tree Rings, Borehole temperatures and Interglacial cycles
3   Climate and Changing Weather:   06
 Concepts of Heat transport, Coriolis Acceleration, Geostrophic motion, Ice
albedo, water vapour feedback, aerosols
 Global Wind Systems: Trade Winds and the Hadley Cell, the Highs and
Lows of the Westerlies, the Vital Importance of Monsoon Rains
 Cloud Formation and Climate: Hurricanes and Global Warming
Open Elective-II/CIVIL/2021-22/Page 6 of 10

 Global Ocean Circulation: The Icelandic Whirlpool, Origin of the Gulf
Stream, The Deep Atlantic Conveyor, El Niño and its Effects
 Global ice sheet degradation: rates, reasons
4   Climate Change Legalities:   06
 The Climate Change Policy Framework: Overview of how the international
legal and policy framework to address climate change developed over time
and key issues under negotiation.
 Key provisions of the UNFCCC, its organizational structure, and different
Party groups under the Convention.
 Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement, COP Simulation
 Towards a Post-2020 Regime
 India’s role in climate change mitigation
6   Climate Change Adaptations and Finance:   08
 Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience: Conducting a Vulnerability
Assessment
 Climate Finance Landscapes
 Economic Development: Linking Adaptation and Development Planning;
international Initiatives to Support Climate Change Adaptation
   International Climate Negotiations
   Policy and Regulation
 National and International financing, Private Finance
   Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF), Green Climate Fund (GCF), WBG
2025 Climate Change, Pilot Program for Climate Resilience (PPCR)
7   Impacts of Climate Change: (Case Studies)   04
 On Ecosystems
 Food security and food production
 Human health, livelihoods and poverty
8   Geoengineering: Future technologies and Mitigation   10
 Overview of emissions levels and mitigation targets per country, ways to
integrate mitigation into development planning, through low emission
development strategies.
 Low Carbon Development, CO₂ Capture and Sequestration; role of basalt
rocks
   Solar Radiation Management, Temperature targets
   Biofuels, gas hydrates
 Slug Theory, stabilization scenarios
 Role of non-governmental organizations and corporate initiatives; voluntary
commitments and actions; disclosure-based initiatives; social cost of carbon
 Economics of Climate Change, main economic sectors where mitigation
actions can be applied
 Short term and Long Term Mitigation
Total   45
Pedagogy:
1. 45 Lectures, including presentations, videos, invited specialist lecture delivery
2. Fieldwork of at least 5 days

Pre-requisite: Nil
Objectives:
● Acquire introductory knowledge of 3D Printing (3DP) and its capabilities in the
modern digital manufacturing industry.
● To get acquainted with the operating principles and applications of most
prominent technologies in the field of 3D Printing
● Explore the Design for 3D printing capabilities of each 3D printing process and to
identify and create complex and novel designs.
Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:
● Understand the fundamental principles of various 3D Printing technologies, material
requirements and cost considerations about each 3DP process.
● Identify critical areas where 3DP can be applied to create value for the entire
product life cycle.
● Apply the necessary skills in selecting the right 3DP process for a given application.
● Develop an enterprising perspective concerning the application of 3DP in the
design of a product, either entirely or partly.
Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)
Unit Description   Duration
1   Introduction to 3D Printing: Introduction to 3DP, history of 3DP,   4
definition, distinction between 3DP, AM, CNC & other digital
manufacturing techniques, reasons to use 3DP, classifications of 3DP
processes, design for Additive Manufacturing (DfAM), 3DP industry:
present and future, 3DP process chain, CAD and file formats for 3DP.

liquefaction, bonding, solidification, support generation, nozzle

material characterization, extrusion of: ceramics, metals, biomaterials,
composites, non-planer systems, contour crafting, concrete printing.

apparatus(SLA), history of SLA, material requirements, workflow:
SLA chemistry, reaction mechanism, scan patterns, applications,
benefits and limitations, other liquid polymer-based systems: solid

Pre-requisite: Object Oriented Programming, Data Structures and Algorithms.
Objective:
1. To impart knowledge of the current theories, methods and techniques in the field
of Artificial Intelligence.
2. To create ability to analyze, design and develop Al-systems.
Course Outcomes: After successful completion of this course, student will be able to:
1. Formulate Artificial Intelligent problem and identify agents and environments.
2. Apply informed and uninformed searching strategies.
3. Apply knowledge representation schemes for expert systems and game playing.
4. Implement supervised and unsupervised learning approaches to solve problems
in AI domain
Detailed Syllabus:
Unit   Description   Duration
1.   Introduction to Artificial Intelligence:
Definitions of AI, Broad overview of application areas of AI (like
vision, Natural language processing, Robotics etc.) Concept of
Modelling, Inference and Learning. Introduction to Machine   5
learning and Deep learning as a subset of AI. Intelligent agents,
concept of rationality, structure of agents, Environment, Properties
of task environment. Real world Examples of agents and
environments.
2.   Solving problems by Searching:
Problem solving agents, well define problems and solutions,   10
formulating problems. What is searching? problem as a state space
search, Informed search and uninformed search.

Uninformed   Search:   Breadth   first   search, Depth   first
search, Uniform cost search
Informed Search: Informed search strategies, Greedy Best first
Search, A* search, Hill climbing, problem with hill climbing such
as Local Maxima, Plateau, Ridge, Genetic Algorithm.
Adversarial Search:
Introduction to Domain of a game, optimal decisions in games,
minimax algorithm, Alpha-beta pruning.
3.   Knowledge Representation:
Prepositional Logic: Syntax, Semantics Knowledge base and
inference.
Predicate logic: Facts, Representation of fact, mapping between
facts and representation, properties and issues of knowledge   8
representation system, Instance relationship, Isa, gt & Lt predicate.
Unification algorithm, resolution in predicate and prepositional
logic.
Rules: Procedural versus Declarative knowledge, forward versus
backward reasoning, forward & backward chaining rule system.
4.   Constraint satisfaction Problem (CSP):
Constraint satisfaction problems, Backtracking search for CSPs,
variables and value ordering, propagating information through   5
constraints, Intelligent backtracking, Local search for CSP. Case
study: Complete example on CSP.
5.   Learning:
Forms   of   learning,   Super-vised   learning-   decision   tree
classification, Unsupervised learning- K means   clustering.   5
Reinforcement learning- passive and   active reinforcement
learning
6.   Expert system:
Expert system: Definition, model, characteristic, architecture,   4
development process, limitations, and knowledge representation
schemes, Case study: JESS’s rule based engine with RETE algorithm.
7.   Case study:
Complete application of AI as Natural language understanding   8
and generation, Robotic Vision and Self driving car.
Total   45

Pre-requisite: Nil

Objectives:

1. To offer students the tools and techniques of film appreciation so that they will be able to actively
engage with cinema as a form of art, expression, history and culture.

2. To expose students to different genres of world cinema so as to make them avid, critical and
active viewers.

3. Through their exposure to arts and humanities, to broaden their horizons and deepen their
sensibilities so that they may respond and engage with the world with increased awareness and
competence.

Outcomes:
After completion of the course, students would be able to:

1. to understand the way that content, form, and contexts work together to create meaning in film.

2. to actively engage with cinema and develop an informed personal response to films.

3. view and appreciate films through an informed understanding of their technique of production,
grammar, cultural and historical context.

Detailed Syllabus: (per session plan)

Unit | Description Duration

1. |What is cinema? 5
¢ Definition of cinema.
e The concept of persistence of vision.

e Film’s relationship to each of the arts: music, dance, literature, theatre,
architecture, photography and painting.

e The relationship between film and 20th-century art movements:
impressionism, cubism, surrealism.

2. | Visual literacy 5
e The vocabulary of film: shot, scene, sequence, frame, composition in depth,

e point of view, transitions, Mise-en-scéne etc.
SVKM’s NMIMS
Mukesh Patel School of Technology Management and Engineering

e The tools of expression- frequency and number of shots, the size of the subject
in the frame, the angle of view, composition and balance, the use of lighting
and

e color, the movement of camera and lens, how images come to express
meanings and its relation with the word-meanings. Film formats: celluloid and
digital

e Element of sound: dialogues, background score, music, silence, ambience.

3. | Film styles and Genres 5
e Image and editing. To what extent does film manipulate reality?
e Different genres. Analysis of recurrent themes, images, and narrative
structures. Action, adventure, comedy, drama, epic/historical, horror, Sci-fi,
war etc. Other formats i.e. short films: fiction & nonfiction
4. | Film appreciation and history 25
e Development of film in Europe, US and India. Important directors and their
¢ contribution to world cinema, film companies and films.
e World cinema: D. W. Griffith, Sergie Enstine, Robert Flaharty, Vittorio De Sica,
Walt Disney, Charles Chaplin, Franscois Trufautt, Jean Luc Godard, Ingmar
Bergmen, Andrei Tarkovsky, Sergei Eisenstein, Alfred Hitchcock, Jean Renoir,
Federico Fellini, Akira Kurosowa, Andre Wajda, Yashizoro Ozu, Steven
Speilberg, Majid Majidi, etc.
e Indian cinema: V. Shantaram, Satyajit Ray, Shyam Benegal, Ritwik Ghatak,
Girish Karnad, Rajkapoor, Guru Dutt, Adoor Gopalkrishnan, Mrinal Sen,
Bimal Roy, Basu Bhattacharya, Maniratnam, and contemporary trend-setting
directors.
5. | Film Studies 5
e Film appreciation, analysis, criticism etc.
e Reviewing films for various media.
e Censorship: need, relevance, Censor Board. Influence of cinema on society,
culture, arts.
e Film institutions: NFDC, NFAI, FTII, Film Festivals Authority of India,
Children Film Society.
e Film Society movement, International film festivals.
e Films as an industry.
e Interrelationship of film industry with other media.
Total 45
